#5782. Democrats Are at COP31 to Show That the US Has Not Abandoned the Fight Against Climate Change

The results of the US midterms on November 3 delivered a resounding victory for the Democrats, and a major loss for US president Donald Trump and the Republican party.

Gaining control of the Senate and the House of Representatives has emboldened the Democrats, giving them a renewed sense of political legitimacy and a mandate to pursue their agenda. But will this shift translate into meaningful changes in US climate change policy?

The Democratic sweep will change the political dynamics around US climate policy and how the country cooperates with the international community on this issue. Although there was no official US presence at the 2025 COP conference, held in Brazil, a coalition of 100 local US leaders, including governors, mayors and other top city and state officials, attended as part of the US Climate Alliance. Former US vice-president Al Gore, and former US secretary of state John Kerry are part of an unofficial US group at the 2026 gathering.

Kerry said in a speech there: “Americans are committed to taking back their future, and we will build and rebuild our partnerships as we do that.”

Being on the ground at COP is important. As the US has a decisive role to play in global climate policy, sending a non-official coalition signals that many Americans are still working to combat climate change.

Trump has repeatedly stated that climate change is a hoax and refused to attend the COP31 climate talks being held in Turkey. But 20 Democratic members of Congress will be attending, although they have been denied official state department funding for the trip.

During the first and second Trump administrations, the US has been an outlier among wealthy countries when it comes to fighting climate change. Trump has actively backed the use of fossil fuels, undermining clean energy projects, and rolled back legislation that stipulated emission standards for vehicles.

Trump also weakened greenhouse gas reporting requirements and methane regulation. Then in February 2026, the Trump administration rescinded the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2009 finding that greenhouse gases threaten the health and welfare of the public, which had regulated the emissions from new cars and other vehicles. This had provided the legal foundation for regulation under the Clean Air Act.

On the international front, Trump was equally determined to undermine global efforts to fight climate change. Famously, he withdrew from the Paris agreement, part of a global initiative to address climate change, and refused to attend COP summits. But the Democrats’ seismic midterm win may be a sign of optimism for those fighting to address climate change.

The biggest issues of the midterms were affordability, corruption and the Iran war, but issues related to fighting climate change were also on voters’ list. There is growing concern about data centres. As many as 56% of US voters felt that data centres and AI were either a major or even crucial factor in influencing who they voted for, with only 13% saying it was not a factor at all.

Data centres require millions of gallons of water for cooling systems, and this is expected to rise to 73 billion litres of water a year by 2028. Over half of planned AI facilities in the US will be situated in areas that have significant water shortages or drought conditions.

After the midterms, Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat, is likely to become the chair of the House of Representatives’ committee on science, space and technology once the new session starts in January. She wants to tackle the administration’s “climate denialism”.

Lofgren’s leadership, along with new Democratic members of the committee, may offer it more power to reverse some of the Trump administration’s changes to science policy.

However, the Democrat midterm wins will not mean that the US is automatically back at the negotiating table at COP nor that the US will be able to rejoin the Paris Accords while Trump is president. Trump still has the power to make these decisions and can continue to keep the US out of international climate initiatives, regardless of who controls Congress. The US Constitution says nothing about withdrawing from treaties, which creates uncertainty for what the Senate’s role might be.

The election, however, does signal that there is considerable domestic opposition to his approach. And while Congress has not passed follow-up legislation prohibiting presidential withdrawal from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has continued to fund several UNFCCC initiatives. During the Biden administration, the US significantly increased climate finance from US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion) a year in 2021 to US$9.5 billion in 2023.

Democrats could also push back on Trump’s current policies, using their power to hold hearings, investigate the administration’s dismantling of climate programmes and challenge cuts to scientific research. The Democrats can also use the power of Congress’s control of spending to protect or restore funding to some of these environmental initiatives.

They could also try to introduce legislation that reinstates some of the clean energy initiatives that had been implemented in past administrations to strengthen emissions standards and support clean energy. The big issue, however, is that Trump has made it clear that he is going to be very active in using his veto power, and without a two-thirds majority in Congress, the Democrats will not be able to override this.

What this all means is that the world cannot expect the US to be a reliable and constructive partner at COP with Trump still in power. Trump will probably continue to forge ahead with expanding fossil fuel production, while weakening international climate cooperation, even if the electorate disapproves of these policies.

Ironically, Trump’s greatest contribution to the fight against climate change was his initiation of the war with Iran, which helped to cut global fossil fuel carbon dioxide emissions by 0.4% due the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But climate scientists note this is not a long-term solution.

While the Democrats’ electoral victory offers a glimmer of hope for renewed climate action, both domestically and internationally, restoring US climate leadership will take time, especially while Trump remains in power.

By Natasha Lindstaedt, Professor in the Department of Government, University of Essex

#5781. At $10,250, Could This 1995 Mercedes-Benz E320 Estate Bring Class To Car Line?

It's arguable that the W124-series was the last of the bank-vault-era Benzes. Today's Nice Price or No Dice E320 estate is one of the most desirable of those vaults to potentially invest in, and it has the rare third row. Let's see if its price tag has us opening up our hypothetical bank accounts.

Perhaps the polar opposite of a Mercedes of any era in build quality, safety, and engineering is the backyard-built kit car. Arising in the late 1950s and carrying through its heyday in the 1970s, home-built kit cars typically started with a donor chassis, often from an old Triumph or VW. A fresh fiberglass body gave that chassis new life, and the builder a sense of pride in creating a working, drivable car.

The Meyers Manx SR2 we looked at on Wednesday was an example—and an extremely rare one at that—of a '70s-era kit car. Created by industry legend Bruce Meyers, the SR2 proved to be his swan song, as his company folded shortly after its launch. That makes the small clutch of original SR2s (about 200 total) far more dear when they do come on the market. Our SR2 came with Corvair power and an interior ready for the next owner's taste in upholstery. At $17,000, however, that wasn't a winning combo. You all expected more for that amount and sent the Manx packing with a massive 93% 'No Dice' loss.

The closest today's 1995 Mercedes-Benz E320 Estate comes to a kit car is that it's the same model year Mercedes-Benz India, Ltd. began building similar models from knock-down kits at its Chakan assembly plant. This is also nearly the last year for the W124 series as a whole, as it was replaced, body style by body style, over the course of the next three years: 1995 (saloons), 1996 (estates), 1997 (coupes), and 1998 (cabriolets). Mercedes is nothing if not methodical.

This generation, which represents the facelifted version of the W124, was also the first to carry Mercedes' new naming convention of a class letter followed by a number indicating—sometimes only semi-accurately—engine displacement. The company has carried on this convention to this day. Because of that simple nomenclature, we can tell from the name that this is a mid-size E-Class (Executive class) model with a 3.2-liter engine. See? Easy-peasy.

That 3.2-liter engine is an M104.992 straight-six with double-overhead cams and four valves per cylinder. In North American guise, it produces a workmanlike 217 horsepower and 229 pound-feet of torque. As in all U.S.-bound cars, here it's matched with a five-speed 4G-Tronic automatic actuated through Mercedes' traditional pixelated snake shift gate.

According to the ad, this car has undergone significant repairs and maintenance over its 159,850 miles. The seller notes that under their ownership, they replaced the engine wiring harness, head and head gasket, radiator, and water pump. In addition, the car has a new climate control panel and has had two failed window regulators replaced. Other plusses include Continental tires with plenty of tread left and "flawlessly working" A/C.

With all that in the rearview, the seller now describes the car as "sorted and in excellent working condition." The receipts for the work will accompany the car in the sale for the next owner's reading enjoyment.

The car's appearance matches its mechanical status. The exterior is painted Smoke Silver, which the seller notes as paint code 702 for those keeping score. Yes, there will be a test later. The ad claims this Benz isn't a show car, but that it's solid enough to take out in public without embarrassment. On the downside, there are noticeable scratches and wear-through areas on the rear bumper and rocker moldings, but otherwise the paint looks to be in top-notch shape. Factory eight-hole alloys lend the car an all-original look, but could stand some work with a Scotchbrite to bring out their best nature.

In the cabin, the seller notes in the ad that the driver's seat shows wear and, wisely (sneakily?), doesn't show us how extensive it is. The rest of the cabin presents well, and the desirable rear-facing foldable third row is present and accounted for. If we're picking nits, we can point out that the (real) wood on the center console around the shifter is showing signs of losing battles with the sun. The seller, clearly appreciative of the car overall, claims it "wears its patina with pride."

On the plus side, a more modern stereo has been installed, but it's a Mercedes unit, so it keeps the vibe alive. Other plusses to consider: the car has a clean title, a passing smog test grade, and carries current registration, so there's no back-due malarkey for the next owner.

Apparently, under its current owner, this Benz has not been pressed into daily driver duty, as the seller claims to use it "as a Sunday driver and for the occasional school run." That's an acceptable compromise to keep the wear and tear at a minimum while still letting the car get some exercise. Based on the seller's description, though, this seems like a solid car to daily, and what a classy ride it would be.

Naturally, that class comes at a cost: $10,250. It should be noted that Mercedes' E-Class estates and their earlier W123 siblings are highly desirable in the present market, making them pricier than the average bear.

The question for you is whether or not this seemingly well-sorted estate is worth the seller's $10,250 asking. What do you think? Is that a fair deal for a classy classic? Or is that too much for something taking pride in its patina?

#5780. The Trump Administration’s Pro-Cancer Agenda

Under Trump, Americans could face an extraordinary increase in exposure to cancer-causing toxics and radiation.

Over the nearly two years of President Donald Trump’s second term, his administration has taken more than 500 actions that harm public health or the environment. When faced with this onslaught of harm, it can be difficult to see the strategic agenda at play. However, NRDC’s new analysis reveals that the Trump administration is executing a sweeping and long planned—but quiet—government-wide campaign to dismember major programs that are intended to prevent exposure to cancer-causing toxics and radiation. In sum, this administration has reversed course: America’s government is no longer fighting a “War on Cancer” but fighting a “War to Promote Cancer.”

This is not an accident. Much of this campaign can be found throughout the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 blueprint and has long been advocated for by industry. But a healthy life should not be treated as an obstacle to somebody else’s profit margin. The freedom to breathe clean air, drink safe water, eat safe food, work without needless exposure to carcinogens, and raise children without avoidable toxic risks should be among the most basic expectations of life in America. Americans should not have to wonder whether the water coming from their taps contains cancer-causing chemicals, whether the air they breathe carries toxic pollution from a nearby industrial facility, or whether going to work means being unnecessarily exposed to carcinogens.

Instead of ensuring these basic freedoms, the Trump administration is creating a system in which polluters are given greater leeway to expose everyone in the nation to cancer-causing toxics and radiation.

#5779. 2028 Honda CR-V Will Go Hybrid-Only, Following The Toyota RAV4's Lead

We've been living with affordable hybrid vehicles for almost three decades now, but it's taken a surprisingly long time for some of the best-selling cars in the U.S. to go hybrid-only, even for models that have offered reliable hybrids for years. Toyota started doing it with the current Camry and new RAV4, and now Honda has confirmed that the next-gen CR-V will only be sold with hybrid powertrains.

Honda says the seventh-generation CR-V will be revealed next year, in time for the SUV's 30th anniversary, and it will ride on a new platform and use the company's new two-motor hybrid system, which our own Andy Kalmowitz got to try out in a Civic prototype last year. This new powertrain is said to be more powerful and more efficient, and the modular architecture is more rigid while being lighter-weight. It should be cheaper for Honda to produce, too, and a new electric all-wheel-drive system will be a big improvement.

Somehow we didn't get a hybrid CR-V in the U.S. until the 2020 model year, when the fifth-gen model was facelifted. Since then, annual CR-V hybrid sales have grown almost tenfold, and it currently makes up more than 50% of total CR-V sales. With the price difference between the hybrid and the regular CR-V being so relatively minor, and the gains in driving experience being so large, it makes sense to just hybridize the entire lineup. This year will be the third straight year in which Honda sells more than 400,000 CR-Vs, and upping the average efficiency of that many cars can make a big difference.

Many U.S.-spec CR-Vs are currently built in Ohio (the rest being made in Indiana), and Honda just announced plans for a new $3 billion plant in Ohio that will focus on hybrids, though gas-only and fully electric cars will be built there as well. Production there won't start until 2029, but Honda envisions an annual capacity of 240,000 units. Honda says it will introduced 15 new hybrids by 2030, most of which will be oriented towards the American market.

One of those hybrids will be the model at the top of this slide, or at least something similar to it. That rakish fastback is officially called the Hybrid Sedan Prototype, and it's probably just the next-gen Accord that's due to come out in the very near future. It wears what will be Honda's new design language, and you don't have to imagine how it'll look on the CR-V — lightly camouflaged prototypes have already been spied, as you can see from the Instagram post below.

I think it's looking pretty good, though it's a shame that the CR-V will seemingly lose its signature vertical taillights. We probably won't have to wait long to see the CR-V; expect an actual auto show debut, simply because a car this popular can actually take the spotlight and be of interest to the regular people who still go to shows. A Detroit Auto Show debut in January seems like a safe bet, but Honda could wait for Chicago in February or New York in March.

#5778. What's The Worst Way You've Abused A Rental Car?

Unless you only travel within driving distance of home or are willing to spend the time and money on shipping, we will all end up in a situation where renting a car is a necessity. There may be plenty of cities with fantastic public transportation systems, but you just need a car to venture out and explore the countryside. Many of us are far more care-free behind the wheel when the vehicle is owned by an abstract corporate entity and not a person with a face.

What's the worst way you've abused a rental car? I'm not talking about returning it with an empty tank. That's just a surcharge that rental companies are more than happy to add to your bill. Abuse is real, lasting damage that's an absolute nightmare to reverse. Let me use a hypothetical beach day in the South of France as an example. You and a few friends take a decent Peugeot 408 to a sleepy village on the Mediterranean. After a fun day of sand and surf, everyone piles back into the sedan right off the beach, covering the interior with sand. That's the appetizer. On the drive back, you get impatient sitting behind a truck on a two-lane road. You pull into the oncoming lane but don't get entirely clear, and you sideswipe the truck. The 408 is far worse off, with its entire right side scratched up. That's abuse!

Besides outright crashing a rental car, the worst thing you could do is race a pack of them. Rental car racing actually is a significant part of NASCAR lore. The mischievous tradition has endured stock car racing's evolution from a moonshiners' pastime to a billion-dollar sport. Several current Cup Series drivers have admitted to racing each other and their team members. In many instances, rental car racing is just a fun way to salvage a rained-out test day. Everyone just piles on to the track once the showers stop and run laps to dry the racing surface. On race day, it's pushing the limit on the drive out of the track. Joe Gibbs Racing driver Chase Briscoe told The Athletic in 2025, "Honestly, the craziest thing, I think, is watching the team guys leave a racetrack. It is like the best racing and just the most chaos you've ever seen in your life."

Remember to leave your stories of rental car abuse in the comments section below. Be sure to mention the make or model of the car that you returned to be someone else's problem.

#5776. Cell Therapy for Knee Osteoarthritis Reverses Damage in Early Trial

— It won't be cheap, but could be the disease-modifying therapy the field has long sought

ORLANDO -- A cell-based therapy for knee osteoarthritis (OA) called OSCA not only improved patients' symptoms in a phase IIa trial and appeared safe, but also showed signs of reversing joint damage within a few months, a researcher reported here.

Standard evaluations including the Western Ontario McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) and Knee Osteoarthritis Outcomes Score (KOOS) showed that a single treatment reduced pain levels by half in the 6-month study, according to Jae-Young Park, MD, PhD, of CHA University in Seongnam, Korea.

But perhaps more importantly, MRI findings at month 6 indicated that some cartilage had regenerated and marrow abnormalities were resolving, he told attendees during a late-breaking abstract session at the American College of Rheumatology's annual meeting.

Orthopedic surgeons should pay close attention: If these results are duplicated with further testing, the treatment could be the first genuine disease-modifying therapy for knee OA, potentially making arthroplasty a quaint relic of a barbaric era in medicine.

OSCA is shorthand for a combination of cord blood-derived mesenchymal stem cells, dubbed osiramestrocel (OS), and cartilage acellular matrix (CAM) taken from pigs, Park explained. He described the proposed mechanism of action as targeting not only the synovium, but also subchondral bone and sensory neurons. The hoped-for result is decreased inflammation, less pain, and structural improvement.

The phase IIa trial tested single doses of this product, injected into the knee joint, in 113 patients randomized equally among two dosing levels (50 or 100 million cells per injection) or placebo. Technically, safety was the primary focus in this early study, with pain, function, structural change, and biomarker effects as exploratory outcomes.

Mean patient age was about 62 and some two-thirds were women. Body mass index values averaged about 25 (which may raise questions about generalizability to the U.S. and other countries where obesity is more common). At baseline, self-reported pain scores on a 100-point scale averaged roughly 67, with mean WOMAC and KOOS values of about 55 and 50, respectively.

Three patients in the lower-dose group and eight receiving the higher dose experienced injection-site reactions, but no other important treatment-related adverse events were noted. Discounting the injection-site reactions, numbers of treatment-emergent adverse events were similar across the three study arms.

Those data may have been the study's primary object, but Park spent most of his talk on the efficacy outcomes. These were all very favorable, even astonishingly so.

Both WOMAC and KOOS scores improved by about 25 points, or approximately half of their baseline values after 6 months. Some improvement was also seen with placebo, but this still left a clinically and statistically significant advantage of 15 points in WOMAC scores and 20-21 points on KOOS. Self-rated pain scores fell 40-44 points from baseline with the two OSCA doses, with differences from placebo of 24-29 points. For the latter outcome, the lower dose outperformed the higher one to a small degree.

Another symptom-focused analysis looked at responses by OMERACT-OARSI criteria, achieved by 77-78% of the OSCA groups versus 39% of the placebo group. Park pointed out that this gap was already apparent just 4 weeks after dosing.

Structural effects were evaluated with the so-called MOCART and WORMS techniques for interpreting MRI images. The former examines cartilage specifically, while the latter was used to assess tibial and femoral bone marrow. The MOCART analysis showed some modest cartilage regeneration -- also greatest with the lower OSCA dose -- and a degree of marrow normalization. For the latter, the higher dose had the greater impact. Notably, the placebo group saw progression of both cartilage and marrow damage.

Finally, serum and urine biomarkers for inflammation and cartilage pathology all showed improvement. For these analyses, the higher dose appeared superior.

Being such a small and short-duration study, many questions remain unanswered. Patients in the current trial will be followed for an additional 6 months, plus a 5-year extension. Those data will give some insight into the therapy's durability. An issue for future studies will surely be whether repeat dosing is needed to maintain or boost structural recovery. Also, the current trial enrolled patients with moderate knee OA, so whether it's more or less effective in patients with milder or more severe disease is another issue that clinicians will want addressed.

Future plans by the developer, Korea-based Kangstem Biotech, aren't yet clear -- a July press release on the study's topline results indicated that the firm is seeking partnerships with global pharmaceutical companies, while making no mention of possible phase III trials.

#5774. The High-Rise Bottleneck: Why EV Charging in Indian Apartments Is an Engineering Puzzle

Most Western clean-energy reporting takes a very specific picture of home charging for granted. You pull into a private driveway, plug into an attached garage wall-box, and pull cheap power while you sleep.

That reality does not exist for most urban drivers in India.

Data from Kazam and the Alliance for an Energy Efficient Economy (AEEE) shows that roughly 70% to 75% of urban households in major Indian metros live in multi-family apartments and cooperative housing societies. Parking means an open ground level slot or a space two levels down in a concrete basement. When someone here buys an electric car, their biggest hurdle isn’t battery degradation or highway chargers. It’s their own building.

As an electrical engineer in India, I watch this play out every week. Someone buys an EV, assumes they can hire a local wireman to pull power from their flat’s meter to their parking bay, and runs straight into transformer limits, cable physics, and nervous managing committees.

Here is what is actually going on beneath the floorboards.

Indian housing societies buy electricity under a bulk “sanctioned load” from their local utility (DISCOM). The utility sizes the local transformer using an electrical diversity factor the simple assumption that not all 100 flats will run their air conditioners, geysers, and induction stoves at the exact same moment.

A domestic geyser pulls 2 kW for ten minutes and shuts off. A 7.4 kW AC wall-box pulls 32 amps continuously for six to eight hours. When several residents plug in around 8:00 PM, that heavy, unbroken draw lands on the transformer right as domestic air conditioning and kitchen loads hit their evening peak.

Let’s look at the numbers on a 100-flat complex running on a standard 250 kVA transformer:

Here is where the grid cracks: just five or six cars charging at 7.4 kW pull 37 kW to 44 kW. That wipes out the 30 kW buffer completely. If eight cars plug in at once (59.2 kW), the transformer goes straight into thermal overload.

When that happens, the main incomer breaker trips plunging common areas and elevators into darkness or the utility slaps the society with massive Maximum Demand penalties on their next power bill. Getting a utility to upgrade a transformer or approve higher sanctioned load requires significant capital, transformer yard space, and months of red tape.

In a detached house, wiring an EV charger means running 5 or 10 metres of cable from your distribution board to the garage.

In an Indian high-rise, your electricity meter sits in a ground-floor panel room or inside a service shaft on the 14th floor. Your car is parked two floors beneath the earth in Basement 2. Connecting the two is an expensive engineering problem:

Even if an owner is willing to foot the entire wiring bill, they still need a No Objection Certificate (NOC) from their housing society committee or Resident Welfare Association (RWA).

Most RWA committees are volunteer residents without technical backgrounds. When handed a request for high-power continuous charging, their hesitation usually comes down to three worries:

The courts are starting to step in. In Amit Dholakia v. The State of Maharashtra (2025), the Bombay High Court pushed state authorities to issue clear guidelines preventing arbitrary NOC rejections. More recently, in early 2026, the Supreme Court of India issued notice on a Public Interest Litigation challenging arbitrary charger bans across states. While the legal momentum is clearly moving toward protecting a resident’s right to charge, taking a court ruling to a heated Sunday morning society meeting rarely makes for a quick installation.

Treating an electric car like an extra microwave where everyone pulls their own line from their domestic meter does not scale. Societies have to build shared electrical infrastructure.

India’s EV transition is moving fast on two and three wheels. But passenger electric cars won’t reach mass adoption until high-rises solve the overnight charging puzzle.

The vehicles are ready, and buyers want them. But until building codes, dynamic load balancing, and society committees catch up with automotive engineering, the hardest part of driving electric in India will simply be charging at home.

#5771. Ibuprofen and Kidney Injury: Study Reveals Who Is Most at Risk

— Higher AKI risk seen only in certain patients

Use of ibuprofen was associated with higher rates of acute kidney injury (AKI) among hospitalized adults, but the excess risk was concentrated almost entirely in certain patients, according to a retrospective active-comparator cohort study.

Compared with patients given oxycodone for acute pain, those who received at least 24 hours of ibuprofen had higher adjusted rates of the following:

The heightened risk was driven primarily by high-risk populations: postoperative patients (IRR 1.70, 95% CI 1.28-2.27) and critically ill patients in the intensive care unit (IRR 1.65, 95% CI 1.29-2.11), reported Todd Miano, PharmD, PhD, of the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, and colleagues.

In contrast, patients deemed low risk -- those younger than 60, not critically ill, not recovering from surgery, and with preserved baseline kidney function (estimated glomerular filtration rate >60 mL/min/1.73 m²) -- had no elevated AKI risk associated with ibuprofen use (IRR 0.94, 95% CI 0.75-1.18).

These findings "suggest that there may be a subset of patients who can safely be treated with NSAIDs [nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs], such as younger patients with preserved kidney function who are not critically ill and are not postoperative," the authors wrote in JAMA Network Open.

However, current hospital practice did not appear to reflect that distinction. Even among low-risk patients in the study, 87% were prescribed oxycodone over ibuprofen.

"NSAIDs cause nephrotoxic effects, primarily through vasoconstriction of afferent arterioles in the glomerulus, which can reduce kidney blood flow, leading to ischemic AKI in vulnerable patients," Miano and team explained. "Most evidence regarding NSAID-AKI risk comes from outpatient settings, where patients often use NSAIDs for extended durations. In contrast, hospitalized patients typically receive NSAIDs for at most a few days."

While low-risk patients may safely tolerate ibuprofen, they "are often prescribed oxycodone," which carries an "extensive adverse-effect profile" and risks long-term dependence, the authors emphasized. "Thus, our analysis suggests that outcomes might be improved with enhanced risk stratification and individualized analgesic prescribing that effectively identifies patients at low risk of NSAID-associated AKI."

For this study, the researchers reviewed records for 78,656 hospitalized adults admitted to three Philadelphia hospitals within the University of Pennsylvania Health System from January 2004 through June 2017. Patients with end-stage kidney disease, baseline serum creatinine over 2.0 mg/dL, recent unresolved AKI, or other contraindications were excluded. Median patient age was 59, 48% were women, 59% were white, and 31% were Black.

Overall, 72,343 patients received oxycodone and 6,313 received ibuprofen. In the unweighted raw data, inpatients given ibuprofen were younger (median age 52 vs 59 years), had fewer comorbidities, and had a lower crude AKI rate (5.1% vs 6.2%) than those given oxycodone. Median follow-up was 3.0 days.

Over 270,472 days of patient follow-up, 4,799 AKI events occurred (17.7 events per 1,000 days). AKI was defined by changes in serum creatinine and initiation of KRT according to Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria and staged over 7 days after onset. Most AKI events were stage 1 (79%), 15% were stage 2, and 6% were stage 3.

In a post-hoc subgroup analysis, the IRR of AKI was 1.48 (95% CI 1.18-1.86) among patients with concomitant nephrotoxin exposure and 1.15 for those without such exposure (95% CI 1.00-1.32).

The authors noted that prescribing decisions cannot hinge on nephrotoxicity alone. "While our analysis was focused on kidney outcomes, other NSAID-mediated adverse effects (e.g., bleeding) also inform prescribing decisions," they wrote. "Research evaluating the broader comparative safety of these classes is needed to optimize inpatient analgesia."

Patients who received both ibuprofen and oxycodone on the index date were excluded, which may limit generalizability to those treated with both drugs.

#5768. A BMW i3 Spent Less Than 3 Hours Charging On A 3,658-Mile Road Trip, Is That Fast Enough For You?

Regardless of how you feel about the exterior styling, interior design, infotainment software, or even driving dynamics of BMW's latest Neue Klasse models, there's no denying the new electric cars are extremely impressive when it comes to range, efficiency and charging. The in-demand Neue Klasse cars have consistently outperformed in real-world range tests, and last year BMW drove an iX3 from Debrecen, Hungary, to Munich, Germany, covering 626 miles on a single charge.

To show off just how road-trip-capable its Neue Klasse cars are, BMW took the new i3 on the Paneuropeana, a long-distance EV rally route devised by Rafael de Mestre, who has circumnavigated the globe in electric cars four times. The car covered 5,886.7 kilometers on the journey, or 3,658 miles rounded up — over 1,000 miles more than you'd drive when crossing the United States. It took 3 days, 2 hours and 41 minutes to complete the drive, and only 2 hours and 46 minutes was spent charging. Is that fast enough for you, yet?

The trip started at the North Cape in Norway, the northernmost point of continental Europe that you can get to by car (about 1,300 miles from the North Pole), and after crossing through eight countries ended in Tarifa, the southernmost point of Europe in the Andalusian region of Spain. Along the way they encounted bad weather and rough roads, so it wasn't a walk in the park. The focus of the drive isn't outright speed, so the checkpoints and stages are organized like "regular road users travelling along country roads, motorways and through towns," according to BMW.

Charging stops weren't pre-determined, though, and BMW says that made for a great challenge: "optimising the route between checkpoints specifically to make the best use of the charging infrastructure, whilst also taking into account external factors such as the weather, traffic jams, etc." The charging stations chosen were public ones, adding to the potential issues. In the video covering the trip, at one point the team got the car down to 0% with 0 kilometers of range left, and in another moment they arrive at a high-power charging station to find no chargers working.

Only one engineer was in the i3 at any given time, with the car being followed by an identical i3 and an iX3 for support. The i3 in question was a 50 xDrive model, which has a 108.7-kWh battery pack, a dual-motor powertrain with 463 horsepower, and an EPA-rated range of up to 468 miles in the States (567 miles on the European WLTP cycle).

The point of the Paneuropeana is to see who can spend the least amount of time charging along the route, and BMW broke the record by more than seven hours. The i3 can charge at up to 400 kW, and on the trip BMW saw an average charging power of 275 kW, which ain't bad. BMW says the i3's average speed was just about 50 mph, and its energy consumption was damn impressive: 12.5 kWh per 100 km, which translates to almost 5 miles per kWh in U.S. figures. That's better efficiency than the i3's WLTP rating.

BMW hasn't said how many times the i3 stopped to charge, or how long the average stop was, but does that really matter? A U.S.-spec i3 can gain 180 miles of range in just 10 minutes of charging, and it can go from 10% to 80% in 21 minutes. At steady highway speeds, the i3 should be able to take you almost 400 miles before needing to be juiced up again. That's got to be good enough to assuage any range anxiety you've still got kicking around in your brain.

However, while Davis called this "important progress," she added that "we can't lose sight of the fact that our nation does not have enough primary care physicians to meet patients' needs."

"We need concrete policy changes to ensure that more people go into primary care and can practice, and stay, in communities that need it the most," she noted.

AAFP said it is supporting legislation focused on residencies in primary care and rural and high-need areas, as well as funding for graduate programs that can help train primary care physicians to work in community-based settings.

AAMC called on Congress to pass the Resident Physician Shortage Reduction Act of 2025, which would gradually increase the number of Medicare-supported GME positions.

Bryan Carmody, MD, MPH, of Eastern Virginia Medical School in Norfolk, who runs a popular blog on medical education, noted an important caveat -- that hospitals can add residency positions even without federal funding, as long as they meet certain educational standards.

Indeed, hospitals have continued to add residency positions since the 1997 cap, "even without Congress subsidizing the cost," he told MedPage Today in an email.

Carmody said he's not sure that expanding federally funded positions will curb any alleged physician shortage; he also questions whether one exists. Instead, he argued that shortages are "distributional" and the "natural result of the incentives in our system."

"I'm not convinced that subsidizing positions in this way is going to do much of anything to address those problems," he added, noting that there's "no requirement that these newly trained residents will practice in a way that improves access for patients."

They may end up in primary care, or "they might work as a sub-specialist in the affluent suburbs," Carmody said. What they choose is more dictated by the incentives in the current system, he suggested, "and I don't see how those incentives are changed in the least by whether or not the hospital received extra public money to train them or not."

#5764. Anticoagulants Reign Supreme in VTE Prevention After Joint Replacement

— Large comparative-effectiveness trial fails to find noninferiority with aspirin

Aspirin didn't prevent venous thromboembolism (VTE) as well as anticoagulants did for patients undergoing elective hip or knee replacements, the randomized PEPPER trial showed.

For the primary composite endpoint of death from any cause or symptomatic VTE over 6 months after 30 days of prophylaxis, 1.26% of aspirin recipients had an event compared with 1.23% of warfarin recipients and 0.94% of rivaroxaban (Xarelto) recipients, reported Vincent Pellegrini Jr., MD, of the Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth in Lebanon, New Hampshire, and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine.

In pairwise comparisons, 6-month risks of a primary effectiveness outcome event were 1.24% and 1.01% for aspirin versus warfarin, 1.24% and 0.94% for aspirin versus rivaroxaban, and 1.13% and 1.10% for warfarin versus rivaroxaban.

The differences between aspirin and the two anticoagulants did not meet the criterion for noninferiority (P=0.09 and P=0.10), although the comparison between the two anticoagulants did (P=0.01).

Risks of a primary safety outcome event -- bleeding, reoperation for wound problems, or myocardial infarction -- were 3.65% and 2.88% for warfarin versus aspirin; 3.70% and 3.02% for rivaroxaban versus aspirin; and 3.59% and 3.61% for rivaroxaban versus warfarin, none of which met the criterion for noninferiority.

"By providing comparative risk-benefit profiles regarding thrombosis and bleeding for medications used for VTE prophylaxis, these findings can help inform preoperative decision making for patients undergoing elective total hip or knee replacement," the authors wrote.

"Aspirin is widely favored among orthopedic surgeons in the United States and Canada because of low cost, minimal bleeding risk, and the absence of required monitoring, in addition to concerns about anticoagulants with regard to increased risks of bleeding and associated wound complications, readmission, or reoperation," they noted. "However, evidence to confirm the effectiveness of aspirin as compared with anticoagulants [had been] scant."

The results might seem to contradict the findings of the EPCAT III trial published earlier this year, which showed that an aspirin-only approach was as effective and safe as rivaroxaban.

"However, at closer glance, I think they tell two parallel stories," Geoffrey Barnes, MD, of the Frankel Cardiovascular Center at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, told MedPage Today.

"Taken together, these two studies suggest that some component of anticoagulant therapy likely benefits patients after hip and/or knee arthroplasty surgery. As such, it might make sense to employ a short course of anticoagulation (e.g., rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for 5 days) followed by aspirin therapy in most hip and knee surgery patients at average risk of postoperative VTE," he argued.

Pellegrini and team noted that EPCAT III and another trial comparing 5 days of rivaroxaban then aspirin versus rivaroxaban alone were much smaller and both had larger noninferiority margins that were equal to the entire projected incidence of VTE and excluded patients at high risk for VTE.

The PEPPER trial randomly assigned patients at 34 centers in the U.S. and Canada who were undergoing elective hip or knee arthroplasty for osteoarthritis to receive open-label treatment with aspirin (81 mg twice daily), warfarin (to a target international normalized ratio of 2.0), or rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) for 30 days.

VTE made up most of the events in the primary effectiveness endpoint. The noninferiority margin for the risk difference in the primary composite effectiveness outcome measure was 0.69 percentage points. Intention-to-treat analyses yielded similar results to those of the per-protocol analysis.

The trial included 15,317 patients in the primary per-protocol analysis: 7,214 with hip arthroplasty and 8,103 with knee arthroplasty. However, a "very large number of patients [more than 3,500] were excluded from both the warfarin and rivaroxaban groups because of crossover and an inability to stay on the assigned drug," Barnes noted. "While measured covariates were balanced across all three groups, this large difference in exclusions may have introduced unmeasured confounding."

Cost and monitoring affected adherence to rivaroxaban and warfarin, respectively, such that fewer patients crossed over from the aspirin group. Indeed, the per-protocol aspirin cohort (6,090 participants) was 22% larger than the rivaroxaban cohort (4,996 participants) and was 44% larger than the warfarin cohort (4,231 participants), "despite similar initial randomization numbers," Pellegrini and team acknowledged.

The researchers agreed that the crossovers compromised the benefits of randomization "but reflect the pragmatic comparative-effectiveness design."

#5762. QuantumScape Has An Osprey Up Its Solid-State EV Battery Sleeve

Federal policy makers orchestrated an EV sales crash in the US last year, only to see electrification stakeholders gradually piece together a comeback focusing on cars that hit the affordability MSRP of $30,000 or less. New, higher-performing solid-state EV batteries are also inching their way towards the market, with the US startup QuantumScape among the innovators contributing some fresh news in recent weeks (for the record, Finland’s Donut Labs is another).

As the name indicates, a solid-state battery replaces the liquid electrolyte of a conventional lithium-ion battery with a solid material. If that sounds like a deep electrochemical challenge, its is. Nevertheless, science loves a challenge, and so do electrification stakeholders who are determined to sharpen the contrast between EVs and gasmobiles. Compared to the current generation of EV batteries, solid-state technology meets a higher bar for energy density and other performance benchmarks, while avoiding the use of volatile chemicals (see more solid-state background here)

High tech ceramics have emerged as one of the options, and that is where QuantumScape has set its sights. The company launched in 2010 and it surfaced on the CleanTechnica radar in 2012, when Volkswagen dropped word of its interest in the solid-state forumula.

QS has been focusing its attention on developing a lithium-metal formula for the anode (the part of a battery that collects a charge), by tweaking the separator, which is the part of a battery that serves as a buffer on the electrolyte.

“A solid-state lithium-metal battery…replaces the polymer separator used in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid-state separator. The replacement of the separator enables the carbon or silicon anode used in conventional lithium-ion batteries to be replaced with a lithium-metal anode,” QS explains.

To ice the solid-state cake, the QS anode does not make an appearance during the battery manufacturing process. It self-forms as part of the battery’s first charging cycle.

QS has accumulated a string of investors and affiliations since 2012, capped by a hookup with the legacy firm Corning last year aimed at developing a manufacturing system that accommodates its ceramic separator.

The latest news takes QS farther into all-solid state technology, this time with a focus on the cathode, under the trade name Osprey.

“Osprey pairs the QS proprietary ceramic separator and anode-free lithium-metal design with a solid cathode, creating an all-solid-state cell,” the company explained in a press statement on November 11.

“Osprey builds on the company’s QSE platform, and opens new licensing and co-development options for current QS customers and expanding its offering to developers of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries,” the company elaborates. The QS blog further explains that Osprey is a “solid-state platform that allows developers of sulfide-based solid-state batteries to incorporate QS technology into their all-solid-state battery (ASSB) development programs.”

Don’t get too excited just yet — the cathode work is still in the early stages of validation — but QS is now confident that its data will stand up under public scrutiny. In addition to safety improvements compared to conventional Li-ion batteries, QS checks a list of additional performance boxes for ASSBs:

“Cycle life: 1,000 full charge cycles with ~80% capacity retention under gold-standard testing conditions

Fast charging: 10% to 80% in five-minutes

Low pressure: Requires only one atmosphere of pressure

Cold-weather performance: Operational to less than -20 °C (-4 °F)

Want more details? Check out the QS blog, where the company takes a deeper dive into the new cathode.

As for why QS is working the sulfide angle, that’s a good question. “Sulfides can react with lithium metal, which shortens battery life, and they typically need to be held under high pressure to operate, which is impractical for vehicles and many other applications,” QS notes. Despite those challenges, QS also notes the sulfide formula continues to attract widespread interest in the solid-state field, due to its high level of conductivity and ease of processing. If all goes according to plan, the Osprey platform will enable solid-state battery developers to continue pursuing sulfide to their hearts’ content.

“The industry has invested heavily in sulfide-based batteries but keeps hitting the same fundamental limits,” explains QS president and CEO Dr. Siva Sivaram, “As the data shows, Osprey can address these limitations.”

As another indication that sulfide stakeholders are not out chasing rainbows, take a look at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, part of a sprawling network of research facilities under the umbrella of the US Department of Energy. ORNL has just published a new study in the journal Energy Materials under the title, “Operando neutron radiography reveals calendar aging-induced lithium redistribution and back-diffusion in thick-cathode all-solid-state batteries.”

As the title indicates, the researchers deployed a neutron radiation tool to probe the inner workings of lithium batteries while they are in operation, enabling them to deliver a precise map of the degradation process that has bedeviled the sulfide field. They also delivered a roadmap for further work:

“Based on these findings from calendar aging, we envision future formation strategies should be redesigned to minimize sustained potential gradients while stabilizing interphases, for example through optimized composite electronic percolation and catholyte or coating materials and validated with time-resolved neutron imaging to establish transport-informed, durability-first conditioning rules that generalize across cathode loadings and operating temperatures.”

Got all that? The real question is why a federal research institution is still delivering advanced analyses leading to the next generation of EV batteries that outperform conventional batteries while improving EV safety and reducing overall costs. After all, US President Donald Trump and the Republican majority in Congress have expended considerable time and effort to stop, if not reverse, EV sales in the US. In addition to prematurely killing off the $7,500 EV tax credit last fall, the President also tried (and ultimately failed) to claw back funds from the federal NEVI public EV charging station program.

Readers, take a guess at the answer in the discussion thread. One possible explanation is the energy storage angle. While the President’s whackadoodle “American Energy Dominance Policy” dials down solar and wind (especially wind), it supports practically every other domestic energy resource including nuclear, biomass, geothermal, and hydropower alongside fossil fuels, with energy storage also making a substantial appearance.

The electronic war of the future is another factor to consider, with crewless vehicles and “anti-idling” kits serving as a sort of gateway drug that demonstrates the logistical and tactical advantages of battery power, silent running, and a lower heat signature compared to diesel fuel.

#5761. Upfront PCI Still Not Beneficial for Stable CAD as Far Out as 25 Years

— No diverging event curves seen in COURAGE and ISCHEMIA long-term outcomes

A longer horizon did not give patients with stable coronary artery disease (CAD) any improved hard outcomes when getting an invasive strategy over conservative management, according to extended results from the COURAGE and ISCHEMIA randomized trials.

There were still no diverging event curves to be found up to 25 years into COURAGE nor 11 years into ISCHEMIA, investigators reported at a session dedicated to these follow-up reports at the American Heart Association (AHA) annual meeting held in Chicago.

COURAGE had shown in 2007 that an initial management strategy of adding percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to optimal medical therapy (OMT) did not reduce the risk of death or myocardial infarction (MI), at a median 4.6 years of follow-up, in patients with stable CAD. A newer trial, more reflective of modern care, came to the same conclusion: 2019's ISCHEMIA failed to show any 4-year benefit from adding early stenting or bypass surgery to optimal medication in patients with stable, moderate-to-severe ischemic heart disease.

Between-group results remained superimposed in the latest data.

The estimated 25-year cumulative incidence of combined death or MI in COURAGE was 93.3% with added PCI and a similar 91.0% with OMT alone (HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.88-1.15), in a report simultaneously published in JAMA.

In ISCHEMIA, all-cause 11-year mortality was also not significantly different between invasive and conservative management groups (25.8% vs 26.9%, adjusted HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.86-1.09) in a report also released in JAMA.

Similarly, 9 years into ISCHEMIA's parallel trial in patients with concomitant chronic kidney disease (CKD), separately published in Circulation, there was no difference in cumulative all-cause mortality or cardiovascular mortality.

It thus remains debatable what the value is of coronary artery bypass grafting or PCI in chronic coronary disease. Of note, PCI did result in angina relief for people with ischemia refraining from antianginal therapy in the sham-controlled ORBITA-2 trial.

"There are several important lessons that will continue to help guide treatment decisions. A conservative strategy is a safe initial approach in most cases of chronic stable coronary artery disease. A conservative strategy has a slightly higher risk for spontaneous MI that should be considered and balanced against initial procedural risks," according to Donald Cutlip, MD, and Robert Yeh, MD, MSc, both of Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School in Boston, in a JAMA editorial.

"As with all trials, the results are an average outcome based on randomized treatment assignments and apply in this case to the initial strategy with ongoing guideline-directed medical therapy and careful monitoring. For individual patients, the question is whether we can do better by personalized shared decision-making; avoiding risk in those unlikely to benefit while pursuing an early invasive strategy in those with increased likelihood of benefit. This is the real long-term goal," Cutlip and Yeh stressed.

The COURAGE investigators reached a median follow-up of 15 years in their post hoc 25-year report.

Individual components of the primary endpoint were consistently neutral between upfront PCI and OMT:

"Deferred revascularization is inherent in the OMT strategy, so this estimate reflects the strategies as practiced and not necessarily the effect of PCI on outcomes. Nevertheless, it is notable that nearly half of patients randomized to receive OMT alone never required revascularization," wrote study authors Neel Butala, MD, of Rocky Mountain Regional VA Medical Center in Aurora, Colorado, and colleagues.

"The high rate of repeat revascularization among patients randomized to receive PCI likely reflects both the use of predominantly bare metal stents and progression of atherosclerosis in nonstented segments," they added.

Included in this analysis were 959 of the original COURAGE participants enrolled at Veterans Affairs hospitals. Mean age at baseline was 62.7 years and fewer than 2% were women. About 40% had diabetes, and mean left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) was just over 59%.

Median follow-up reached 9 years in ISCHEMIA-EXTEND, the extension study of ISCHEMIA, and 8 years in ISCHEMIA-CKD.

Both were strategy trials that randomized people to upfront coronary angiography (and revascularization when feasible, via PCI or coronary artery bypass graft surgery) and guideline-directed medical therapy or medical therapy alone (invasive management later allowed for failure of medical therapy).

In the main trial, estimated cardiovascular mortality at 11 years was 15.8% and 17.1% (adjusted HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.75-1.02), respectively, and noncardiovascular mortality 9.1% and 8.1% (adjusted HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.96-1.45).

"These results support shared decision-making between patients and their clinicians, clarifying that while a routine invasive strategy improves quality of life for symptomatic patients through at least 4 years over an initial conservative strategy, there is no survival advantage over approximately a decade," reported Judith Hochman, MD, of NYU Grossman School of Medicine/NYU Langone Health in New York City, and colleagues.

Similarly, the ISCHEMIA-CKD trial showed that in patients with at least moderate ischemia and advanced CKD, cumulative all-cause mortality (57.4% vs 56.8%, adjusted HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.87-1.28) and cardiovascular mortality (40.3% vs 38.4%, adjusted HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.84-1.34) were still unimproved with the upfront invasive strategy, according to Sripal Bangalore, MD, MHA, also of NYU Grossman School of Medicine.

All 5,179 participants randomized in the ISCHEMIA trial were included in ISCHEMIA-EXTEND. At baseline, median age was 64 years, 23% of participants were women, 42% had diabetes, and median LVEF was 60%.

ISCHEMIA-CKD had 777 people randomized. Median age at baseline was 63 years, 31% were women, 57% had diabetes, 53% were on dialysis, and median LVEF was 59%.

Cutlip and Yeh cautioned against extrapolation of the numerical trend toward excess late noncardiovascular mortality in ISCHEMIA.

"The findings must also be interpreted in the context of the study's design as a strategy trial that included subsequent invasive angiography in 26% of patients assigned to the conservative strategy during the early phase," they noted. "Given that any differences in outcomes between the two randomized treatment arms would be mediated by the different rates and timing of revascularization in each group, the absence of this information makes interpretation of the study findings, and in particular the effect sizes, difficult."

#5760. That Mystery SUV Spied In Moab Is An Audi-Bodied Test Mule For The New Scouts

A few days ago, Reddit user CapnDangerPony took to the r/whatisthiscar subreddit with a far-away photo of a very strange-looking test mule driving around in Moab. The poster only got a good photo of the side of the mule, and another from further away that gave a glimpse of its front end, neither of which revealed any details aside from a strange shape, lots of camouflage, and some sort of body-on-frame platform. Now our spies have gotten a better look at the test mule, and I know exactly what it is: This is an early prototype for the new Scouts.

Somehow, I don't think I saw a single comment online thinking that it was a Scout mule based on the Reddit photos, but that's definitely what it is. This time, it wasn't spied in Moab but at a secret Audi test facility in Germany, which is one of the few giveaways as to its identity — another obvious one being the tow hooks. I've already been surprised that Scout test mules haven't been regularly spied by now, since just this week Scout announced that it's starting to construct "validation builds" at its factory in newly blue South Carolina, and prototypes with closer-to-production bodies have apparently already been out there for months. This one is likely an older mule that's still out there racking up test miles, which is probably fine since since the Scouts have been delayed so much.

So, all of you distraught internet commenters can rest easy now. The mystery is solved. This weird test mule is for the Scout Terra and Traveler — my guess is the Traveler because of its shorter wheelbase — and despite how strange it looks, there's still some information we can glean from it.

There have been persistent rumors that Audi wants to build a competitor for the Mercedes-Benz G-Class using a modified version of the Scout's platform (and at the same factory), which seems to be at least partially why Volkswagen wanted to resurrect the brand at all, and could also be a reason for some of the trucks' delays and development problems. Audi has yet to green-light that project, so it's highly unlikely this mule is testing out a new Audi model, but the company is clearly helping out with the vehicle's engineering.

It is wearing an Audi body, though, specifically one from a Q6 E-Tron. It's basically just a placeholder, so Scout can test out the platform and powertrain without needing to put a real design on top yet. It's got huge fender flares tacked on, and you can see that the wheelbase is longer than the Q6's, with the wheels sitting in cut-outs made in the wheel arches. There's clearly a big battery pack under there, with rudimentary side steps added on in a similar fashion to the GMC Hummer EV, and the chunky six-lug wheels wear BFGoodrich all-terrain tires.

The rear tow hooks are just likes the ones on the Scout show trucks, as are the overall shapes of the bumpers, and the bits we can see of this mule's suspension setup appear to align with what Scout has shown us of its architecture. There's no tells as to whether this test mule is running the fully electric setup or is the range-extender hybrid model that will use a four-cylinder Volkswagen engine behind the rear axle; it's likely the latter, as the vast majority of Scout reservations have been for the EREV, and Scout will start production with them.

Scout first broke ground on its plant in Blythewood, South Carolina, two and a half years ago, with the project being part of a $2 billion investment that hopes to create more than 4,000 jobs. Now the company says it's starting early validation builds "to validate vehicle engineering, buildability and parts maturity while confirming that newly installed equipment is set up and functioning as expected." The company has started welding, assembly and painting operations, and in the background of a released photo we can see a couple bodies-in-white of the Traveler SUV.

750 robots help to put together 160 individual parts using 5,000 weld points, and don't worry, there's "AI-supported weld monitoring" so that everything is perfect. An "advanced metrology system" is also used to match the body against the engineering specs, checking thousands of measurements. Scout says the body shop can process up to 40 vehicles per hour, but right now the company is just testing things to make sure it all works properly before real manufacturing starts. Next it's sent through "an electrified automotive paint shop" before the truck goes to assembly, where the painted body is attached to the chassis and humans put all the components together.

The company says "validation vehicle builds will continue and mature into 2027 as Scout Motors prepares for its next phase of pre-production vehicle builds. As engineering, buildability and parts maturity advance, the manufacturing team will progress from equipment set up and functionality to proving manufacturing processes and ultimately scaling those processes toward production speed." There's no word as to updated production timelines beyond that, apart from Scout saying first deliveries are planned to start "in 2028." According to MotorTrend, the company has 210,000 pre-orders with that number expected to increase to 400,000, or about 12 to 18 months of confirmed sales, and executives deny any further delays.

#5757. GLP-1 Drugs Linked to Improved Survival After Liver Transplant

— Reasons for lower mortality risk weren't clear in retrospective study

Liver transplant patients who took a GLP-1 receptor agonist had a lower risk of death than those who weren't on a GLP-1 drug, according to a retrospective three-center cohort study.

Among 2,402 patients, those on GLP-1 receptor agonists after their transplant were 45% less likely to die over a median 3.9 years of follow-up (adjusted HR [aHR] 0.55, 95% CI 0.38-0.80, P=0.002). That mortality risk advantage held whether or not transplant patients had type 2 diabetes, though the protective effect was greater among those without diabetes.

A replication cohort of 1,443 liver transplant recipients drawn from a U.S. claims database mirrored those results, showing 45% and 55% lower post-transplant mortality risks linked with GLP-1 use in two analyses (aHRs 0.55 and 0.45), reported Zhihao Li, MD, of the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual Liver Meeting in Denver.

"Several points support a real effect here," Li said in a presentation at the meeting. "The results were replicated in an independent cohort, they're similar to what's been reported in other organ transplants, and there are plausible cardiovascular and anti-cancer pathways."

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is on pace to become the leading cause of liver transplant in the U.S. While a transplant cures liver disease, it doesn't remove a patient's metabolic or metabolic-related risks, Li noted. GLP-1 drugs deliver cardiometabolic and kidney benefits for patients with liver disease, but their value among liver transplant patients isn't clear, he added.

The primary study cohort included adults who underwent a liver transplant between 2015 and 2025 at one of three Mayo Clinic sites. Patients' transplant indication was either metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) or another etiology with type 2 diabetes or a body mass index (BMI) of at least 30 kg/m2. The replication cohorts were drawn from claims data in the OptumLabs Data Warehouse.

Median patient age was 61.2 years, 65.4% were male, 77.5% were white, and the median Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD)-Na score was 20. More than one-third (35.5%) had a MASH or metabolic indication for liver transplant. All patients had metabolic risk factors before liver transplant. Most patients had type 2 diabetes (58.9%), hypertension (65.3%), or a BMI of at least 30 (64.8%).

Among the 841 transplant patients who took GLP-1 drugs, 72% started them after their transplants. Median time to first GLP-1 dose was 1.5 years after transplant, and the median time spent taking the drugs was 1.2 years. Those on GLP-1 drugs were more likely to have MASH, diabetes, hypertension, obesity, or to be on statin therapy.

GLP-1 drug use was associated with a 14.2% drop in LDL cholesterol, an 8.3% drop in total cholesterol, and a 2.6% decline in HbA1c. Body weight fell by 5% in the 2 years after patients started a GLP-1 agonist.

Despite those changes, the reasons for the lower mortality risks weren't clear, Li said. Those on GLP-1 drugs weren't significantly less likely than their non-GLP-1 drug counterparts to experience a major adverse cardiovascular event (aHR 1.03, 95% CI 0.56-1.92) or, specifically, myocardial infarction (aHR 0.78, 95% CI 0.29-2.09).

The same was true for major adverse kidney events, sustained estimated glomerular filtration rate decline of at least 40%, or kidney transplant after liver transplant, though trends favored use of GLP-1 drugs. Li noted that a possible signal emerged for kidney failure in favor of GLP-1 drugs, but the difference just missed significance (aHR 0.46, P=0.06).

Most people who die after a liver transplant have a functioning graft, Li noted. Instead, malignancies, cardiovascular events, infections, and renal failure account for the majority of post-transplant deaths. Transplant patients on GLP-1 drugs were less likely than nonusers to die from those non-liver causes, including cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events, malignancies, infections, or graft failure. "This helps explain the survival benefit we observed," he said.

Limitations included the study's lack of power to detect differences in major adverse cardiovascular or kidney events. The cause of death wasn't known in 23% of patients, and drug exposure was relatively short. Sicker transplant recipients started GLP-1 drugs less often, Li noted.

#5756. Scientists discover a hidden driver of high cholesterol and a way to stop it

Heart disease linked to high cholesterol continues to be the leading cause of death worldwide. Although doctors have more treatment options than ever, many people still struggle to lower their cholesterol to safe levels. Others experience side effects that make existing medications difficult to take.

Researchers at the University of California San Diego School of Medicine have now identified a previously unknown biological pathway that helps explain why diets high in cholesterol can gradually weaken the body's ability to remove harmful low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol from the bloodstream. Even more promising, they have identified an experimental drug that has already undergone safety testing in humans and could potentially interfere with this process.

The findings, published in Nature, could open the door to a new approach to treating high cholesterol.

"We've known for a long time that a high-cholesterol diet reduces the liver's ability to clear cholesterol from the blood, but we didn't fully understand why," said senior author Alan Saltiel, PhD, professor of medicine at UC San Diego School of Medicine and director of the UC San Diego/UCLA Diabetes Research Center. "This new discovery explains a critical piece of that puzzle."

The liver plays a central role in controlling cholesterol levels. It removes cholesterol from the bloodstream so it can be processed, broken down, and used by other parts of the body.

To accomplish this, liver cells rely on structures called LDL receptors. Located on the surface of these cells, the receptors work much like docking stations, capturing LDL cholesterol circulating in the blood and bringing it inside for processing.

The number of available receptors matters. When liver cells have more LDL receptors, they can remove more cholesterol from circulation. This is one reason widely used cholesterol medications, including statins and PCSK9 inhibitors, are effective. They help maintain or increase the number of receptors available to clear LDL cholesterol.

Scientists Uncover a Hidden Cholesterol Pathway

Using experiments involving mice and human cells, the researchers discovered a previously unrecognized process that interferes with the liver's ability to clear cholesterol. Over time, this mechanism reduces the number of LDL receptors, making it harder for the body to keep blood cholesterol under control.

The process begins with a protein known as Ral, which Saltiel had previously investigated in fat cells. The team discovered that consuming high amounts of dietary cholesterol activates Ral, setting off a chain of events that leads to the loss of LDL receptors. As Ral activity increases, fewer receptors remain available to remove harmful cholesterol from the bloodstream.

The researchers then identified another critical piece of the mechanism: an enzyme called cathepsin A (CTSA). This enzyme helps drive the process responsible for depleting LDL receptors.

When scientists used a small molecule inhibitor to block CTSA, the results were striking. LDL receptors became more stable, and levels of circulating LDL cholesterol dropped dramatically in mice.

The discovery is especially significant because the newly identified pathway is different from those targeted by current cholesterol medications. That distinction could make it possible to develop treatments for patients who do not respond adequately to existing drugs.

"There's still a real need for new cholesterol-lowering options, since some people can't get to safe levels even with the drugs we have now," said Saltiel. "This new pathway we discovered is completely separate from anything that existing drugs target, so it gives us a new opportunity to fill that gap."

A Previously Tested Drug Could Accelerate Treatment

Discovering a new biological target is usually only the beginning of a lengthy drug development process. Researchers often need years of additional work to identify a suitable compound and determine whether it can be used safely in people.

In this case, however, the scientists may already have a promising candidate.

A drug designed to inhibit CTSA had previously been developed as a potential treatment for heart failure. Although the program was eventually discontinued for strategic reasons, the experimental medication had already progressed through a Phase 1 clinical trial, where it was successfully evaluated for safety in humans.

That earlier work could provide an important advantage. Rather than beginning drug development from scratch, researchers believe the existing CTSA inhibitor may be ready to advance into a Phase 2 clinical trial to investigate its effectiveness against high cholesterol.

The findings are still at an early stage, and the drug has not yet been shown to lower cholesterol in humans. Nevertheless, its previous clinical testing could shorten the path toward determining whether this new treatment strategy works in patients.

"Luckily, there's an experimental drug sitting on the shelf that's already been shown to be safe in humans," said Saltiel. "We hope to test whether this might be effective by conducting a clinical trial -- which could potentially bring a new treatment option to patients much sooner than would have been expected."

Co-authors of the study include Xue Feng, Shuo Zhang, Yuqi Wang, Twisha Kurlagunda, Allyssa Sit, Sadatsugu Sakane, Se Yong Park, Churaibhon Wisessaowapak, Kaylee Nguyen, Jamie Yan, Himani Pothulu, Catherine Dinh, Felicia Chu, Yuyao Ren, Bichen Zhang, Patrick Secrest, Chao-Wei Hung, Preethi Veeragandham, Yuliya Skorobogatko, Tatiana Kisseleva, and Amit R. Majithia at UC San Diego; Priya Jaishankar, Pusu Yang, and Adam Renslo at the University of California, San Francisco; Linmeng Han and Peng Zhao at the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio; and Philip L.S.M. Gordts at the University of Utah.

The research received partial funding from the National Institutes of Health (Grants P30DK063491, R01DK117551, R01DK128796, and R01DK135289) and an American Diabetes Association postdoctoral fellowship (1-25-PDF-76).

#5755. BYD Is Combining Solar Energy Storage, Five-Minute Flash Charging, And Robotic Arms For Its New Charging Stations

Despite not selling any cars in the U.S., China's BYD is quietly taking over the EV world. It has surpassed Tesla as the world's largest electric carmaker by global sales, and it's also been hard at work trying to dethrone Tesla as the provider of the world's most advanced EV charging network. Now it's announced the latest big step toward that goal. On Tuesday, BYD announced that it will combine clean solar power, its proprietary Flash Charging tech that uses local energy storage, and robotic arms into one EV charging system.

The core of this system is BYD's Flash Charging, which draws power from the grid like any other EV charging station. Unlike others, though, it stores the electricity in two on-site 185-kilowatt batteries. That stored energy can then be pumped into your EV way quicker than it would be if it were drawing from the grid directly, BYD says.

Each Flash Charger has two connectors, capable of up to 1,500 kW charging if only one is in use, or 1,000 kW if two cars are sharing. For context, Tesla's new V4 Superchargers top out at 500 kW, regular superchargers hit 250 kW, and the fastest DC chargers from Electrify America can do 350 kW. BYD's quoted charge times are 10% to 70% in five minutes, 10% to 97% in nine minutes, and in cold weather, 20% to 97% in 12 minutes given an ambient temperature of minus 30 degrees Fahrenheit.

BYD is now incorporating solar generation into the equation, drawing power from the sun to those same local 185-kW batteries, presumably via solar panels placed on top of the charging station's canopy. This means the system is less reliant on the grid, which is huge in remote, sun-soaked regions like, say, the desert in the United Arab Emirates where BYD launched all this.

Then there are the robotic arms. The idea is far from new or original — Tesla promised them a decade ago, and EV makers like Volkswagen, Hyundai, and China's Xiaomi have since built their own renditions. It's a simple premise: A robotic arm locates your car's charging port, opens the cover, and inserts the connector automatically.

BYD plans to install 6,000 Flash Charging stations worldwide by the end of next year. Don't expect all or even most of them to get solar power or the robot arms initially, but if BYD can actually normalize five-minute charging with solar and robot arms sometime in the next couple of years, we might be looking at the new charging network king.
