#5754. Four of Seven Dutch Green Hydrogen Projects Have Been Cancelled. The Subsidies Keep Coming.

The Netherlands awarded €783.5 million in subsidies to seven green hydrogen projects in 2022. Together they were supposed to deliver 1,150 MW of electrolysis capacity. Four years later, four projects representing 550 MW have been cancelled, and none of the original seven is operating. The November 2 parliamentary answers also confirm that the government cannot say when electrolytic hydrogen will become commercially viable without dedicated subsidies. Another €780 million is reserved for a future subsidy round anyway.

The TFIE Strategy Briefing follows what happened to the Dutch projects, what the government’s own cost and demand revisions imply, and which industrial activities could prosper without the hydrogen market originally forecast.

The €783.5 million was awarded, not spent. Roughly €150 million had been disbursed under the programme when the parliamentary answers were published. That distinction matters, especially when assessing potential losses to taxpayers. It does not make the project record look good. The Dutch state has spent four years supporting a group of plants that has so far delivered no operating capacity, while almost half the planned megawatts have been withdrawn.

The price assumptions were difficult to defend from the start. Officials say the original subsidy decisions reflected expectations that renewable hydrogen would cost around €2/kg by 2030 and become competitive with fossil-derived hydrogen within a decade. Making a kilogram by electrolysis typically requires about 50–55 kWh of electricity. Even at €50/MWh, a very cheap assumption for dependable electricity supplied to a European industrial facility, that power costs €2.50–€2.75 per kilogram before capital recovery, maintenance, water treatment, compression or delivery. Buying electricity only during the cheapest hours lowers the energy bill but leaves the electrolyser idle for longer, increasing the capital cost per kilogram produced. Eurostat’s latest industrial electricity data show how low the €50/MWh assumption is relative to ordinary non-household electricity prices, although large electrolysers would negotiate different contracts.

There are established industrial uses for hydrogen, particularly in chemicals and refining. The Dutch policy went considerably further, assuming domestic electrolysis could grow into a competitive source of energy for processes where direct electricity would often be cheaper. The cancellations have arrived alongside retreat from those anticipated markets, not as an isolated string of engineering setbacks. Lower-than-expected demand and expensive production are undermining the case for both the plants and the infrastructure intended to connect them.

The government’s September energy planning already gives hydrogen much less work in building heat and electricity generation. It also projects substantially less industrial hydrogen demand than earlier plans. Nevertheless, the proposed response includes more production subsidies, obligations for some industrial customers to buy renewable hydrogen, and measures to support a national pipeline network. Those choices keep public policy committed to volumes that commercial buyers have not shown they can afford.

The network has its own deteriorating economics. The Netherlands Court of Audit found that estimated investment had risen from €1.5 billion to €3.8 billion. Gasunie/Hynetwork Services estimated startup losses of up to €2.5 billion against a €750 million grant. These are forecasts, not bills already paid. But a pipeline system designed for a large future hydrogen market becomes harder to finance when that market contracts. Higher tariffs would make hydrogen less attractive to the customers it needs. Additional subsidies shift the burden elsewhere. The Court of Audit laid out the problem in December 2025.

Dutch chemical manufacturing, steel processing and port industries do not need to disappear as hydrogen expectations shrink. Some energy-intensive feedstocks can be produced where clean electricity is cheaper and imported for further manufacturing in the Netherlands. Industrial heat pumps and direct electric processes avoid producing and transporting hydrogen in the first place. Smaller refineries will also need less hydrogen as petroleum demand declines. These changes have different consequences for particular companies and workers, but they offer a more credible starting point for an industrial strategy than a hydrogen-volume target.

The government now faces another subsidy round with evidence it did not have in 2022: cancelled projects, higher costs, much smaller demand expectations and a pipeline investment whose customers are uncertain. It should evaluate the industrial products being made, the cost of the available decarbonization routes and the amount of hydrogen that those routes actually require before funding another large tranche of production capacity. Otherwise the next awards risk preserving yesterday’s forecasts at tomorrow’s expense.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing analysis examines the project record, subsidy assumptions, pipeline exposure and alternatives for Dutch industrial production. It includes the implications for ammonia, steel and refining that are beyond the scope of this CleanTechnica article.

#5752. Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer

Scientists at the University of Virginia Comprehensive Cancer Center have developed a promising experimental strategy for treating glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive malignant brain tumor in adults. The new approach could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles that have limited the effectiveness of existing brain cancer treatments.

The research team, led by UVA's Roger Abounader, MD, PhD, identified tiny genetic molecules known as "microRNAs" that can interfere with several genes responsible for the development and growth of glioblastoma. To deliver these molecules into the brain, the researchers combined specialized nanoparticles, focused ultrasound and microscopic bubbles. Together, these technologies offer a way to temporarily cross the brain's protective barrier, which normally prevents many treatments from reaching brain tumors and other neurological conditions.

"This new approach could help target numerous molecules that promote cancer growth, including those for which no drugs exist, at the same time to achieve better therapies," said Abounader, a professor at UVA's School of Medicine in the Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Cancer Biology, as well as its Comprehensive Cancer Center and Center for RNA Science and Medicine. "We are hoping to translate our findings into future clinical trials for patients with glioblastoma and other brain tumors."

Why Glioblastoma Is So Difficult to Treat

Glioblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults and one of the most aggressive forms of cancer. It claims more than 13,000 lives in the United States each year. One reason it is so difficult to treat is that cancer cells spread into surrounding healthy brain tissue, making it nearly impossible for surgeons to remove the entire tumor.

Another major challenge is the brain's natural "blood-brain barrier." This protective system helps shield the brain from harmful substances, including toxins and infectious agents. Unfortunately, it also blocks many drugs that could otherwise be used to attack brain cancer.

Current treatment generally begins with surgery to remove as much of the tumor as possible. Patients then receive radiation therapy and chemotherapy to help control the remaining cancer and extend survival. Despite these efforts, glioblastoma remains exceptionally difficult to manage.

The UVA researchers are pursuing a different strategy. Instead of relying on drugs that target individual cancer-related processes, their approach uses microRNAs, small pieces of genetic material capable of suppressing the activity of multiple problematic genes at the same time.

By disrupting several genes that help glioblastoma grow and survive, the treatment could potentially slow or even stop tumor growth. This ability to target multiple cancer-driving mechanisms is especially important because combining several conventional cancer drugs can produce harmful side effects. In addition, many of the molecules involved in cancer growth cannot currently be targeted by available medications.

Using Ultrasound to Deliver Cancer-Fighting Molecules

Getting these genetic molecules into the brain presents another major challenge. To overcome it, Abounader's team uses focused ultrasound guided by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), allowing researchers to direct sound waves precisely toward the intended area.

The ultrasound works with tiny "microbubbles" to temporarily open the blood-brain barrier. This creates a brief opportunity for nanoparticles carrying the microRNAs to pass through the barrier and enter the brain, where they can act on genes involved in tumor growth.

The researchers tested this approach in laboratory experiments and animal models of glioblastoma. Their findings showed that the microRNA treatment slowed tumor growth and helped the animals survive longer.

Although these results are encouraging, the strategy remains experimental and will require additional research before it can be evaluated in human patients. Abounader believes the findings provide an important early indication that the technology could eventually benefit people with glioblastoma and potentially those with other types of cancer.

"This approach could have broad applications for several brain and other human diseases," Abounader said. "We and many others are intensively working to lighten the burden of cancer, and hopefully also completely cure it, but this requires a continued investment in cancer and medical research."

UVA Expands Focused Ultrasound Cancer Research

UVA Health has been at the forefront of focused ultrasound research since the technology's early development. Over the years, its scientists have built an extensive research program investigating how precisely directed sound waves might be used to treat a wide range of medical conditions.

Recognizing the technology's potential in cancer care, UVA partnered with the Charlottesville-based Focused Ultrasound Foundation to establish the Focused Ultrasound Immuno-Oncology (FUSION) Center. It is the first center in the world devoted specifically to investigating how focused ultrasound can be combined with cancer immunotherapy. Researchers believe this combination could lead to major advances in cancer treatment during the 21st century.

The effort also supports the broader missions of UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center and UVA's Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology, both of which are working to improve care through new medical discoveries.

UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center is among just 57 cancer centers nationwide to receive the National Cancer Institute's prestigious "comprehensive" designation. The recognition reflects its excellence in cancer research and patient care.

The Manning Institute was established to speed the discovery and development of new medicines and potential cures for some of the most difficult diseases. Its work is supported by a statewide clinical trials network designed to make emerging treatments more accessible to patients as they move through research and testing.

Abounader and his colleagues published their experimental approach and initial laboratory findings in JCI, the Journal of Clinical Investigation. The study is open access and can be read free of charge.

The research team included Shekhar Saha, Ying Zhang, Myron K. Gibert Jr., Collin Dube, Farina Hanif, Elizabeth Qian Xu Mulcahy, Sylwia Bednarek, Yunan Sun, Pawel Marcinkiewicz, Xiantao Wang, Gijung Kwak, Ahsan H. Polash, Haolin Li, Kadie Hudson, Manikarna Dinda, Tapas Saha, Matthew McCord, Fadila Guessous, Nichola Cruickshanks, Rossymar Rivera Colon, Lily Dell'Olio, Rajitha Anbu, Wenjie Liu, Songy Choi, Benjamin Kefas, Pankaj Kumar, Alexander L. Klibanov, David Schiff, Jung Soo Suk, Justin Hanes, Jamie Mata, Markus Hafner and Abounader. The researchers reported having no financial interest in the work.

Funding came from the National Institutes of Health's National Cancer Institute through grants U01 CA220841 and P30 CA044579, along with the NIH's National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke through grants R01 NS122222 and R21 NS122136. Additional support was provided by a UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center pilot grant, a Schiff Foundation grant, the Ben and Catherine Ivy Foundation, and the Focused Ultrasound Foundation.

#5751. Perioperative Therapy Tops Prostatectomy Alone in High-Risk Prostate Cancer

— PROTEUS substudy shows a 62% lower risk of recurrence or death with apalutamide plus ADT

Results from a substudy of the phase III PROTEUS trial presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) congress showed that adding apalutamide (Erleada) and androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) before and after radical prostatectomy reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 62% compared with prostatectomy alone in patients with high-risk localized prostate cancer.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, Mary-Ellen Taplin, MD, of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, discusses the findings.

Following is a transcript of her remarks:

At ASCO 2026 in the plenary, the PROTEUS main study was presented, which was a very large, 2,100-patient study, which looked at the effect of 6 months of neoadjuvant apalutamide and ADT compared to placebo and ADT, followed by prostatectomy. And then everyone received another 6 months of the therapy they had been assigned to. So that study was positive. It showed a 20% reduction in metastasis or death by central imaging review and a 26% reduction by investigator assessment.

And to complement that data, there was a substudy done, which was what was presented at ESMO during one of the oral sessions. So the substudy compared what I'll refer to as the PROTEUS regimen, so 6 months of ADT and apalutamide before and after prostatectomy to standard-of-care prostatectomy alone. There was a 3:1 randomization to the prostatectomy alone to obtain more patients for a comparison to the prostatectomy.

So the primary endpoint of the substudy was a little bit different than the primary endpoints of the main study. So the main study had two co-primary endpoints, which was pathologic response and MFS (metastasis-free survival). The primary endpoint of the substudy was event-free survival at 3 years. So event-free survival includes relapse by any means -- so PSA [prostate-specific antigen], local recurrence, [and] imaging relapse, which included PSMA [prostate-specific membrane antigen] PET or conventional imaging.

So this primary endpoint was very, very positive. There was a 62% reduction in the risk of recurrence or death with the 6 months of apalutamide and ADT before and after surgery, prostatectomy. And this was true controlling over time for the analysis at the longer time points when accounting for testosterone recovery. In addition, there was a 51% lower risk of death or metastasis -- again, metastasis by PSMA PET or conventional imaging. Fifty percent fewer patients received subsequent therapy at all by 3 years. And importantly, there was a 50% reduction in any radiation after receiving the neoadjuvant ADT and apalutamide. So in summary, the primary endpoint, event-free survival, and all the secondary endpoints including MFS and first subsequent therapy were all very positive for the combined neoadjuvant apalutamide, ADT, and prostatectomy.

Safety is very important to assess. The main side effects were similar, I would say, to what is known for apalutamide and ADT. Can't be ignored, but in general are easily managed in the clinic and include fatigue, hot flashes, and incidence of rash. The rash with apalutamide is different than a rash say with antibiotics. It's less of an allergic type rash and more immune-mediated where patients can continue the drug with a dose reduction or a short interruption.

Hypertension is a known class side effect of androgen pathway receptor inhibitors. Importantly, there was no increase in surgical complications. This is a nice study designed to analyze that with the neoadjuvant and the adjuvant therapy combined with prostatectomy compared to prostatectomy alone.

Notably, to me, is that in the control arm the patients who had prostatectomy, 70% of patients relapsed by 3 years. So these are men who -- prostatectomies alone are not curing them, and they need subsequent therapy which may or may not put them into remission.

So I think that's important to take into consideration when thinking about the best treatments for patients. You have to dissect the pros and cons of surgery, androgen deprivation, and radiation, and think about the general health of your patient, their age, their goals. Is ADT and an androgen pathway inhibitor safe? And is surgery versus radiation safe? And those are the types of analyses that the treating physician needs to make when thinking about these patients with very high-risk localized prostate cancer.

#5750. Novel Sjogren's Drug Passes First Phase III Test

— Barring catastrophe in second trial, approval seems likely

ORLANDO -- An investigational CD40L antagonist called dazodalibep looks to be nearing the finish line on the way to approval for Sjögren's disease, based on results from a 48-week phase III trial reported here.

With scores on the EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Disease Activity Index (ESSDAI) as the randomized trial's primary outcome measure, patients on the active drug saw reductions of 5.2 and 5.6 points by week 48, depending on which of two doses they received, compared with a 3.8-point decline with placebo (P<0.05 and P<0.001, respectively), reported Ghaith Noaiseh, MD, of the University of Kansas in Kansas City.

Clinically significant reductions of 3 points were achieved by about two-thirds of patients receiving dazodalibep; fewer met more stringent response levels, but even so, fully half of patients on the higher of the two doses had ESSDAI scores drop by 7 points, Noaiseh said during a late-breaking abstract session at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting. Despite a strong placebo response in the trial, the drug held a statistically significant advantage.

In addition, safety findings were better than unremarkable, with fewer serious adverse events than were seen with placebo.

This was one of a pair of phase III trials conducted by drugmaker Amgen, which took control of dazodalibep when it bought the original developer, Horizon Therapeutics, in 2023. The other has not been completed but should be soon, the company has said. These studies follow encouraging results from phase II trials reported in 2023.

Dazodalibep is intended to disrupt interaction between the CD40 receptor and its ligand, CD40L, which should have a wide range of effects, Noaiseh explained. It "disrupts CD40L-mediated costimulatory interactions between T cells, B cells, glandular epithelial cells, and other antigen-presenting cells," he said. That leads to decreased production of inflammatory mediators as well as autoantibodies.

Also of note, although it's a biologic drug, it's not a monoclonal antibody -- rather, it's a fusion product based on an antibody but with the Fc portion removed, Noaiseh said, noting that previous efforts to target CD40L with an antibody led to unacceptably high rates of thrombosis.

For this first phase III study, the investigators enrolled 648 Sjögren's disease patients, randomizing them to three arms: placebo, dazodalibep 3,000 mg every 12 weeks (low dose), or the drug at 1,500 mg every 4 weeks (high dose). Their mean age was 53, and 94% were women. Some 56% were from Europe and North America, 7% from Japan, and the rest from a variety of other countries.

Baseline ESSDAI scores averaged 10.2, with about 20% having scores of 14 or higher, indicating high activity. A key secondary outcome measure was the EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Patient-Reported Index (ESSPRI); scores at baseline averaged 7.07. Another outcome that was developed specially for these trials was a Diary for Assessing Sjögren's Patients Index (DASPRI), in which patients recorded their symptoms daily, including dryness at four separate body locations -- a complement to ESSPRI, which asks patients about symptoms during the previous 2 weeks and only rates overall dryness.

In general, the higher dazodalibep dose was more effective. This was most clearly seen in data on dryness, with a decrease of 2.5 points on ESSPRI's dryness domain, and a 1.98-point decrease in DASPRI dryness -- compared with -1.33 and -1.05 with placebo, respectively (P<0.001 for both comparisons). Dryness relief with the lower drug dose came in about halfway between the high dose and placebo, missing statistical significance.

Overall rates of treatment-emergent adverse events were similar across all three arms, affecting some 85% of patients. Those considered treatment-related were a bit more common with the high-dose drug (37% vs 25% for placebo), but only five events were rated as serious in the entire study sample, two of which were in the placebo group. Likewise, discontinuations because of adverse events were about the same in the three arms, with 24 total among the 648 participants.

The investigators also examined "special interest" events that could potentially arise from this novel biologic agent targeting a range of immune functions. These included allergic and hypersensitivity reactions, thromboembolism, opportunistic infections, and various malignancies. There were very few of any of these, and none were more common with either dazodalibep dose versus placebo. In total, 40 such events were seen, including 14 with placebo, 12 in the low-dose group, and 14 with the high dose.

#5749. Scientists finally discover how a common gut bacterium can trigger colon cancer

For nearly two decades, scientists have known that a common gut bacterium can produce a toxin that damages the colon and helps drive the formation of tumors. What they could not explain was how the toxin first attaches to intestinal cells and begins its attack. Now, researchers have uncovered that missing step, revealing a surprising vulnerability that could lead to new ways of protecting the colon.

The breakthrough comes from a team led by scientists at the Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center, its Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, and the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine. Their findings, published in Nature, identify a protein called claudin-4 as the essential docking point for a bacterial toxin known as BFT.

Even more promising, the researchers have already used this discovery to develop a molecular decoy that intercepts the toxin before it can damage colon cells. The strategy successfully protected mice from the toxin's harmful effects, suggesting a possible new approach to preventing bacterial damage associated with colorectal cancer. The research received partial support from the National Institutes of Health.

"We've made several attempts over time to identify the receptor, so this is an exciting moment," says senior author Cynthia Sears, M.D., Bloomberg~Kimmel Professor of Cancer Immunotherapy and professor of medicine at Johns Hopkins. "Understanding how bacterial toxins work can open doors to new approaches for detection and therapy for associated diseases, including diarrhea, colorectal cancer and bloodstream infections."

How a Common Gut Bacterium Can Promote Colon Cancer

The investigation centers on Bacteroides fragilis, a bacterium that can be found in the intestines of up to 20% of healthy people. Although the presence of this bacterium does not automatically mean someone will develop cancer, certain strains produce a powerful toxin capable of disrupting the colon's protective lining, causing inflammation, and encouraging tumor growth.

The toxin, known as B. fragilis toxin or BFT, has been under investigation for years. In a landmark 2009 study published in Nature Medicine, Sears and her colleagues demonstrated that the toxin could promote the development of colon tumors. Their work helped establish an important connection between toxin-producing gut bacteria, chronic inflammation, and colorectal cancer.

Earlier experiments also revealed that BFT damages a protein called E-cadherin, which helps hold neighboring cells together and maintain the colon's protective barrier. When this protein is broken apart, the barrier becomes compromised, potentially allowing harmful substances and bacteria to interfere with the surrounding tissue.

However, one critical question remained unanswered. Although BFT could break down E-cadherin, the toxin did not appear to attach directly to that protein. Researchers suspected that another molecule was helping the toxin reach its target, but repeated attempts to identify it had failed.

Scientists Identify the Missing Link Using CRISPR

To solve the mystery, the researchers turned to CRISPR, a powerful gene-editing technology that allows scientists to selectively disable genes and investigate what they do.

Maxwell White, an M.D./Ph.D. candidate working in Sears' laboratory, led a genome-wide CRISPR screening effort in collaboration with Matthew Waldor's laboratory at Harvard Medical School. The team systematically switched off genes in colon epithelial cells, the cells that form the inner lining of the colon, to determine which ones were necessary for the toxin to attach and cause damage.

One gene stood out dramatically. It produces claudin-4, a protein that helps neighboring cells form tight junctions, the seals that limit the movement of substances between cells and help maintain the intestinal barrier.

When the researchers disabled the gene responsible for claudin-4, BFT could no longer bind to the colon cells. Without that initial attachment, the toxin was unable to attack E-cadherin.

The finding revealed that claudin-4 acts as a receptor for the bacterial toxin. In effect, the toxin must first latch onto this protein before it can carry out its damaging activity.

"It took a while to get the assay working and validate the approach, but once we were able to do the screen, claudin-4 was a clear, resounding top hit," says White. "That was an exciting moment."

An Unexpected Discovery Reveals a New Bacterial Attack Strategy

The identity of the receptor surprised the scientists.

Sears and other researchers had expected BFT to interact with a protein involved in cellular signaling, such as a G protein-coupled receptor. These receptors act somewhat like communication switches, allowing cells to respond to signals from their surroundings.

Claudin-4, however, serves a very different purpose. Rather than functioning primarily as a signaling receptor, it helps maintain the physical connections between neighboring cells.

The discovery also revealed an unusual way for a bacterial toxin to operate. BFT belongs to a class of enzymes called proteases, which cut other proteins. Most proteases act directly on their targets, but BFT appears to require a separate receptor before it can reach and damage E-cadherin.

When the team reviewed previous scientific research, they could not identify another toxin known to use the same mechanism.

To establish that BFT and claudin-4 truly bind to each other, the Johns Hopkins researchers collaborated with structural biologists F. Xavier Gomis-Rüth and Ulrich Eckhard at the Molecular Biology Institute of Barcelona.

Using techniques that measure how molecules interact, White and the Barcelona team showed that BFT and claudin-4 form a tightly bound complex in laboratory experiments. Each toxin molecule paired with one receptor molecule, providing direct physical evidence of the connection.

A Clever Molecular Decoy Blocks the Dangerous Gut Toxin

Identifying the receptor did more than explain how the toxin works. It also gave the scientists an idea for stopping it.

If BFT needs claudin-4 to attach to colon cells, perhaps a substitute could lure the toxin away from its intended target.

To test that possibility, the team developed a molecular decoy. This was a soluble protein carrying sequences from claudin-4, designed to attract BFT without allowing it to attack the colon's protective lining.

The researchers then worked with Min Dong's laboratory at Harvard Medical School, including Kang Wang and colleagues, to investigate the approach in mice. These experiments allowed the scientists to examine how the toxin behaves in the more complicated environment of a living intestine.

The results were encouraging. Instead of binding to claudin-4 receptors on colon cells, BFT attached to the decoy proteins. By intercepting the toxin, the decoys successfully protected the mice from BFT-induced damage.

The finding suggests that it may be possible to interfere with the toxin's first step rather than trying to repair the damage after it occurs.

"This approach could be iterated upon with small molecules or other biologics that have better pharmacological properties," says White. The team is now exploring which molecular approaches might be most successful to block the toxin.

Small molecules are compounds that can sometimes be developed into medicines, while biologics are treatments made from or involving biological materials, such as proteins. Future versions of the decoy strategy could potentially be designed to work more effectively in the body or be easier to administer.

What This Discovery Could Mean for Colon Cancer Prevention

Although the findings identify a promising new target, important questions remain.

Scientists have established that BFT attaches to claudin-4 and that blocking this interaction can protect mice from toxin-induced damage. However, they have not yet captured the exact experimental three-dimensional structure showing how the two molecules fit together.

Even advanced artificial intelligence tools, including AlphaFold, have been unable to fully resolve the interaction. Understanding its precise structure could help researchers design more effective compounds that prevent the toxin from binding.

Further experiments will also be needed to determine whether the decoy approach can safely and effectively prevent toxin-related disease in humans. The mouse experiments demonstrated protection against tissue damage, but they did not establish that the strategy prevents colorectal cancer.

Nevertheless, the discovery resolves a major question that has persisted since the connection between BFT and colon tumor formation was established in 2009. By identifying the toxin's previously unknown point of attachment, researchers have uncovered a potential way to interrupt a harmful biological process before it begins.

The findings could ultimately support new strategies for detecting or treating conditions associated with bacterial toxins, including colorectal cancer, diarrhea, and bloodstream infections.

Additional researchers who contributed to the study include Jason Chen, Shaoguang Wu, Abby L. Geis, and Jessica Queen of Johns Hopkins, along with Hailong Zhang, Karthik Hullahalli, and Jie Zhang of Harvard Medical School.

Funding was provided by the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, Janssen Research and Development, Cancer Research UK, the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R01 AI042347, R01 NS080833, R01 NS117626, R01 AI170835 and R01 AI189789) and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute.

#5748. Novel GLP-1 Cut Heavy Drinking Days in Alcohol Use Disorder

— 42% of patients on pemvidutide achieved zero heavy drinking days by week 24

The investigational glucagon/GLP-1 dual receptor agonist pemvidutide significantly reduced the number of heavy drinking days (HDDs) per week in patients with moderate-to-severe alcohol use disorder (AUD), the phase II RECLAIM trial showed.

After 24 weeks of treatment, HDDs per week decreased by 4.20 days with pemvidutide versus 2.75 days with placebo (P=0.0014), reported Henry R. Kranzler, MD, of the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, during the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual meeting in Denver.

In addition, more patients receiving the drug achieved zero HDDs by week 24 (42.2% vs 17.4% with placebo; OR 3.8, 95% CI 1.4-10.4, P=0.0066), as well as higher rates of ≥2-level WHO Risk Drinking Levels (64.4% vs 34.8%; OR 3.3, 95% CI 1.4-7.7, P=0.0049).

"In the context of alcohol use disorder -- which can be a life-threatening condition -- the positive effects are meaningful, and the adverse events are tolerable," Kranzler told MedPage Today.

Of note, patients on pemvidutide also achieved reductions in serum phosphatidylethanol (PEth) levels compared with increases in the placebo group (least-squares mean change from baseline -153.4 ng/mL vs +22.0 ng/mL, P<0.0001).

PEth is a "highly sensitive, highly specific measure of alcohol consumption that doesn't depend on self-reporting, and is objective," Kranzler said, adding that pemvidutide showed a "very robust" effect on PEth, while the placebo group showed a small increase, "which suggests that they were reporting greater reductions in drinking than they were actually experiencing."

"Even though the primary outcome was [a reduction in heavy drinking days], I'm most impressed by the PEth findings," he noted.

According to the 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health, 57.9 million current alcohol users ages 12 and older engaged in binge drinking in the past month, while 27.9 million had AUD in the past year. Excessive alcohol use leads to 178,000 deaths annually, with about one-third from binge drinking.

While the FDA has approved three therapies to treat AUD, only a small percentage of people with the disorder access these drugs.

Pemvidutide has balanced 1:1 glucagon/GLP-1 dual receptor agonist activity that reduces liver fat, inflammation, and fibrosis. A previous phase IIb trial showed that pemvidutide led to resolution of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) without worsening of fibrosis, but did not improve fibrosis without worsening of MASH.

Studies of other GLP-1 receptor agonists have shown that they reduce drinking in people with AUD, and there's also evidence that they affect the reward system in the brain, in addition to having peripheral effects in the gastrointestinal tract.

Thus, this study in AUD was a "logical next step," Kranzler said.

In RECLAIM, 100 patients with moderate-to-severe AUD were randomized to receive subcutaneous pemvidutide or placebo once weekly for 24 weeks, together with a standardized behavioral intervention.

Participants had to be engaging in heavy drinking (28 drinks per week for men, 21 for women) with at least 3 HDDs per week (≥5 drinks per day for men, ≥4 for women) over 28 days prior to screening.

Mean age was about 50, 52% were women, mean body mass index was about 32, and roughly 75% were categorized as having severe AUD. The average number of HDDs per week was 5.6 in the placebo group and 5.9 in the pemvidutide group.

Of the 100 participants randomized, 78% and 80% in the placebo and pemvidutide groups, respectively, completed treatment, while 92% and 90% completed the study.

More participants in the pemvidutide group versus the placebo group had an increase in percent days abstinent (38.9% vs 20.5%, P=0.0075) and the drug led to a higher numerical reduction in the number of drinks per drinking day (-4.9 vs -3.8), though this was not significant.

Pemvidutide also led to reductions in body weight (percent change -8.7% vs +0.4%, P<0.0001) and Fibrosis-4 scores (-0.3 vs +0.2, P=0.0301).

Overall, the most common adverse events (AEs) were mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal events (62% in the pemvidutide group and 34% in the placebo group).

Serious AEs occurred in two patients in the pemvidutide group (including a patient with hyponatremia possibly related to the drug) and one patient in the placebo group.

There were three severe AEs related to pemvidutide (including the patient with hyponatremia, one patient with migraine, and one with fatigue, night sweats, nausea, and gastroesophageal reflux disease).

Drug-related AEs leading to treatment discontinuation occurred in 10% of patients in the pemvidutide group.

#5746. Reflux Drugs and Dementia Risk; Epstein-Barr's Link to IBD; Managing Hepatitis Delta

— News and commentary from the world of gastroenterology and hepatology

Use of proton pump inhibitors in older adults was associated with a modestly increased risk of incident dementia, according to a meta-analysis of nearly two dozen studies published in Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics.

And watch out for the increased pancreatic cancer risk in patients with PRSS1-associated hereditary pancreatitis, researchers warned. (Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology)

#5745. Google enters decision model market with Gemini Decisions API

Google LLC today launched Gemini Decisions API, an artificial intelligence service designed to answer user questions in a cost-efficient manner.

It’s powered by a new AI model called Gemini Decision 1.

Traditional large language models are designed to answer a broad range of prompts. Gemini Decision 1 has a much narrower focus: It can process just three types of questions. The upside is that it answers those questions at a significantly lower cost. According to Google, the model is nearly five times cheaper than its entry-level Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite LLM.

The model can answer yes-no questions, multiple choice questions and prompts that ask it to rate an item on a user-specified scale. A cybersecurity team, for example, could ask the model to rate the severity of an antivirus alert on a scale of 1 to 10.

Gemini Decision 1 prompts include two items: the user’s questions and the dataset to which those questions pertain. The dataset can include up to 256,000 tokens worth of text, audio, images, video or some combination thereof.

LLMs usually generate verbose free-flowing text in response to user questions. Gemini Decision 1, in contrast, outputs terse answers such as “yes” or “no.” It also displays a score that indicates how confident it is in the accuracy of a given response. That score helps applications decide whether they should make use of the output.

Neural networks designed to generate brief answers to simple questions are known as decision models. The first such model, Jev, was launched in mid-September by a startup called TypeSafe AI Inc. It gained a million users within a few days. Three weeks after the launch, TypeSafe raised $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation.

Decision models can answer the narrow set of questions for which they’re optimized faster than LLMs. Additionally, they’re easier to integrate into applications. An application that powers some of its features using an AI model must check the model’s output for errors and filter redundant details before ingesting it. Decision models’ concise, structured responses make both tasks simpler.

“Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request,” Google DeepMind product manager Min Choi and principal scientist Felix Yu wrote in a blog post.

Google checked how Gemini Decision 1 compares to Jev and OpenAI Group PBC’s Decisions API, a competing service that launched last month. The search giant says that its model performed better across seven of the nine benchmarks it tested. However, Jev proved to be slightly more cost-efficient.

Gemini Decision 1 is available through the Gemini Decisions API for 10 cents per 1 million input tokens. Google doesn’t charge for output tokens. The algorithm is also accessible through a limited free tier in Google AI Studio, a service that developers can use to familiarize themselves with the search giant’s models.

#5744. Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease

A pesticide used for decades in agriculture may be linked to a much greater risk of Parkinson's disease, and scientists have uncovered a possible explanation for how it damages the brain.

Researchers at UCLA Health found that people with long-term residential exposure to chlorpyrifos, a widely used pesticide, had more than 2.5 times the risk of developing Parkinson's disease compared with those who were not exposed. Laboratory experiments also revealed how the chemical can interfere with the brain's ability to remove damaged proteins, leading to the loss of nerve cells essential for controlling movement.

The study, published in Molecular Neurodegeneration, goes beyond identifying a connection between pesticide exposure and Parkinson's. By examining what happens inside affected brain cells, the researchers uncovered a biological mechanism that could eventually provide new ways to protect the brain from damage.

A Common Pesticide With a Troubling Link to Parkinson's

Parkinson's disease affects nearly one million Americans. The progressive neurological condition gradually damages brain cells involved in movement, often causing tremors, muscle stiffness, slowed movement, and difficulties with coordination.

One of the defining features of Parkinson's is the loss of neurons that produce dopamine. This chemical messenger allows nerve cells to communicate and helps the brain coordinate smooth, controlled movements. As dopamine levels decline, the brain becomes less capable of regulating those movements.

Although inherited genetic factors can influence who develops Parkinson's, researchers have increasingly focused on environmental exposures that may also contribute to the disease. Pesticides are of particular interest because some chemicals used to kill insects or other agricultural pests can also interfere with biological processes in the nervous system.

Chlorpyrifos has been used extensively in agriculture for decades. Its residential use was banned in the United States in 2001, and agricultural applications faced additional restrictions in 2021. However, the pesticide remains in use on many crops in the United States and continues to be widely applied in other countries.

Because exposure may have occurred years before symptoms appeared, understanding the potential long-term effects of chlorpyrifos is particularly important. Identifying specific chemicals associated with Parkinson's could help researchers develop prevention strategies and determine whether previously exposed individuals might benefit from additional neurological monitoring.

Researchers Find More Than Double the Parkinson's Risk

To investigate the connection, UCLA scientists examined information from 829 people diagnosed with Parkinson's disease and 824 people without the condition. All participants were enrolled in the university's long-running Parkinson's Environment and Genes study, which investigates how environmental exposures and inherited factors influence Parkinson's risk.

The researchers combined California's detailed pesticide application records with participants' residential and workplace address histories. This allowed them to estimate how much chlorpyrifos individuals may have encountered over time based on where they lived and worked.

The results revealed a striking association. People with prolonged residential exposure to chlorpyrifos had more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease compared with those who had no such exposure.

Although this population analysis could not establish that the pesticide directly caused Parkinson's, the researchers took an additional step to investigate whether chlorpyrifos could produce the kinds of brain damage seen in people with the disease.

The team exposed mice to chlorpyrifos in aerosol form for 11 weeks. The inhalation approach was designed to resemble a common way people may encounter pesticides in the environment.

The exposed mice developed movement difficulties and lost neurons responsible for producing dopamine. This was particularly significant because the degeneration of these same nerve cells is a central feature of Parkinson's disease.

The researchers also detected inflammation in the animals' brains, along with abnormal accumulations of a protein called alpha-synuclein.

Under normal conditions, alpha-synuclein is found in nerve cells and plays a role in their functioning. However, the protein can accumulate in abnormal clumps that are closely associated with Parkinson's disease. These deposits are a major focus of research into why certain brain cells gradually deteriorate.

Together, the findings showed that chlorpyrifos exposure could reproduce several important characteristics of Parkinson's in laboratory animals, strengthening the biological evidence behind the human population findings.

Scientists Uncover a Breakdown in the Brain's Cleanup System

The researchers then turned to zebrafish to investigate exactly how chlorpyrifos harms neurons. These small fish are frequently used in neuroscience research because they allow scientists to study biological processes involved in nerve cell development and survival.

Their experiments pointed to a disruption in autophagy, a natural cellular maintenance process that helps remove damaged proteins and other unwanted material.

Autophagy functions much like an internal recycling system. Cells use it to break down worn-out or defective components so that potentially harmful material does not accumulate. This process is especially important for neurons, many of which must remain functional throughout a person's lifetime.

When chlorpyrifos interfered with this cleanup system, damaged material accumulated inside neurons, contributing to their deterioration.

The researchers also made an encouraging discovery. When they restored the cellular cleanup process or removed synuclein protein in their experiments, the neurons were protected from damage.

This finding suggests that the pesticide's harmful effects may depend partly on a biological pathway that researchers could potentially target with future treatments.

A Potential New Strategy for Protecting Against Parkinson's

The discovery raises the possibility of developing therapies that strengthen the brain's cellular cleanup mechanisms and help protect vulnerable neurons. Such treatments might eventually prove useful for people exposed to chlorpyrifos or other pesticides that disrupt similar processes.

However, the protective effects have so far been demonstrated in laboratory models. Additional research will be needed to determine whether enhancing autophagy can prevent or reduce pesticide-related brain damage in humans.

Scientists also want to investigate whether other commonly used pesticides interfere with the same cellular mechanisms. Although chlorpyrifos use has declined in the United States, many people were exposed before restrictions were introduced, and related agricultural chemicals remain widely used.

The findings could also help identify people with a history of substantial pesticide exposure who may benefit from closer neurological monitoring. Earlier recognition of possible changes in brain function could become increasingly important as researchers work toward treatments that slow or prevent Parkinson's progression.

Dr. Jeff Bronstein, professor of Neurology at UCLA Health and the study's senior author, emphasized the importance of identifying a particular chemical rather than treating all pesticides as a single category.

"This study establishes chlorpyrifos as a specific environmental risk factor for Parkinson's disease, not just pesticides as a general class," said Dr. Jeff Bronstein.

"By showing the biological mechanism in animal models, we've demonstrated that this association is likely causal. The discovery that autophagy dysfunction drives the neurotoxicity also points us toward potential therapeutic strategies to protect vulnerable brain cells."

Materials provided by University of California - Los Angeles Health Sciences. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5742. New diabetes implant uses electricity to lower blood sugar and promote weight loss

An experimental electronic implant could offer an entirely new way to treat type 2 diabetes. Rather than relying on insulin or conventional medications, the device uses electricity to convert excess blood sugar into a substance that the body can eliminate. In early tests with diabetic mice, the technology successfully regulated blood sugar and also led to weight loss.

The development comes as type 2 diabetes continues to affect a growing number of people worldwide. Unlike type 1 diabetes, type 2 is frequently associated with obesity, limited physical activity, and consuming more energy than the body needs over long periods.

Insulin injections can help reduce blood sugar by allowing muscle cells to absorb glucose from the bloodstream. However, insulin does not eliminate the underlying problem of excess energy. When the body does not use the glucose it absorbs, the surplus can eventually be converted into fat. This helps explain why some people with diabetes continue gaining weight even while receiving treatment.

Researchers led by Martin Fussenegger, a professor in the Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering at ETH Zurich in Basel, have developed an implant designed to address this problem differently. Their findings were published in the journal Science.

A New Diabetes Treatment Powered by Electricity

Fussenegger and his colleagues have spent years developing technologies capable of controlling blood sugar. Their previous designs used engineered genetic networks, but these systems depended on living cells and other biological materials.

That dependence introduced several complications. Biological components can create challenges involving immune compatibility, long-term stability, production, and regulatory approval.

The researchers have now taken a different approach by creating a catalyst made entirely from inorganic materials. It performs its function without requiring living cells, enzymes, or other biological components.

At the heart of the implant is a piece of graphite felt covered with tiny clusters of gold. These gold structures are coated with even smaller platinum particles, creating a specially engineered surface that enables the chemical reaction needed to process glucose.

The researchers designed this nanoscale surface themselves. According to Fussenegger, the materials also demonstrated excellent biocompatibility during experimental testing, suggesting they can interact with living tissue without causing significant adverse reactions.

The system includes an electronic controller enclosed in a 3D-printed housing. Instead of relying on a conventional wired power connection, the implant receives energy wirelessly at a frequency of 13.56 MHz. This frequency is internationally allocated for industrial, scientific, and medical applications.

How the Implant Removes Excess Blood Sugar

The technology works by transforming excess glucose into gluconate, a substance that can be eliminated from the body through urine.

Normally, glucose provides energy for cells. When more glucose is available than the body needs, some of that excess energy can ultimately be stored as fat. By converting part of the glucose into gluconate, the implant prevents that portion from being metabolized and stored in tissues, potentially helping reduce fat accumulation.

The entire process is designed to happen automatically, responding to changes in blood sugar as they occur.

A conventional glucose sensor, similar to those worn on the upper arm by many people with diabetes, continuously measures glucose concentrations in tissue. When levels rise too high, such as after a meal, the sensor communicates through Bluetooth with a smartphone or smartwatch.

The connected device then activates the implant, supplying the electrical energy needed for the catalyst to convert glucose into gluconate.

Once glucose levels return to the desired range, the implant automatically shuts down. This feedback system, known as closed-loop control, is intended to prevent blood sugar from dropping dangerously low.

Blood Sugar Control and Weight Loss in Diabetic Mice

To evaluate the technology, the researchers first conducted a laboratory experiment using a reservoir containing 5 liters of a nutrient solution with glucose. That volume is approximately equal to the amount of blood circulating in an adult human body.

The experiment demonstrated that the catalyst could convert glucose in a solution of this scale, an important step toward assessing its potential for medical applications.

The researchers then implanted the system in diabetic mice. The results showed that the device could precisely regulate the animals' blood sugar levels. The mice also lost weight, suggesting that converting excess glucose rather than allowing it to contribute to fat storage could offer an additional metabolic benefit.

Over six weeks of testing, the implant continued functioning reliably and was well tolerated by the animals.

"The system operates at a very low voltage, and our experiments showed no evidence of tissue damage from either electrical or thermal effects," says Fussenegger.

Although these findings are promising, the device has not yet been tested in humans. Additional research will be necessary to determine whether the technology can operate safely and effectively in people with diabetes.

Could Electronics Transform the Future of Diabetes Treatment?

Fussenegger believes the technology could represent a fundamental change in how diabetes is managed. Rather than using medications to influence how the body processes glucose, an electronic device could directly control the amount of glucose available.

"For decades, we have treated diabetes by telling the body how to manage glucose. We are now showing that we can take control of glucose directly, using electronics rather than drugs," he says. "And the catalyst only activates when glucose levels are too high."

The approach also creates opportunities to connect medical treatments with digital technologies, including the Internet of Things. This refers to networks of devices that exchange information and respond automatically to changing conditions.

The researchers envision electronically controlled treatments that could be manufactured at scale and integrated with existing digital health systems.

Their next objective is to turn the experimental implant into a medical device suitable for further development and eventual clinical testing.

One potential advantage is its relatively simple glucose conversion mechanism. Because the catalyst does not rely on cells or enzymes, the researchers believe some of the technical challenges associated with biological treatments could be easier to overcome.

Much of the supporting technology is also already available. Wireless power transmission systems and external electronic controllers are commercially established, meaning the team would not need to develop every component from scratch.

If future studies demonstrate similar benefits in humans, this approach could open the door to a new class of diabetes treatments in which smart electronic devices help regulate blood sugar directly, potentially reducing reliance on conventional medications.

Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5741. Doctor Behind Mass Shooting in D.C., Police Say

— Emergency physician accused of shooting multiple people -- one fatally -- before killing himself

Emergency physician Matt Lambert, MD, was named by NBC News as the gunman in Thursday's mass shooting in Washington, D.C., citing law enforcement officials.

According to police, Lambert fatally shot a man at a gym and left another in critical condition before fleeing and shooting others. He then killed himself after barricading himself in an apartment.

Lambert described himself on his website as a clinician and entrepreneur. Lambert holds active medical licenses in West Virginia and Montana, according to DocInfo.org. Neither license lists any disciplinary action.

An X account that appears to be associated with Lambert posted a manifesto on Thursday morning, which included a screenshot of a document with Lambert's name on it.

"My manifesto is an engineering report," the post stated. Police had said earlier in the day their suspect apparently had a dispute with the building's homeowners association.

The X account, OfMiceandMold, hosts dozens of images and complaints about problems with the condo and building. Lambert's name is mentioned several times in documents or screenshots of documents, including a lawsuit in which Lambert is the plaintiff.

The address on Lambert's website is on 15th Street, where the shooting occurred.

The shootings occurred around 8 a.m. in Logan Circle, about a mile north of the White House. Much of the block on 15th Street Northwest was cordoned off as police urged people to avoid the area, which includes a VIDA fitness center, St. Luke's Episcopal Church, residences, and a Whole Foods supermarket. Schools were locked down.

Law enforcement SWAT teams and other officers had their guns drawn on the roof of an apartment building and on the ground below.

Witness James Spellman, who was at the gym, said there were about 50 people there around 8 a.m. when the shooting began.

"Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out," he said. "One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck."

Spellman said he and others dashed out of the gym. He said he heard about two shots fired in the gym and about five or six fired outside.

Officials believe Lambert shot another person in a parking garage elevator, and then barricaded himself on the seventh floor of the building, the official said.

Another witness, Ryan Dubicki, said he was in his nearby apartment around the same time when he "heard about five bangs."

"They were really spread out so I thought it was construction," he said. A short time later, "there were cops everywhere."

The Logan Circle neighborhood has seen violence before. In early August 2025, a onetime member of President Donald Trump's Department of Government Efficiency was assaulted early on a Sunday morning in the neighborhood by a group of teenagers attempting to carjack him and a woman, authorities said.

Days later, Trump fulfilled his threat to bypass local authority and imposed direct federal control over the city, sending in hundreds of National Guard members to reduce crime. That deployment continues today.

The Associated Press contributed to this story.

“We made progress on infrastructure projects to comply with hospital seismic regulations,” Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Kathy Lancaster said in the release. “We also continued to invest in the facilities and technology members need to receive care in the setting they prefer, including inpatient, ambulatory and telehealth services.”

The system also outlined “nearly $1.0 billion in charitable grants, loans and investments to strengthen the healthcare infrastructure of communities” that included about $315 million in financial assistance and charity care.

Last year, it logged $1.4 billion in operating income (1.1% operating margin) across 12 months, as well as $9.3 billion in net income and $4.8 billion of capital spending.

The organization’s quarterly financial update comes ahead of a more granular regulatory disclosure, typically filed within a few additional weeks. That document could include additional information about its plans for Risant to absorb $3.3 billion, Oklahoma City-based Integris Health, which comprises 10 acute and 10 specialty hospitals. That deal is expected to close early next year, though its announcement was short on any financial details.

#5739. Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half

The liver may hold an unexpected key to fighting two of the most serious diseases associated with aging: Alzheimer's disease and heart disease. Scientists have discovered that restoring the function of aging liver cells can dramatically reduce harmful substances in the bloodstream, raising the possibility of treating diseases that affect organs far beyond the liver itself.

In a new study involving older rats, researchers at the Keck School of Medicine of USC found that an experimental drug called cinaciguat reversed important signs of aging in specialized liver cells. After just two weeks of treatment, levels of amyloid beta, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease, dropped by half. Levels of LDL, commonly called bad cholesterol, also returned to those seen in younger animals.

The findings, published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry, also revealed a previously unknown way that liver cells communicate with one another. This discovery could help scientists develop treatments that restore the liver's ability to remove potentially harmful substances from the blood, possibly reducing the risk of Alzheimer's disease and atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty deposits accumulate inside arteries.

Why the Liver Could Be Important for Alzheimer's

Although Alzheimer's primarily affects the brain, scientists are increasingly interested in how other organs might influence the disease. The liver plays a central role in filtering the blood and removing unwanted compounds, including substances that may contribute to disease when they accumulate.

The USC findings suggest that restoring this natural cleaning process could offer a different approach to preventing certain age-related illnesses. However, the results have so far been demonstrated only in rats, and additional studies are needed to establish whether the same benefits occur in humans.

"We need to do further translational work to see whether our findings might point to new therapies," said corresponding author Laurie DeLeve, MD, PhD, professor and vice chair for scientific affairs in the USC Department of Medicine. "We're hopeful, though, because the findings line up with a lot of epidemiological results showing age as a major risk factor for Alzheimer's and atherosclerosis, and liver damage as a risk factor for Alzheimer's."

Targeting the liver could be particularly valuable in Alzheimer's research, where efforts to develop treatments acting directly in the brain have faced an estimated 98% failure rate in clinical trials. One major obstacle is the blood-brain barrier, a protective system that limits which substances can enter the brain from the bloodstream. While this barrier helps shield the brain from harmful compounds, it also makes delivering certain medications extremely difficult.

"If we're right that the liver is impactful, what do we do about that?" said first author Sam de Leve, MA, a USC lab technician and child of Laurie DeLeve. "Rather than trying to get a drug through the blood-brain barrier, which is obnoxiously difficult, we could direct drugs to the liver, an organ where there might be more therapeutic impact and certainly an easier job of drug delivery."

Scientists Restore the Aging Liver's Natural Filters

To understand how liver aging affects the bloodstream, the researchers focused on a relatively understudied group of cells known as liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs).

These cells form the lining of tiny blood vessels inside the liver. Unlike most blood vessel walls, they contain numerous microscopic openings that function somewhat like the holes in a sieve. These openings allow larger molecules circulating in the blood to reach neighboring cells called hepatocytes, which carry out much of the liver's work processing and removing substances from the body.

As the liver ages, the openings in LSECs gradually become smaller or disappear. This makes it harder for certain large molecules to reach the cells responsible for clearing them, allowing more of these substances to remain in circulation.

One substance affected by this change is amyloid beta. This protein is especially important in Alzheimer's research because it can accumulate in the brain and form plaques, one of the disease's defining features.

Previous observations showed that the liver becomes less effective at removing amyloid beta as it ages. The researchers suspected that the gradual closing of the openings in LSECs might help explain why more of the protein remains in the bloodstream of older animals.

To investigate, they administered cinaciguat to aged rats for two weeks. They then compared the treated animals with two untreated groups, one consisting of older rats and the other of younger rats.

The results were striking. Cinaciguat restored the structure and function of the aging LSECs, reopening their microscopic pores and improving their ability to help clear substances from the blood. Amyloid beta concentrations fell by approximately 50%, reaching levels comparable to those in young rats. The untreated older animals showed no similar improvement.

The researchers also measured low-density lipoproteins (LDL), often referred to as "bad" cholesterol because elevated levels contribute to fatty deposits inside arteries. Over time, these deposits can restrict blood flow and increase the risk of heart disease.

Initially, LDL was included as a comparison measure rather than a substance expected to respond to treatment. Unlike larger molecules, LDL particles are small enough to leave the bloodstream without passing through the microscopic openings in LSECs. The scientists therefore expected cinaciguat to have little or no effect on LDL levels.

Instead, they discovered that LDL concentrations in treated older rats also fell to levels observed in young animals.

"We said, 'Wait, why did that go down? Clearly, there's more to this story,'" Sam de Leve said.

The unexpected finding suggested that the drug was doing more than simply reopening the liver's aging filters. It appeared to be restoring another important aspect of liver function.

Because previous research had shown that hepatocytes function better when LSECs are present, the team began examining how these two types of cells communicate.

Their investigation uncovered a previously unknown sequence of biochemical signals that helps coordinate the liver's ability to remove substances from the bloodstream.

A Hidden Communication Pathway Between Liver Cells

The researchers found that cinaciguat activates an enzyme called soluble guanylate cyclase inside LSECs. This triggers the cells to release a growth factor known as HB-EGF, which sends a signal to nearby hepatocytes.

In response, hepatocytes alter their surfaces in ways that allow them to capture more LDL and amyloid beta from the blood. This helps explain why the treatment reduced both substances, even though they do not rely on the same filtering mechanism.

Normally, aging interferes with the ability of LSECs to release HB-EGF. Cinaciguat restored this signaling process, allowing the liver cells to communicate more effectively and supporting the removal of substances that otherwise tend to accumulate with age.

The discovery identifies a potential new target for future drugs. Rather than focusing exclusively on the physical openings in LSECs, researchers may be able to develop therapies that restore the chemical signals responsible for helping the liver work efficiently.

Could Liver Rejuvenation Help Prevent Alzheimer's and Heart Disease?

According to the researchers, this is the first study to demonstrate that a drug can fully restore the structure and function of aging LSECs, including their ability to support the clearance of substances from the bloodstream.

It is also the first to show that a treatment directed at the liver can bring age-related elevations in circulating amyloid beta and LDL back to youthful levels.

These findings raise the possibility that cinaciguat, similar medications, or treatments targeting HB-EGF could eventually be used to counteract certain effects of liver aging. If those changes translate into meaningful protection against disease, they could provide new strategies for preventing Alzheimer's and cardiovascular problems.

For now, however, the findings represent an early step. Lowering amyloid beta in the bloodstream does not necessarily mean that amyloid plaques in the brain will decrease or that Alzheimer's disease can be prevented.

The researchers plan to continue studying cinaciguat in rats to determine whether its effects on amyloid beta actually translate into measurable protection against Alzheimer's disease.

They also hope the findings will encourage scientists studying other conditions, particularly atherosclerosis, to investigate how restoring liver function might influence disease development.

"We hope that people who are in fields like atherosclerosis research read this, and want to grab the idea for themselves," Sam de Leve said. "There are six different ways someone could go with this, and we can't do them all. So please, scoop us. We'd love it."

Additional researchers involved in the study include Xiangdong Wang, Helia Alavifard and Lily Dara, all affiliated with the Keck School of Medicine of USC.

The research received federal funding from the National Institutes of Health [R56AG071480, 5R01DK100580].

#5738. Google Cloud rolls out Gemini for healthcare

Google Cloud rolls out Gemini for healthcare" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Google launched Tuesday Gemini for healthcare, an agentic artificial intelligence platform aimed at connecting complex clinical, financial and administrative workflows used by healthcare providers and payers.

The platform was developed alongside clinical and health plan leaders and is built to support HIPAA compliance, the tech giant said.

“The fundamental challenge in healthcare isn't a lack of information—it's the immense friction of making that data actionable across a highly regulated ecosystem," said Thomas Kurian, Google Cloud CEO, in a statement. “By working directly alongside our healthcare customers, we've built a platform that resolves chronic bottlenecks so that the industry can put its focus entirely back on human health.”

There are four main components to the “integrated, fully governed” system: skills for healthcare work, connectors to various administrative systems, [an] open healthcare partner ecosystem and a secure, governed platform with open model choice.

It directly integrates with electronic health records (EHRs), billing systems, security and compliance platforms, clinical guidelines and workflows, coding, enterprise productivity platforms and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) datasets.

Gemini for healthcare is available in preview as of Nov. 10. Gemini Enterprise Standard and Gemini Enterprise Plus customers will be able to access the platform, and can choose between per-user subscriptions and pay-as-you-go pricing.

Dozens of companies from all corners of the industry are partnering with Google on the launch, including GoodRx, Epic, IMO Health, Oracle Health, Infinitus, Suki and more.

Infinitus CEO Ankit Jain told Fierce Healthcare the opportunity for healthcare AI is “much bigger than making existing workflows faster or more efficient.”

“It's about fundamentally changing what's possible—enabling healthcare organizations to support more patients, move care forward faster, and deliver at a scale that wasn't possible before,” Jain said. “But that requires AI that can do more than answer questions. It needs to take action, navigate complex systems, and handle the administrative work that too often gets in the way of patients getting care.”

Jain continued, “That's what this partnership with Google Cloud represents. By bringing Infinitus agents into Gemini for healthcare, we're making it easier for healthcare teams to put AI to work on the processes that connect patients to care. It's another step toward a future where more people get the care they need, without the complexity of the healthcare system standing in their way.”

Several major health systems have also teamed up with Google for the launch, including HCA Healthcare and Northwell Health. Other organizations include Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts, the American Society of Clinical Oncology and Highmark Health.

“Making it easier for physicians to access and understand a patient’s medical history helps them spend less time gathering information and more time focused on patient care,” said Michael Schlosser, M.D., HCA Healthcare EVP and chief clinical officer, in a statement. “Through our work with Google Cloud, we’re exploring how Gemini can interpret and synthesize complex patient information from multiple electronic health record systems and care settings, connecting data from different sources to give clinicians a more complete and cohesive understanding of a patient’s medical history.”

#5737. Senators Investigate Whether RFK Jr. Lied to Congress About Samoa Trip

— HHS has maintained that the Samoa visit "was unrelated to vaccines"

Two Democratic senators are launching an investigation into whether Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. lied to Congress about his reason for a 2019 trip to Samoa after the Associated Press and the Guardian published documents in August refuting his testimony.

The new inquiry is one of a vast array of investigations planned into the Trump administration after Democrats regained control of the House and Senate from Republicans in the midterm elections.

Sens. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) said in a letter Wednesday to Children's Health Defense (CHD), a nonprofit group known for anti-vaccine activism that was formerly chaired by Kennedy, that they were starting an investigation.

The lawmakers asked the group for a broad range of documents related to Kennedy's Samoa travel, his 2024 presidential campaign, and his Senate confirmation process. The letter also requested all communications between the group and federal government officials since President Donald Trump's second term began in January 2025.

AP and Guardian reporting in August showed that while Kennedy repeatedly told lawmakers who held the key to his confirmation last year that his visit to Samoa before a deadly measles outbreak had "nothing to do with vaccines," a letter he sent to the Samoan prime minister ahead of the trip on CHD letterhead showed otherwise. In the letter, Kennedy used the words vaccine or vaccination eight times.

"We intend to hold Secretary Kennedy accountable for the grave harm he has caused to vulnerable children," Wyden and Alsobrooks wrote in their letter. "We also intend to hold him accountable for any false statements made to Congress, a crime that undermines the Senate's ability to fulfill its constitutional duties."

HHS has maintained that the Samoa visit "was unrelated to vaccines." In response to an AP inquiry in August, it said "any claim or insinuation based on these letters that Secretary Kennedy lied under oath or to Congress is not only false but outright defamatory."

Kennedy was not under oath during his confirmation hearing. Knowingly giving material false testimony to Congress is a crime that carries a possible prison sentence regardless of whether a person is under oath, though it is rarely prosecuted.

Wyden is expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee, which has oversight into Kennedy's health department, when Democrats retake Congress in January. Alsobrooks serves on the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which also oversees the department.

The same senators on Wednesday announced a separate investigation into hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of gifts reportedly given last year to Kennedy by a donor and former employee.
