#5638. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns following affairs scandal

Nvidia Corp.’s board of directors today announced the resignation of Jensen Huang, now former chief executive and president of the artificial intelligence chipmaker, amid a scandal, naming Colette Kress, current executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO.

The news arrives following numerous industry reports that the board intended to replace Huang as CEO after revelations of a second extramarital relationship with an executive at Nvidia, coming mere days after he admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

News initially broke over the weekend that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, no relation, an executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed International Pte. Ltd. and an alleged Chinese spy. The Information reported on Tuesday that Alice Huang facilitated $7.5 billion in chip sales to China. According to another report, Jensen Huang also had a relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, who serves as vice president of healthcare.

The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities concluded Alice Huang acted as a Chinese intelligence asset. Upon revelations of the affair, the Associated Press reported that President Trump announced that the Federal Bureau of Investigation was looking into the allegations, while adding, “I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

Late Wednesday, the Nvidia board met to decide whether to oust Huang and discussed a potential replacement as CEO. Huang has no obvious single successor and owns about 3.6% of Nvidia’s stock. Reportedly, the board sought counsel from an outside firm to find someone to fill the role.

With the announcement, Nvidia stock was falling more than 5% in trading today, backing off an even steeper loss at the opening. Yahoo Finance calculated that Nvidia has lost more than $600 billion in market value since the previous Thursday, likely with more shocks to come.

“Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Kress. “We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead.”

Kress has served as executive vice president and CFO since joining in September 2013. Her accolades include leading the company’s finance organization and working to build the company’s dominance in the AI chip industry. Before joining Nvidia, she spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco Systems Inc. and Microsoft Corp.

The CFO was intimately involved with Nvidia’s widespread financing of AI compute providers, in particular its backing of not only AI leaders OpenAI Group PBC and Anthropic PBC — the latter set to go public as early as next week — but also neoclouds such as CoreWeave Inc. and Nebius Group NV. Those financings have been criticized by some as “circular,” meaning Nvidia essentially invested in customers so they could use the money to buy more of its graphics processing units.

The potential successors to Huang, who had 30 direct reports, include no one obvious choice and a succession plan apparently was not in place. Candidates that some have speculated about include Arm Ltd. CEO Rene Haas, who worked at Nvidia years ago, Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, and Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing and creator of its CUDA software considered the real moat for its business.

“The sudden resignation of Jensen Huang is about more than succession at the world’s most important AI chipmaker,” Forrester Vice President and Group Research Director Stephanie Balaouras told SiliconANGLE in an email. “Nvidia’s leadership crisis is a stress test for the AI boom. If Nvidia stabilizes quickly under new leadership, the AI infrastructure boom will have demonstrated resilience. If its stock, financing relationships or ecosystem commitments remain under sustained pressure, that would add evidence to the fragile side of the AI bubble ledger.””

Balaouras added that “tech leaders shouldn’t overreact, but they should treat Nvidia’s CEO transition as a prompt to reassess concentration risk across their AI infrastructure, suppliers and investment plans.”

Huang is best known for co-founding Nvidia in 1993 in a San Jose Denny’s and has served as its CEO since. His departure will likely send further ripples through the AI silicon and software industry. He has been deeply involved in Nvidia’s product strategy and built longstanding customer relationships, helming the company as it became the behemoth it is today.

Nvidia commands roughly 80% of the data-center AI chip market, although industry estimates vary by methodology. Epoch Artificial Intelligence Inc. puts its share of AI computing power shipped at 63% in the second quarter of 2026. Other market carve-outs include custom chips built by cloud companies within the broader supply, including Google LLC’s tensor processing units at 25%, Amazon Inc.’s custom silicon at 5% and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.’s AI hardware accelerators at 4%.

Nvidia is expected to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings on Nov. 17.

#5637. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5636. Hurricane Season Is Over Early, but El Niño Is Not Done With Us Yet

In a typical year, the Atlantic hurricane season runs from June to the end of November. But 2026 has been anything but a typical year.

In fact, the meteorologists at AccuWeather have announced that tropical activity for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season is over, three weeks before the official end of the season on Nov. 30.

"El Niño has played a significant role in limiting tropical activity across the Atlantic," said AccuWeather lead hurricane expert Alex DaSilva.

"While tropical storms can still develop this late in the season, the weather patterns we're seeing give us confidence that the United States will avoid additional direct tropical impacts this year. It's an unusually quiet conclusion to a season that defied expectations and broke a 121-year-old hurricane record.”

But while the hurricane season might be bowing out early, the country still needs to prepare itself for the coming winter months in a big way.

AccuWeather originally forecasted 11 to 16 named storms for the season last spring, but once El Niño arrived and strengthened much earlier in the year than usual, the forecast dropped to eight to 11 named storms and three to four hurricanes.

To date, only 10 named storms came to fruition, the fewest since 2014, when there were only eight storms. Only one reached hurricane status, with Hurricane Isaias making a destructive Category 2 landfall on the Florida Panhandle in October.

It was the first time since 1925 that there was only one hurricane in the entire season.

That’s not to say that the season wasn’t destructive. The first storm of the season, Tropical Storm Arthur, dumped more than 20 inches of rain in some spots across the Gulf in June and caused an estimated $4 billion to $6 billion in total damage and economic loss, according to a preliminary estimate from experts at AccuWeather.

While the hurricane season is over, homeowners across the country still have to continue with a deluge of wet weather on the way.

Again, all thanks to the Super El Niño still churning away.

Notably, the El Niño could influence winter weather across the United States, bringing warmer-than-average temperatures to Northern states and wetter-than-average conditions to the South and East Coast, according to NOAA’s U.S. Winter Outlook.

Wetter-than-average conditions are most likely across the southern tier, from the Southwest to the Southeast, and along the East Coast. But if the temperatures stay up, the likelihood of snow is slim.

But even without the snow, the storms could be significant for this area this year.

“As we know from decades of observations, a very strong El Nino will likely bring a southward and eastward shift to the jet stream for the contiguous U.S., which tilts the odds toward stormier weather across the South,” said Ken Graham, director of NOAA’s National Weather Service.

“While higher chances of rain and snow may bring relief to drought-afflicted areas, too much precipitation on dry soil can fuel destructive flash floods and mudslides. Now is the time for communities and individuals to plan ahead for the upcoming winter.”

Meanwhile, more snow than average is favored across parts of the Intermountain West, the Plains, and the Appalachians this winter because of El Niño's active storm track, according to The Wall Street Journal.

In fact, most models that were reviewed showed above-average snowfall across the Plains, from South Dakota to northern Texas, and a swath of the central and southern Appalachians.

#5635. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

#5634. How Agents Can Chart a Course for No Buyer Remorse

The bidding war is over. Some of the decisions made are harder to undo. As an agent or broker, is it part of your professional obligation to discuss where the buyer might be in five years financially and family-wise? Probably, even if it might occasionally put them off a purchase.

A recent survey of 1,000 U.S. property owners found that 80% had at least one regret about their home, location or buying experience. Location bothered 45%, while 58% reported regrets about the home or homeownership itself.

For homeowners who bought during the pandemic frenzy, moving on can carry an added complication: the mortgage may be more attractive than the house.

A recent study in the Journal of Banking & Finance found that for every percentage-point increase between a homeowner’s fixed mortgage rate and current market rates, the probability of selling falls 18.1%. Researchers estimate mortgage lock-in was associated with 1.72 million fewer home sales between Q2 2022 and Q2 2024.

That pressure is particularly relevant now. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached 7.28% in early October, its highest level in nearly three years.

For Nick Nastos, a real estate broker and founder of Chicago’s Property Shop, that creates an unusual form of buyer’s remorse.

“You can regret the house and still have a mortgage you’d hate to give up,” he says. “That’s what makes these decisions difficult. Someone may know the home no longer fits their life, but replacing a 3% mortgage with today’s rate can completely change the math.”

Nastos gives five reasons a pandemic purchase may feel different now.

Nastos says regret alone should not determine whether someone sells.

“Start with what you would change about the house, then price out what changing homes would actually cost,” he says. “Sometimes the answer is to move. Sometimes that low mortgage makes improving the home you already own the better option.”

Suzy Minken, a real estate advisor with Compass working out of Northern Virginia, said looking toward the future while purchasing a house today is key to avoiding buyer remorse.

“It’s not something that is talked about enough,” she says. “I’ve even had buyers speak to my architect (relationships are key) while touring the house to see if they could do an addition. The architect did a review of the property and said it could be done. The buyers submitted an offer (multiple bid situation) and bought the house. They proceeded with a two-story addition before they moved into the house.”

Minken stresses that there is a need to distinguish between buyer’s remorse and the frustration of having fewer options than originally anticipated.

“Consider the young family who purchased a starter home with the intention of moving to a larger home in five years,” she explains. “Perhaps they’ve welcomed another child and need an additional bedroom. But with higher home prices and mortgage rates, the move-up home they envisioned may no longer be financially practical.

“In many ways, today’s move-up buyer has become today’s renovation buyer. Rather than moving to a larger home, homeowners are looking for ways to make their existing homes accommodate their changing needs.”

But what happens when renovation isn’t an option either?

“When buyers fall in love with a home, I encourage them to think about whether it’s already ‘maxed out’ or has room to grow with their changing needs,” says Minken. “Is there room to expand? Could an unfinished basement become additional living space? Is there flexibility in the floor plan to accommodate a growing family?

“I also encourage buyers to look beyond the house itself. Why are the current owners selling? Did they outgrow the home after having another child? Is there something about the layout or the property that made adapting it difficult? These questions can reveal important clues about how a home might serve its next owners.”

Minken encourages buyers to think beyond what they need today and consider how their needs might change over time. That includes family circumstances, the need for additional space and even commuting considerations if their employer requires them to spend more time in the office.

“We can’t predict changes in interest rates, home prices or family circumstances,” she says. “But we can ask the right questions before they make one of the largest financial decisions of their lives. Sometimes the regret isn’t buying the wrong home. It’s discovering that the next step, whether moving to a bigger house or renovating, is no longer within reach.”

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5633. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

#5632. Low Rates or Lots of Leverage? Buyers Rarely Get Both.

If you’ve been watching mortgage rates lately, you might feel a little stuck. Rates climbed above 7% this year, and a lot of buyers have decided to sit tight and wait for them to come back down.

But rates are only half the story. When you buy a home, you usually get one of two things: low rates or negotiating power. It’s rare to get both at the same time. And right now, you have a lot more of that second one than you might think.

Think back to 2020 and 2021. Rates were near 3%, and buyers rushed into the housing market. Those low rates sounded great, but they came with a catch. There were a lot of buyers just like you that you had to compete with – and there weren’t enough homes for sale to meet that demand.

That’s why homes got multiple offers, buyers paid over asking or waived inspections, and sellers held all the cards. Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com, shows just how one-sided things got:

“Seller’s markets peaked at 98 of 100 metros in spring 2022 after two years of mortgage rates near 3%.”

Then, in the second half of 2022, rates went up. As a result, the number of people buying homes went down, inventory grew, and the balance slowly started tipping from sellers back to buyers. Fast forward to today, and that flip is officially here.

In a recent report, Realtor.com found about two-thirds (66) of the top 100 metros now lean in favor of buyers (see graph below):

And while you may want lower rates, this shift in power has its own perks.

There are more homes for sale than there have been in years. And in a more buyer-friendly market like that, it means sellers have to work harder to get their homes sold. As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Higher inventory and lengthening days on market give buyers improved negotiating power.”

That shows up in the deals buyers are getting. According to Redfin, nearly half of buyers now get some kind of concession from the seller – like help with closing costs, money for repairs, or even the seller paying to buy down your mortgage rate (see graph below):

So when you find a home you love, even if the rate isn’t what you necessarily wanted, there are other levers to pull. Ask about a price cut or a seller-paid rate buydown, too. It could take some of the sting out of today’s rates.

And just in case you’re still thinking you’ll just hold off until rates drop, here’s what you should know. Experts at Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo don’t expect rates to fall much through 2027 (see graph below):

And here’s the whole point. Even if rates did drop in a big way, a lot of buyers would rush back in. More competition means fewer deals, fewer concessions, and sellers getting the upper hand again.

So waiting comes with a trade-off. You might land a better rate down the road, but you’d probably give up the bargaining power you have today.

That doesn’t mean you have to move right now. You should only buy when the numbers work for you. But if you’ve got a real reason to move, today’s leverage could help make your numbers work – even at today’s rates.

Buyers rarely get low rates and strong negotiating power at the same time, and today’s market is handing you the leverage. Connect with a local real estate agent to find homes where sellers may be open to covering a rate buydown or closing costs, so you can see if today’s market can work for your budget.

It’s also the fourth-highest residence to be sold in the mountain town, beating out a number of single-family homes.

"Add the views, proximity to downtown restaurants, the private elevator, and a true lock-and-leave setup. The buyers recognized it as a one-of-a-kind opportunity."

#5629. Today's Market Could Be a Win for Veterans Looking To Buy a Home

If you’re a veteran or active-duty service member who’s been hoping to buy a home, you may have more going for you in today’s housing market than you realize.

VA home loans already come with some pretty powerful benefits. But now, with more homes for sale and buyers having more room to negotiate in many markets, those benefits could go even further.

And if you’ve ever heard that buying with a VA loan is harder, takes longer, or puts you at a disadvantage, there’s something else you should know… a lot of what people believe about VA loans simply isn’t true.

Today, nearly 4 million service members and veterans have an active VA home loan. And according to the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), more than 343,000 homes were purchased using VA loan benefits in its most recent reported fiscal year. And it’s easy to see why.

For eligible veterans and service members, VA loans offer advantages that can make buying a home more affordable, including:

No down payment required for many eligible borrowers.

No monthly mortgage insurance, even with no down payment.

Competitive mortgage rates that can help lower monthly payments.

Benefits like this are powerful in any market – and even more so today. That may be why VA loan usage has grown for the last two years in a row.

A few years ago, when homes were getting multiple offers and buyers were competing for nearly every listing, VA buyers sometimes had a harder time getting their offers accepted.

A 2021 survey from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), found 89% of sellers were likely to accept an offer from a buyer using a conventional loan. But only 30% were likely to accept one using an FHA or VA loan.

The reason? Some sellers were concerned that VA financing would take longer, be more difficult to close, and require them to pay more in costs and repairs. But those concerns don’t necessarily reflect how VA loans actually perform.

A white paper from Vetted VA based on 2025 mortgage data busted a lot of VA loan myths:

Myth #1: VA loans get denied more often than other loans.

The Reality: VA loans actually have the lowest denial rate. Just 8.2% of VA purchase applications were denied, compared to 15.0% for conventional loans, 12.8% for FHA loans, and 12.5% for USDA loans.

The Reality: 90% of VA home loan applications that reached underwriting made it to closing, compared to 81% for conventional loans.

The Reality: VA loan appraisals typically take 7–10 business days, similar to conventional and FHA loans.

Myth #4: Sellers have to pay all the closing costs for VA buyers.

The Reality: VA buyers can pay many standard closing costs themselves. Buyers and sellers can also negotiate which eligible costs the seller will cover.

Since there are more homes for sale and fewer buyers competing in many areas, sellers may be more open to different financing options than they were a few years ago. And the opportunity doesn’t stop at getting your offer accepted.

Depending on the house and your local market, you may also be able to negotiate a lower price, ask for repairs, or request help with closing costs.

VA guidelines allow sellers to cover the buyer’s normal closing costs, plus concessions of up to 4% of the home’s value.

Think about what that combination could mean. You may be able to buy with no down payment, avoid mortgage insurance, and negotiate help with some of the other expenses that come with buying a home.

That could mean keeping thousands of dollars in your savings instead of spending them upfront, giving you more breathing room after you get the keys.

#5628. Computer vision startup Tristar AI pulls in $12.4M to automate quality control for manufacturers

All too often, manufacturing defects seem to slip past human eyes, with the result that high-speed production lines turn into expensive scrapheaps. Computer vision startup Tristar AI Inc. has just raised $12.4 million in early-stage funding in order to try to put an end to these costly mistakes.

Today’s Series A round was led by Isogon Ventures and saw participation from Blackhorn Ventures, Ford Street Ventures, NextView Ventures, TenOneTen and Capgemini’s ISAI Cap Venture Fund.

Tristar AI is gearing up to transform quality assurance in manufacturing at a critical moment for the industry. Manufacturers have found themselves squeezed by a combination of rising raw material costs and growing labor shortages, and these problems have been made even more acute by the U.S. government’s insistence on bringing more manufacturing back home.

According to data from the Capgemini Research Institute, 48% of U.S. companies have invested in reshoring projects this year. But 83% say they’re worried about the lack of skilled industrial workers needed to fulfill those initiatives.

One of the major challenges for manufacturers is that they’re still encumbered by inefficient inspection protocols that rely on either manual checks, or in a best-case scenario, rigid, rule-based machine vision systems. Quality control is essential for any manufacturing operation, but the inefficiency of these protocols makes it a significant roadblock too.

It forces companies to take skilled workers off production lines and sometimes even bring their entire operations screeching to a halt. Yet there are many occasions where they still miss subtle flaws in their products, resulting in wasted materials, downtime, missed deadlines and sometimes even very expensive customer claims.

Founder and Chief Executive Salem Karani is all too familiar with the inefficiency of manual inspection. He told SiliconANGLE that while growing up, he would often accompany his father to his family’s plastic film manufacturing plant in Houston, turning up at all hours of the day and night in order to troubleshoot production issues that could spring up at any moment. Because the company’s margins were so tight, any period of extended downtime could threaten its profitability, so he would spend hours with his dad frantically troubleshooting line errors.

It was this experience that ultimately inspired Karani, who studied computer vision at Harvard and MIT, to develop an automated quality inspection system that can operate continuously without slowing down production. “The problem was never that people didn’t care about quality,” Karani said. “It’s that people catch problems after the fact, once they’ve already cost time, materials and customers. Tristar gives every production line a live record so teams can act when it matters most.”

Computer vision in manufacturing operations is not a new concept, but where Tristar differs is through its use of more sophisticated artificial intelligence models that can adapt to changing conditions, materials and defect types. The startup’s platform looks at machine telemetry, the quality of the products coming off the line and the activity of human operators, allowing it to uncover issues the moment they emerge and immediately understand where the problem is, and why it occurred.

Best of all, the system can integrate with factories’ existing systems, such as cameras, sensors, programmable logic controllers, enterprise resource planning systems and so on That enables them to get up and running without an expensive overhaul.

Isagon Ventures General Partner Paco Riberas said he’s backing Tristar because manufacturers are losing far too much money to avoidable defects. “In today’s industry, precision isn’t optional, and Tristar makes it possible,” he said. “Its AI vision catches defects in real time, directly on existing production lines. Salem and his team are building the quality standard for modern manufacturing.”

Tristar’s early traction has been encouraging. Its system already monitors more than 500 production lines across North America and Europe.

Customers include global packaging giants such as Amcor, DuPont and Klöckner Pentaplast, and also some of the biggest suppliers to automakers such as Toyota, Honda and Mercedes, Karani said. Those customers report defect detection accuracy rates of between 95% and 99%, and say the platform pays for itself in an average of just four months.

Karani said the goal now is to expand Tristar’s platform into new manufacturing sectors and enhance the capabilities of its computer vision AI to try and improve its accuracy even further. Ultimately, he sees the company as the operational system of record for factory floors, giving manufacturers more visibility into everything about their production operations, from the raw materials to the finished product.

“Physical AI will play a critical role in the future of manufacturing,” said Capgemini Ventures’ Matthieu Eyriès. “Tristar combines advanced AI capabilities with a strong understanding of industrial environments, addressing concrete manufacturing challenges with measurable impact.”

#5627. The Housing Market Is on Solid Ground, Even with More Foreclosures

It’s been nearly two decades since the 2008 housing crash, but the word “foreclosure” can still make people uneasy. And if you’re planning a move, you may be wondering if more foreclosures will flood the market with homes for sale – especially if you’ve seen the headlines lately.

Buyers may be hoping for a rush of bargains. Sellers may be bracing for more competition. The latest data points to neither, and knowing why can help you plan your next move with confidence.

Completed foreclosures are up 33% from last year, according to ATTOM. That sounds like a big leap, but context helps.

Even with that increase, foreclosures are still about 26% below where they were in the first half of 2020.

Zoom out further, and today’s activity is a small fraction of what the market saw during the 2008 crash. Lenders completed about 28,000 foreclosures in the first half of 2026, according to ATTOM. Compare that to the crash years in red, when lenders often completed more than 200,000 in the span of a few months (see graph below):

Experts say today’s numbers reflect a housing market that’s still in good shape. As Rob Barber, CEO at ATTOM, explains:

“While some homeowners are still facing financial challenges, overall foreclosure volumes remain well below historical norms and the broader housing market continues to demonstrate resilience.”

And here’s why we can absorb the slight uptick in foreclosures we are seeing.

During the crash, a lot of homeowners either lost their homes to foreclosure or were forced to sell, which left the market overwhelmed with houses for sale. That isn’t happening now.

One way to see this is through months’ supply, which measures how long it would take to sell every home on the market at the current pace. Four to six months is considered balanced.

Right now, it’s about 4.8 months, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). That’s pretty well-balanced, and less than half of where it peaked around the last crash (see graph below):

If foreclosures were really surging, you’d see it in the number of homes for sale. As Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . a surge of actual foreclosures in 2026 would have easily put the inventory data much higher in 2026.”

Equity is a big reason there’s no surge of distressed sales. Data from the Census Bureau and ATTOM shows nearly two in three homeowners have paid off their mortgage or have more than 50% equity. And Cotality says the average homeowner has about $310,000 in equity.

If a homeowner with equity hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house, pay off the loan, and walk away with money in their pocket instead of facing foreclosure. That’s an option many people didn’t have during the crash. According to HousingWire, nearly one in four homes were underwater back in 2010.

Being underwater means owing more on your mortgage than your home is worth, which makes selling a lot harder. Today, just 2% of homeowners are considered seriously underwater (see graph below):

Not every homeowner has that kind of equity, but most do, and that’s what puts a ceiling on how high foreclosures can go.

If rising foreclosures have you questioning where the housing market is headed, the data says it’s in good shape. The supply of homes for sale is balanced, and most homeowners have plenty of equity.Have questions about what you’re seeing online, your local market, or about how much equity you have? #5626. Kylie Jenner Faces Fourth Household Staff Lawsuit—Former Housekeeper Alleges Dog Bite, Being Trapped in Closet

Kylie Jenner's former housekeeper is suing the beauty mogul, claiming that she was trapped inside Jenner's closet, bitten by her dog, and pepper-sprayed in the face.

The lawsuit, which is the fourth filed by a member of Jenner's household staff since April, was brought by Dinora Cabria Amaya, who began working for the reality TV star in March 2025.

In the 20-page filing, which was obtained by The Rolling Stone, Amaya claimed that she was denied overtime and experienced a hostile work environment.

She also claimed that she suffered workplace injuries, including being hit with pepper spray, which allegedly caused “severe burning and vision problems.”

According to the lawsuit, she messaged her manager, “Sorry to interrupt you, I had an accident at work, someone left pepper spray and took off safety." The manager then allegedly replied, "Thanks for letting us know."

They then requested that the housekeeper fill out a report and provide it to Jenner's security before seeing a healthcare professional.

She then claimed she experienced “significant eye pain, blurred vision, headaches, burning, irritation, and sensitivity," but received no accommodations due to pain.

“The more plaintiff complained that she was hurt, the harder defendants made her job,” the lawsuit claimed.

Amaya then claimed that she was often "confined in a room because defendant Jenner did not want to see her” and that her “repeated reports of ongoing pain” were not regarded with importance.

In one alleged incident, she described using a passcode to enter the TV personality's closet, only to became locked inside and suffer a panic attack.

“No one is at the house that can let you out, and I cannot give the password to anyone else; you just have to wait,” the housekeeper's manager allegedly replied when Amaya told her she was locked inside.

Amaya claimed that her manager "mocked her" during their call.

The housekeeper then recalled the alleged incident that saw Jenner's dog biting her while she was cleaning the doghouse.

“Again, no meaningful assistance was provided. Plaintiff purchased over-the-counter medication and treated the injury herself. She continued reporting that her eyes hurt, her arm and wrist hurt from the dog bite, and her back hurt from the increasingly physical work," the filing states.

Amaya was fired on Feb. 6, 2026, after requesting mileage reimbursement for her trips to Jenner's homes.

Jenner owns multiple homes in the Los Angeles metropolitan area and a property outside of Palm Springs.

The housekeeper is now claiming that she was fired because she spoke up about her treatment.

The filing names the beauty mogul, her company Kylie Jenner Inc., staff supervisors Laura Dooley and Itzel Sibrian, Tri Star Services, and La Maison Family Services.

The lawsuit claims wrongful termination, false imprisonment, disability discrimination, failure to provide reasonable accommodations, whistleblower retaliation, failure to prevent discrimination and retaliation, and intentional infliction of emotional distress.

Amaya is seeking unpaid wages, past and future monetary earnings, and damages. The housekeeper is being represented by lawyer Della Shaker.

Amaya earned $40 an hour working for Jenner—$23 more than the state's minimum wage. Amaya worked six days a week.

Jenner’s lawyer, Michael Rhodes, noted that Shaker is the same lawyer representing the other members of Jenner's staff who sued earlier this year.

“It’s clear that this lawyer wants to use publicity to try to extract an unwarranted payday. We’re not going to be intimidated into doing that. As such, we’ll defend these meritless cases vigorously and look forward to telling our side of the story," Rhodes told The Rolling Stone.

In response, Shaker told the outlet, “For employees working in high-profile households, the fear of losing future employment opportunities can be overwhelming. When your livelihood depends on discretion, references, and powerful professional relationships, speaking out can feel impossible. But no employer has the right to retaliate against workers for protected complaints. The truth should never be buried behind wealth, fear, or silence.”

Amaya's lawsuit comes after former housekeepers Angelica Hernandez Vasquez and Juana Delgado Soto also filed suits against Jenner, also alleging mistreatment and whistleblower retaliation.

#5625. Amanda Seyfried Reveals What It Was Like To Be in Elizabeth Holmes’ Texas Home While the Theranos Founder Was in Prison

This article contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything.”

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary “You Can See Everything” gives viewers an unprecedented look into the home life of Elizabeth Holmes.

The disgraced Theranos founder invited the filmmakers to document the 34 days before she reported to the Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, TX, on May 30, 2023. Two years later, the A24 production team would pick up cameras again, joining Holmes’ partner, Billy Evans, and the couple’s two young children at their home in Austin, TX.

In a surprise twist to viewers, Amanda Seyfried, who portrayed Holmes in the Hulu miniseries “The Dropout,” becomes an important part of the narrative in the second half of the documentary.

The actress opened up about the experience in a Rolling Stone interview with Fielder and Oppenheim, and described what it was really like to enter the family’s Texas home while Holmes was away in prison.

Seyfried—who had been shown footage Fielder and Oppenheim captured in the days leading up to Holmes reporting to prison—explained that she had some preconceived notions about Evans.

She chose to put those feelings aside before visiting the home—a four-bedroom, three-bathroom luxury residence that’s currently on the market for $2.25 million with Amy Deane of Moreland Properties.

“I wanted to turn my disdain off a little bit, because I’m in his house now with his children—with their children,” she emphasized. “I always want to give people the benefit of the doubt, and I felt bad that I had talked a bunch of sh-t about him up until that point.”

The “Mamma Mia!” star noted that although she didn’t particularly “like” Evans, she was careful with her words because she was “coming into this man’s house.”

She explained that “trying to engage with Billy” was “going fine” until he received an unexpected call from Holmes.

“That was just ... what an experience for somebody to have, to say the least,” she reflected, adding that everything she felt was plainly visible on her face in that scene.

“We didn’t know she was gonna call right then. I am sitting there with her children and cuddling with her dog! While she’s in prison!” the star recalled.

Later, the documentary would show Fielder, Seyfried, and Evans having dinner together—a moment that grew tense quickly, due to a stark difference in political opinions between Seyfried and Evans.

“I don’t want to provoke him, but at this point, it’s kind of like, the gloves are off,” she recalled. “I was in the frame of mind where I’m like, ‘OK, this guy is disrespectful, and I’m here in his home, I’m gonna argue this because I actually have a pretty solid stance on things.’”

Seyfried revealed that the dynamic was difficult to balance, as she was torn between being “protective” of herself and “trying to set the record straight,” but she was also hoping to maintain “some kind of rapport” with Evans, so filming could resume in the home without the entire production crew getting kicked out.

The documentary eventually leverages Seyfried’s acting skills—and unique knowledge of the source material—to create a series of reenactments to key the audience into moments that happened before cameras picked up.

These reenactments would take Seyfried and the crew to the ultraprivate Del Mar, CA, beach home Holmes had rented in the weeks leading up to her prison stay.

In the Rolling Stone interview, Fielder remarked that Seyfried had been very “curious” about the objects that were found on the re-creation sets, and wanted to learn which items were placed by the production design team and which had existed in the home when Holmes lived there two years earlier.

“I was just grasping at anything that could ground me back into this world, because it had been so long, and I think I was also experiencing some kind of weird, like, meta-vortex, because I had just seen Elizabeth Holmes in this house, and the house is so specific,” Seyfried explained.

The four-bedroom, four-bathroom home certainly is specific, and became an instantly recognizable location from the moment the “You Can See Everything” trailer dropped. It’s one of just about a dozen residences in the ultraexclusive community called Sandy Lane, about a half-hour from San Diego.

The single-story home was built in 1948 and includes direct access to a private beach. It features tall ceilings, exposed beams, and sizable windows that connect the moody space to its serene surroundings.

The actress said it was “just crazy” to be in the “same place” she had seen Holmes in, through footage Fielder and his team had previously captured.

“Nobody had been in Holmes and Evans’ beach house for two years, or whatever,” she said. “And suddenly, it’s like I’ve time-traveled two years into the past.”

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5624. What’s Next for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac After the Midterm Elections

President Donald Trump has suggested that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac's government conservatorship should end. But whether that will happen under his administration remains unclear after the midterms.

Since the federal bailout in 2008, Fannie and Freddie have remained under conservatorship for 18 years, with the terms subjecting them to strict oversight and regulation by the Federal Housing Finance Agency.

For years, the U.S. Treasury has collected nearly all profits from the two entities, an amount surpassing $300 billion and exceeding the government's outlay in the bailout. Trump has floated the idea of ending the conservatorship since his first term in office, an idea that regained attention when he returned to the White House in 2025.

Trump suggested this could mean an initial public offering of the two mortgage giants, with both companies valued at up to $1 trillion combined and selling between 5% and 15% of their stock.

Key Democrats have expressed reservations about privatizing Fannie and Freddie or otherwise ending the conservatorship, raising questions about whether the Trump administration will pursue the matter with Democrats in control of Congress.

Trump has said little about the matter in recent months. Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, who has long pushed for an end to conservatorship, believes that the Trump administration wanted to wait until after the midterms to take action.

“The reason why it’s not being touched right now is, you know, midterms,” he told CNBC on Election Day.

Before the election, a senior Trump administration official said the end of conservatorship for Fannie and Freddie could still be on. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested the government could take up the matter again in 2027 or 2028.

U.S. Federal Housing Finance Agency Director William Pulte supported the idea this spring. He said that changes to their credit scoring requirements introduced this year could increase the chances of success. But only Trump knew the timing, he said.

“We stand ready every day to execute the president’s vision, and if and when he decides he wants to do something, we are locked and loaded and ready to go," Pulte said.

But starting in January, the Trump administration may face stiff opposition in Congress to privatizing Fannie and Freddie, a move that many economists have warned could put upward pressure on mortgage rates.

Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA), who's running to chair the House Financial Services Committee, has consistently opposed administrative efforts by regulators to rapidly release Fannie and Freddie from conservatorship without comprehensive congressional oversight, public transparency, and safeguards for affordable housing and racial equity.

"To address the affordable housing crisis, Congress must ensure that Fannie and Freddie meet their mission to provide liquidity, sustainability, and affordability to all housing markets in the U.S., and at all times," Waters said at a hearing in April.

Legal and political analysts are divided on whether the executive branch could end the conservatorship by fiat, but such a push would almost certainly face stiff opposition from Democrats in Congress.

The White House didn't respond to a Realtor.com® request for comment about the future of the conservatorship. Waters also didn't respond.

Even as he discussed the end of conservatorship, Trump used Fannie and Freddie as tools to try to help improve affordability in the market. That meant directing them to purchase $200 billion in mortgage-backed securities in an effort to improve the housing market.

Trump's former Federal Housing Commissioner Frank Cassidy told Realtor.com that privatization is a lever Trump could pull without his party controlling Congress. But it needs to be structured in a way that benefits the market. One worry is that the lack of government backing would drive up mortgage rates.

"It hasn't been a priority yet. It would need to be worked on very quickly because it will take some time," Cassidy said. "How do you structure it in a way that makes it more favorable? The idea under conservatorship is implicitly a government guarantee."

In the meantime, the Mortgage Brokers of America reiterated that a positive outcome is still possible.

"MBA continues to believe that GSE release must preserve what works to ensure that it continues to deliver what consumers need and investors expect," it said. "And importantly, any release must include an explicit federal backstop—passed by Congress and paid for by the GSEs—of their mortgage-backed securities to protect consumers, taxpayers, and our best-in-the-world housing finance system."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5623. EXCLUSIVE: Olympic Champion Tara Lipinski Shares Her ‘Controversial’ Christmas Decorating Rule—and Why She’s Starting Now

Olympic figure skating champion Tara Lipinski is picking sides in some of the most divisive holiday decor debates of all time as she hosts HGTV’s "Big Bargain Holiday Showdown."

The 44-year-old Lipinski, who earned gold in the 1998 Winter Games, reveals her holiday decor rules to Realtor.com® ahead of the Nov. 10 premiere of the new six-episode competition series.

She covers everything from when it's appropriate to start decorating to when decorations should be removed, and whether Christmas lights are better in multicolor or monotone.

On the show, two teams of family, friends, and neighbors go head-to-head in a holiday-themed design battle where they have just 48 hours and $500 to overhaul one room in their respective homes.

DIY experts Ashley Dixon and Clinton Tharp are on hand to help wrap things up before designers Stephen Brown and Pelar Fullilove judge the spaces and declare the winner of a $2,000 cash prize.

"I know it's very controversial, but I am starting to decorate this week. I am skipping Thanksgiving," Lipinski, who stays in her lane as a neutral host on the HGTV show, tells Realtor.com.

"The older I get, the wider the window has become. I really don't think it can be too early. It's just so fun to walk into your house when it's full of Christmas lights and so cozy and idyllic and warm. ... I like to stretch it as much as I can. That’s why in November, you have a ton of time, you can just relish in it."

Lipinski clarifies that, although she'll set her table to host Thanksgiving, it's jingle all the way until the start of the New Year.

"I always used to take it down right away. I do get a little tired of it when holidays are actually over, so I feel like you've got, like, one week after and then you've got to zip it up," she says.

In Lipinski’s house, which she shares with husband Todd Kapostasy and their 3-year-old daughter, Georgie, the holiday magic is spread in multiple spaces.

"We usually go [for] a more traditional Christmas, the classic, the red, the green," she shares. "Other rooms, we change it up. We do our bedroom a whole winter wonderland, white and gold and silver. And then Georgie, my daughter's room, we do a really fun pink Christmas so we can branch out.

"I feel like it's evolved throughout the years, and there's always adding and subtracting."

There is only one thing that never changes: the Christmas tree.

“We have a lot of artificial trees in the house, but for the one in the living room, our main one, we do a real one,” says Lipinski. “My husband loves that, so that's been his thing since we got married. We've always done a real tree. It's fun. That day we make it a tradition and get dressed up in our Christmas outfit and we go and pick out a tree and make it festive.”

The decision to go faux with trees everywhere except the living room has always been unanimous, but the couple have clashed in the past.

“My husband and I have gotten into a full-blown argument about the amount of Christmas lights that need to be on a tree. He fully understands now that it has to be every inch covered,” she says.

As for whether the Christmas tree lights should be a string of assorted colors or all white, Lipinski says for her house, it depends on the tree’s location.

“I like it to be the multicolored ones. That’s my go-to. Although the ones in my bedroom, since it's all the white theme, we do just the white,” she details.

Lipinski has been honing her holiday home design technique for decades. She credits her mother for inspiring a passion for all the pageantry.

“My mom was meant to be an interior designer, so I grew up with someone who was constantly making our house a home and making it so special, that loves decorating, and I have that same gene,” she shares.

“We are big holiday people. We have a storage unit of not just Christmas [decor]. We decorate every single holiday, so this show just feels like it was meant for both of us. After all the things I've done in my career, I feel like she's probably going to be most proud of this one because it's so spot-on.”

The annual task of decorating the home has become a festive event for the whole family.

“What's fun is my mom and dad still come over, and they decorate with me,” says Lipinski. “My dad's the handy one and my mom is so creative. I couldn't do it without them. We pull out the boxes, we put on Christmas music, we have some hot cocoa, and we decorate together. It's really become a tradition, and now [with] my daughter, it feels like the three generations all together doing it still.”

The family’s dedication to holiday decor already seems to be something Lipinski’s daughter is developing herself.

“The art of decorating, making it special, and doing it with family is what I'm passing down to my daughter—and that we do it together. She loves it,” shares Lipinski. “This year, she's finally really clocking what Christmas is. When I told her it's time to decorate, her eyes lit up, and I just thought, 'Oh, my goodness, I'm creating a little monster here.’”

This year, Lipinski and her team of holiday fanatics plan to spruce up their space with even more trimmings thanks to the seasonal inspiration the show’s creative contestants have gifted.

“Really opening your mind ... the way they utilize the space of the room, like using the chandelier, there [were] some really beautiful entries," she says.

"It felt super immersive and even more magical, so I'm going to try to up the ante this year on my own Christmas decorating from learning those things.”

'Big Bargain Holiday Showdown' premieres on Nov. 10 at 9 p.m. on HGTV and streams the next day on HBO Max.

Karli Mullane is a celebrity and entertainment journalist at Realtor.com. She previously worked at Celeb Map, POPSUGAR, and NBC, covering pop culture, lifestyle, travel, and news of all kinds. #5622. Former CFO Sues NAR for Withholding Retirement Payments

The National Association of Realtors® (NAR) may spend the holidays in court, as the association is being accused of failing to pay a former employee promised retirement based on the financial strain of previous legal issues.

John Pierpoint—NAR’s former and long-time chief financial officer, who was succeeded by Matthew Cendella in 2025—filed a lawsuit against NAR in the Circuit Court of Cook County in Chicago on Wednesday, Nov. 11. He claims that NAR has refused to pay him a retirement benefit that the association regularly provides to retiring senior executives.

According to a release from Pierpoint’s attorneys, NAR “improperly withheld one year of salary in retirement compensation despite having recorded the anticipated payment in its own financial records for more than a decade.”

The release also points out that NAR has maintained the executive retirement compensation practice for approximately two decades, and pays retiring senior executives a year’s worth of their base salary.

In 2024, Pierpoint received over $872,000 for his role as CFO, according to NAR’s 2024 990 form.

While the Burnett settlement burdened NAR with a $418 million payment, Pierpoint’s attorneys claim that retirement compensation is held in reserve, specifically set aside for those payments.

“Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” David Fish, an attorney representing Pierpoint, stated. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives. We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees.”

NAR had not yet commented on the lawsuit at press time.

This is a developing story. Stay tuned to RISMedia for updates.

Desirae Sin is an assistant editor for RISMedia. She graduated from the University of Connecticut in 2025 with a double major in Journalism and Political Science. #5621. With $23M in funding, Luminal is the latest startup to put Nvidia’s CUDA moat in its crosshairs

Luminal AI Inc. has outlined a plan to tear down Nvidia Corp.’s formidable software moat in the artificial intelligence chip industry after raising $23 million in early-stage funding.

Today’s Series A round was led by Standard Capital and saw participation from existing investors such as Y Combinator, SagaVC, Liquid 2 and Felicis, bringing Luminal’s total amount raised to date to more than $28 million. It comes about a year after the startup raised $5.3 million in seed funding.

Everybody knows about Nvidia these days. The chipmaker has ridden the generative AI wave to a staggering $5 trillion market valuation, surpassing rivals such as Apple Inc., Alphabet Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. to become the most valuable publicly traded company in the world. But anyone who assumes that it’s solely Nvidia’s graphics processing units that set it apart would be mistaken, for the real reason for its dominance of the AI computing industry is not just silicon, but software.

For almost two decades, Nvidia’s proprietary Compute Unified Device Architecture or CUDA software framework has been the real differentiator, serving as a virtually impenetrable barrier that prevents rivals such as Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Google LLC and Amazon Web Services Inc. from stripping away its market lead. Though those rivals have developed some very powerful GPUs and custom application-specific integrated circuits for running AI workloads at lower costs than Nvidia’s hardware, they haven’t been able to match the scale of Nvidia’s software ecosystem.

Virtually every major AI framework, including TensorFlow and PyTorch, has been built natively on Nvidia’s CUDA software, enabling developers to run their AI models on Nvidia’s GPUs without any modifications. But to run their models on alternative chips, developers need to rewrite much of the underlying code, which is challenging and time-consuming work. That’s why the vast majority of AI workloads still run on Nvidia’s chips.

Many developers don’t want to be paying the exorbitant fees needed to rent Nvidia’s GPUs or purchase them outright, but they also don’t want to spend months at a time fine-tuning their codebases to get their AI models to run optimally on alternative hardware, and it’s this challenge that Luminal intends to solve for them.

The startup’s solution is a two-pronged architecture platform that consists of its proprietary search compiler and a fully managed inference cloud that combine to eliminate the hassles of bringing AI workloads onto different chips.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Joe Fioti told SiliconANGLE that the compiler works by systematically exploring different ways of running neural networks on the target chip in order to come up with the most optimal path. It benchmarks each variation until it finds the best possible solution, and then it automatically generates the code developers need.

Once the code is ready, it caches the implementation so it can be reused across recurring inference workloads. In this way, it allows developers to run their AI applications across heterogeneous chip architectures with minimal fuss, Fioti said.

“We started out building in the open on GitHub as AI adoption took off, and quickly saw how much demand there was for a more efficient way to run AI models across different hardware,” Fioti said of the company’s origins.

Luminal’s compiler and inference cloud are designed primarily for running high-throughput, continuous-uptime AI applications that demand massively scalable inference. Think applications such as AI coding tools, automated image generation engines, AI video generators and real-time voice agents.

“The cost of running AI shouldn’t limit who gets to build it,” Fioti said. “We’re building the infrastructure to make high-performance inference more accessible, giving developers more choice beyond Nvidia’s ecosystem without forcing them to compromise on speed or cost.”

Luminal launched its compiler and public cloud-based inference infrastructure just four months ago and adoption is growing rapidly. It’s already processing more than 45 trillion tokens per month – a number that’s roughly equivalent to 10% of the total tokens consumed so far by Together AI Inc., an $8 billion-valued infrastructure unicorn that has been serving the market for more than four years already. The startup has established a strong partnership with AWS, and runs a significant amount of its workloads on that company’s Tranium processors.

Going forward, Luminal’s plans include expanding its engineering team, scaling its go-to-market operations and optimizing its compiler and inference infrastructure to support more chip hardware and AI models.

Standard Capital’s Dalton Caldwell said he’s betting on Luminal because AI inference is the fastest-growing market in the world. “We backed it because of its deep technical expertise and its demonstrated proof that it can squeeze fantastic performance out of heterogeneous hardware,” he said. “Luminal’s ability to get the most out of GPUs that have already been purchased … is incredibly high leverage.”

Though Luminal has had a promising start, it’s certainly not the only company trying to break Nvidia’s CUDA stranglehold on the AI industry. Both Google and AWS have their own things going on, notably launching alternative AI frameworks to PyTorch that make it easier for developers to create AI models and applications that can run on their native processors.

Luminal also faces competition from startups such as Spectral Compute Ltd., which offers a programming toolkit and compiler that enables CUDA-based code to run natively on any AI-accelerated chip. There are also open-source efforts such as the UXL Foundation’s OneAPI, which converts CUDA code into software that can easily run on any silicon.

#5620. Strategy MSCI Verdict Nears as Anthropic IPO Puts Billions on the Line

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Wall Street faces two major tests of institutional appetite as the Strategy MSCI decision approaches. The index provider will publish its November review results shortly after 11:00 PM CET today. Strategy’s inclusion remains a major concern for Bitcoin investors.

Meanwhile, Anthropic is preparing one of the largest IPOs in history. The Claude developer is targeting up to $64.4 billion from its share offering, with a valuation reaching $1.02 trillion before dilution. Its listing will test if institutional investors still have an appetite for enormous technology bets after SpaceX.

Anthropic's bankers are preparing to raise its IPO price above the $70-$78 range, lifting its valuation to $1.5 trillion or more.That would push total fundraising above $100B, including the $26B private placement and the underwriters' option to buy extra shares.Source: FT pic.twitter.com/b3UonmMSWP

The timing creates an interesting contrast for financial markets. Strategy could face billions in potential passive fund selling, while Anthropic is asking investors to commit billions more to artificial intelligence. Each could reveal where Wall Street wants its next wave of capital to go.

Strategy position in MSCI indexes faces scrutiny under new eligibility rules targeting non-operating companies. The methodology could affect businesses whose financial structures resemble investment funds rather than traditional operating companies.

Strategy holds an enormous Bitcoin treasury, and its business model revolves around raising capital through equity and debt offerings to accumulate more BTC.

JUST IN: Global index fund giant MSCI will announce today its final decision on excluding Strategy $MSTR and Metaplanet $MPJPY from its indexes as non-operating companies.JP Morgan said MSCI exclusion could trigger about $2.8 billion outflows from Strategy $MSTR.Strategy… pic.twitter.com/kc8qtwchqd

MSCI previously identified Strategy and Japan’s Metaplanet among companies potentially affected by its review. Now, other digital asset treasury companies also face scrutiny under the new framework.

The potential financial consequences are substantial. JPMorgan previously estimated that removing Strategy could trigger $2.8 billion in selling from passive funds tracking MSCI indexes. But exclusion would not force Strategy to liquidate its Bitcoin holdings. Index-tracking funds would sell MSTR shares, potentially weakening its valuation and access to equity financing.

Yet, a weaker share price could make future fundraising more expensive. This could eventually reduce the company’s ability to accumulate Bitcoin at its previous pace.

MSCI’s announcement is scheduled for shortly after 11:00 PM CET on November 11. Any changes will become effective after the November 30 market close.

While Strategy faces potential exclusion, Anthropic is preparing to raise an extraordinary amount of institutional capital. The company plans to sell 825 million shares at $70 to $78 apiece, potentially raising $64.4 billion. Its valuation could reach $1.02 trillion before dilution, or $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

The offering also includes a separate $26 billion private placement involving major investors, including Google, Nvidia and AMD. Combined proceeds could reach $90.4 billion.

Anthropic’s growth makes the offering difficult for investors to ignore. Its annualized revenue run rate reached $17 billion quarterly, according to its IPO filing.

However, the company also faces enormous infrastructure commitments. Its computing agreements with partners approach $900 billion, showing the extraordinary costs behind the AI expansion.

The Anthropic IPO arrives at a complicated moment for technology stocks. Investors are questioning whether AI companies can generate enough revenue to justify their infrastructure spending and enormous valuations.
