#5619. How Bravo Star Joey Zauzig Turned an 1,100-Square-Foot WeHo Rental Into His Postdivorce ‘Sanctuary in the Sky’

Food influencer Joey Zauzig has worked closely with famed interior designer Jeff Lewis in broadcasting for years, yet the luxury West Hollywood apartment where he often delivers his signature saucy meal reviews and motivational speeches is one he decorated without help.

Zauzig, 34, is a fan favorite on Lewis’ SiriusXM show, “Jeff Lewis Live,” and a recurring cast member on “Still Flipping Out,” Bravo’s new spinoff of Lewis’ original “Flipping Out” series.

On both programs, Zauzig and Lewis have had their differences, but Zauzig reveals to Realtor.com® in Celebrity Sanctuary that when it comes to the style of his L.A.-area home, he believes they’re totally aligned.

“We have a similar sense of taste when it comes to homes and when it comes to renovations,” states Zauzig, while clarifying that Lewis hasn’t been by his place but is always welcome to visit. "I’ll let him see it whenever he wants to come over. I think he'll like it."

The former “The Real Friends of WeHo” star moved into the 1,100-square-foot, two-bedroom, two-bathroom rental unit located inside a high-rise residential tower in West Hollywood in October 2024. At the time, the Virginia native was seeking a safe place to start over following the breakup of his marriage and an unsettling break-in at a previous WeHo residence.

Today, Zauzig’s “small, but perfect” dwelling is his preferred space to comfortably work on his personal brand—and work on himself. It’s where he filmed one of his most popular social media posts “in a tux, shooting the sh*t, eating a shrimp cocktail in the kitchen,” and where he intentionally watched his Bravo debut alone so he could learn and grow through some serious self-reflection.

“To just be in my own home, watch it by myself, and be able to go through those emotions by myself—I was under the covers with a heating pad, face mask on,” recounts Zauzig.

“The best therapy you can ever get is to be able to watch yourself back on TV,” he continues. “I’m by no means perfect. We all make mistakes. We all have things we want to tweak about ourselves when it comes to the journey of becoming your best self. Mine got accelerated from the show, and that's a great thing. Joey 2.0 is going great.”

In this edition of Celebrity Sanctuary, Zauzig details how he’s gotten to “a good place” as he and his carefully curated West Hollywood home continue to be “works in progress.”

I really got this place because of the views. I was going through a divorce. I needed a little sanctuary in the sky, and that's what I got, and it just makes me happy because it's mine and it's beautiful.

I always had my eye on this building. A lot of cool people from my industry live here. It’s [got a] full-time security doorman, marble, light oak wood in all of the hallways. I was like, “If I move into a building in L.A., it has to be this building specifically.” I really was dead-set on that and also safety. I wanted somewhere that I felt, [as] someone that travels so much, could just pick up and leave without any worry.

I definitely made a lot of changes to the place. Farrow & Ball did all of the painting. They sent a paint specialist over. I went really dark. I did a sexy, dark-brown chocolate bedroom, and then my closet is all dark-brown lacquer. The roof is also lacquer, so it reflects [and] it looks bigger. The rest is this taupe-beige. It's a muted white. I didn’t want stark white walls, because it gives rental.

I changed a lot of light fixtures because that was important to me. There was this bubble light fixture in the kitchen, these glass bulbs. It was awful, and it was stark white light. I changed that to this Lulu and Georgia overhead, and I changed the placement of the lighting so it's over my island now, which is really nice. Then there [were] these alien-looking lights! They're not cute, so I changed those into CB2 canister lights. They're a dark black, which goes really nice with the tan [paint]. It feels more warm, cozy.

Other than that, I just made it my own. I made some custom cushions for the balcony outside.

[With] a rental, you never know if you could make changes, but there’s still some tweaks I want to do. Definitely some changes in the kitchen. I hate the green subway tiles. If I felt like putting money into this place, that's what I would change because I am in the kitchen so much. They've got to go. I’m not a subway-tile kind of guy. I would do a marble.

My family room is definitely my sanctuary because I have this white boucle chair where I sit. That's where I edit all my content.

You know when you can't wait to get home and go into that one spot that you're going to relax in, chill in, scroll for hours, watch TV? That's my family room and my specific chair. I love a swivel chair. They help my anxiety a little bit. I just can't wait to get home, get into that boucle chair. I work, I eat, I watch TV. It really is my sanctuary.

The swivel chair is vintage from Mid-Century Modern in Burbank, CA. It was my first vintage piece, and it's special to me. He re-covered it in white boucle. It's so comfortable.

I should probably separate [work and home life] better, but I like to feel comfortable when I'm doing my work, especially when I'm editing. When I need to focus, I like to be in a comfortable chair. I am a really tall guy, so I need to be chillin’ and cozy.

Once I put my phone and my work stuff away, I can actually make the sanctuary a relaxing space.

It's a mix of vintage and Design Within Reach. I have one of those Design Within Reach consoles, this really beautiful silver and glass coffee table, and a CB2 silver lamp. It goes well together with the white boucle and the Design Within Reach dark wood. Then I have a huge Lulu and Georgia Jake Arnold rug, and it's so fluffy and comfortable. It's a smaller family room, so you can have people on the floor and sitting down around the coffee table. It's a really fun little gathering area, and it's comfortable.

Then I have a huge 80-inch TV because I do watch a lot of TV, so I need it to be big. I know a lot of people say you shouldn't have the TV in the family room because it's trashy—I’ll have a TV in my family room all day long, no matter where I live. I think it's chic. I want people to know I'm a TV watcher. I think it adds a little something.

I have this [Pierre] Jeanneret chair to the right of my other chair, and that was a piece that I got as a gift to myself when I was filming my first reality show. It's an original Jeanneret chair. It has one of the red inscriptions in the back, which is one of the most rare Jeanneret chairs. The wicker part had to get redone because someone sat in the chair, broke it, and fell through, so that [part] is not original, but it's fine.

I’m going to change some things for sure soon. I need a new couch.

Just as I'm a work in progress, so is my sanctuary. It's getting there, it’s just not there. It actually makes perfect sense for where I'm at right now. We're all works in progress, and I'm becoming Joey 2.0, so I'm excited.

#5618. Vanta launches AI Governance, Risk Quantification and a Vanta Agent for entire jobs

Compliance automation company Vanta Inc. today launched AI Governance by Vanta, a product on its Agentic Trust Platform said to give security teams a single view of every artificial intelligence system in a company.

Also making their debut at VantaCon 2026 in San Francisco this week are Risk Quantification, Autonomous Vendor Assessments and a new version of the Vanta Agent that the company claims can take on entire jobs.

Vanta is pitching the new products at security teams that are under pressure to move faster on AI. According to job-title data compiled by Vanta, the number of AI security engineers and architects has tripled so far this year compared with all of 2025.

AI governance roles, which did not appear in the company’s figures before 2024, have grown tenfold in two years. A complete inventory of the AI tools in use is still out of reach for many security teams, Vanta said.

Chief Product Officer Jeremy Epling, who is due to demonstrate the products at a keynote later today, said security teams are usually being held accountable for AI with the same headcount they had before it arrived.

“Plenty of tools can list the AI running in your company,” Epling said. Vanta also checks whether that AI is doing what a customer approved, he added, with the Vanta Agent taking on the follow-up work once someone signs off.

Point products for AI security often detect threats without the business context to judge how much they matter, according to Vanta. The company claims to be the only vendor tying an AI agent’s live security telemetry directly to an organization’s compliance controls.

On the risk side, Vanta’s unified risk view, which draws on live signals from across a customer’s compliance program, now includes Autonomous Vendor Assessments. According to the company, Risk Quantification, also added to the view, is meant to show leaders the financial impact of their most critical risks.

Entire jobs can now be handed to the latest version of the Vanta Agent. Once it has learned how a customer runs its program, the agent is said to bring staff in when a decision calls for human judgment. Users can also reach it natively inside Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and Slack.

Vanta also named Fredrick “Flee” Lee its new chief information security officer. Lee joins on Nov. 16 from Reddit Inc., where he led security before, during and after the company’s initial public offering. Gusto Inc., where he ran security before Reddit, was a Vanta customer at the time. At Vanta, he is expected to act as what the company calls “customer zero” in pushing the product road map.

The company has been valued at $4.15 billion since July 2025, when it raised $150 million in a Series D round led by Wellington Management Co. LLP.

#5616. Only a Quarter of U.S. Households Have Children at Home

Household composition is a fundamental driver of housing demand, influencing everything from floor plans and bedroom counts to community amenities and long-term land strategies. Understanding how household composition is changing can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to serve different types of buyers.

As of 2024, 25.4% of U.S. households had children under age 18 living at home, according to Zonda’s analysis of U.S. Census data. Put another way, nearly three out of every four households did not have children at home.

The finding is consistent with trends visible among home buyers: the 2025 Home Buyers and Sellers Generational Trends Report from NAR showed that only 24% of buyers had children under 18, a historic low.

Several structural demographic forces help explain this shift, including fertility rates below replacement levels, later family formation, and an aging population that has contributed to more empty nesters, retirees, and older adults living independently. At the same time, households without children, including DINKS (dual income, no kids), represent an important part of housing demand.

These shifts highlight the changing composition of household types shaping housing demand and reinforce the importance of segmentation over assumptions. The traditional family household remains an important customer, but understanding the needs of other household types can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to reach a broader range of buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

Zonda’s experts provide objective analysis on housing trends, supply and demand dynamics, and economic drivers. The team of economists, researchers, and analysts blends proprietary data with expert interpretation to help you navigate changing markets and make smarter decisions.

#5615. NYC’s First Pied-à-Terre Tax Bills Are Coming—and Buyers Are Recalculating

New York City's new tax on high-value second homes was designed to raise revenue. But changes to the tax code can also influence how people buy and sell property.

"There's always the risk of avoidance," explains Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com®. "Tax bases are famously mobile—especially across municipal boundaries—and that's doubly true for wealthier individuals."

With the first surcharge bills expected to be mailed in the coming days, Realtor.com analyzed the nearly 1 million property and residential-unit records in the city's supplemental tax roll, identifying 24,218 potentially exposed homes that met the relevant valuation thresholds.

Of those, 2,536 (10.5%) sat within just 5% above the minimum valuation required for taxation, while 560 (2.3%) fell within 5% on either side of a higher tax-rate threshold.

Which side of that divide a home falls on can come with huge financial stakes for owners—and agents say buyers are already taking notice.

"The biggest change since July is that buying a second home in New York has become a much more calculated decision," says Donald Brennan, a real estate broker with Engel & Völkers.

In at least one building, two apartments with government-assigned market values just $6,009 apart could face a $37,813 difference in annual surcharges simply because they fall on opposite sides of a tax-rate threshold—assuming neither qualifies for an exemption.

New York City has long attracted wealthy buyers looking for a second residence, whether for work, leisure, or the opportunity to spend part of the year in the city.

"I might be biased, but it's a fantastic place to live, especially if you can afford it," says Krimmel.

His caveat is telling: if you can afford it. With an estimated 52% of New York City renters already burdened by housing costs, wealthy second-home owners present a tempting target for Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s tax-the-rich agenda.

But the new tax will add considerable expense even for those who can afford multiple homes.

For condos and co-ops, the surcharge starts at 4% of their Department of Finance market value at $1 million. One- to three-family homes face an initial rate of 0.8% beginning at $5 million.

The city values houses using comparable sales but condos and co-ops based on their potential rental income, so their tax thresholds aren't directly comparable. At either entry point, however, the annual surcharge starts at approximately $40,000.

Brooklyn accounts for 560 of the 713 Class 1 properties just above the minimum threshold, while Manhattan accounts for 1,700 of the 1,823 condo and co-op units in the equivalent position.

But local brokers point out that many of these properties may never face the surcharge at all.

"In Brooklyn, I think this creates a slightly different conversation because so many of our luxury buyers are purchasing homes they actually intend to live in," says Jessica Peters, a Brooklyn-based broker with Douglas Elliman.

Already, thousands of owners have secured exemptions from the new tax. Of approximately 17,000 notices mailed to owners, close to 11,000 exemption applications had been submitted and more than 8,800 approved as of Oct. 29, Gothamist reports.

That leaves a great deal of uncertainty around how much revenue the city will actually be able to bring in.

While the city budgeted $500 million in annual revenue from the new tax, an April report from City Comptroller Mark Levine warned that exemptions and other behavioral changes could reduce collections to between $340 million and $380 million.

But exemptions aren't the only factor affecting what owners could owe. There's also the matter of the threshold values.

Condo and co-op rates rise to 5.25% above $3 million and 6.5% above $5 million. Rates for one- to three-family homes, meanwhile, increase to 1.05% above $15 million and 1.3% above $25 million.

And because the higher rate applies to the property's entire value, even a small difference in valuation can trigger a monumental increase. The owner of a $3 million condo or co-op subject to the 5.25% rate, for example, would owe just over $157,000.

These higher-rate thresholds have a much narrower geographic footprint, too. Of the 270 records sitting within 5% above a higher-rate threshold, 264 are in Manhattan, including 33 in ZIP code 10022 and 29 in 10021.

Krimmel says owners could respond by reconsidering where they buy or how they use their properties.

"The question is whether there are other places which act as a close substitute for the newly taxed properties," he says.

Brennan sees that calculation emerging among buyers who may spend only a few months a year in New York.

"When you're looking at a multimillion-dollar apartment that you might only use a few months out of the year, that additional tax becomes part of the conversation very quickly," he says.

Some may decide to rent rather than purchase, he adds.

Those decisions could ultimately help free up housing for other buyers or tenants, as Krimmel notes. At the same time, those sales could also reduce the number of properties generating surcharge revenue.

Owners are also challenging the tax in court. Three lawsuits have been filed, two of which remain pending.

A Nov. 4 appeals court ruling dismissed a lawsuit challenging the city's rollout on standing grounds, while the remaining cases challenge its constitutionality.

But homeowners don't need to overturn the law to challenge what they might owe. They can also dispute the city's valuation of their properties—and for those sitting just above a tax threshold, even a small adjustment could eliminate the surcharge entirely.

Narrowing the analysis to properties within just 1% of a tax threshold identified 602 records, including 496 just above the minimum valuation required for taxation.

An additional 106 records fell within 1% of a higher-rate cutoff, including 61 just below and 45 above. All were in Manhattan, and of those, 66 were condos or co-ops near the $3 million threshold, where the annual surcharge increases from 4% to 5.25%.

From a bird's-eye view of the city, those differences might seem negligible. But when looking at a specific building, they are more dramatic.

At 111 West 57th St., a luxury condominium tower near Central Park, unit 57 has a DOF market value of $2,999,794—just $206 below the higher threshold. Unit 38, meanwhile, is valued at $3,005,803.

That $6,009 difference in valuation translates to a $37,813 difference in potential annual surcharges, with the higher-valued apartment facing a charge of approximately $157,805.

A similar disparity appears at 768 Fifth Ave., where two units separated by $19,337 in DOF market value face a $38,317 difference in potential annual charges.

That’s no small sum, even for a wealthy homeowner.

"If they're already paying substantial carrying costs, they're going to look for ways to offset that expense, whether through the purchase price or other concessions," says Ben Jacobs, a Douglas Elliman broker specializing in Manhattan and Brooklyn.

A lower asking price wouldn't automatically reduce the government's valuation or the tax owed, but it could help buyers offset the cost of carrying the property.

Krimmel sees another potential consequence: The surcharge could change what economists call a property's option value—the value of being able to use it differently in the future. Condominiums, for instance, typically offer more flexibility to rent out than co-ops, making that potential rental income part of what a buyer is purchasing.

The same principle could apply to homes that buyers might eventually want to use as second residences.

Even if a property is exempt today, the possibility of a future surcharge could become another consideration in negotiations. Jacobs adds that uncertainty can create its own complications.

"Buyers want to know exactly what their exposure will be before they commit," he says. "When those answers aren't immediately clear, it can slow down a transaction."

To his point, there are early signs of a sharper slowdown in New York City's luxury condo and co-op market since the city began notifying potentially affected property owners in July.

New condo and co-op listings initially priced between $1 million and $3 million fell 11% year over year from July through Nov. 7, compared with a 1% increase between April and June, according to an analysis of Realtor.com listing data.

The decline was even steeper among properties priced between $3 million and $5 million, where new listings fell 16% year over year after July, following a 5% decline in the preceding three months.

By comparison, new listings priced below $1 million fell just 1% year over year since July, after rising 7% between April and June.

Of course, the pied-à-terre tax can’t shoulder all the blame for the slowdown. The luxury market was already showing signs of weakness before the city began sending tax notices, and rising mortgage rates have added another headwind.

Brokers, meanwhile, say some second-home buyers are approaching purchases with greater caution.

"I don't think this means wealthy buyers are suddenly abandoning New York. They still want to be here," Brennan says. "But they're looking much more closely at the numbers."

Peters expects some prospective second-home buyers to delay their decisions or consider renting until they have a better understanding of their potential tax bills.

"What concerns me more is how the additional cost could influence decisions before buyers even start looking," she says.

The first surcharge payments are due on Jan. 1, 2027, and the larger market response—if there is one—will likely take even longer to untangle from the myriad other factors affecting buyer and seller behavior.

But for now, two things are clear: Thousands of potentially affected properties sit close to tax thresholds with huge financial consequences, and new luxury condo and co-op listings have slowed considerably since the city began notifying owners.

Whether those developments are connected—and whether the tax ultimately changes the number of second homes in New York City—remains to be seen.

#5614. Century Communities Promotes Jim Francescon to President

As part of its long-term succession planning process, Century Communities has promoted Jim Francescon to president, effective January 1, 2027. Francescon currently serves as executive vice president, corporate operations.

“Today’s announcement reflects the implementation of a succession plan that our board, Rob, and I have been planning and executing over the past two years,” says Dale Francescon, executive chairman of Century Communities. “We have been very thoughtful in how we have approached succession, with the goal of best positioning Century for long-term alignment with shareholders, success, and growth.”

Dale Francescon will continue to serve as executive chairman and Rob Francescon, who currently serves as CEO and president, will solely serve as CEO. As president, Jim will oversee the company’s home building operations, land, and related corporate functions and will help drive the company’s strategy and growth.

“Jim has played an integral role in shaping our strategic direction and our growth into one of the largest home builders in the country, including leading our recent acquisitions that have deepened our footprint and strengthened our platform,” says Rob. “I look forward to continuing to work closely with Jim and our entire executive team as we position Century for continued success.”

Before serving as executive vice president, Jim was president of Century Living, the company’s multifamily platform, and prior to that served as corporate vice president. Jim also serves as a trustee of the University of Denver, Children’s Hospital Colorado Foundation, and ACE Scholarships Colorado.

“I am honored to take on this role and grateful to our board, Dale, and Rob for their confidence,” adds Jim. “We have built a strong operating platform and a talented team, and I am excited about the opportunities ahead as we continue to grow and deliver on our promise of “A Home for Every Dream.””

#5613. Andersen Partnership Helps Build Accessible Homes for Wounded Veterans

Since 2018, Andersen has worked with Jared Allen's Homes for Wounded Warriors, a nonprofit organization that builds injury-specific, accessible mortgage-free accessible homes for veterans who sustained severe injuries during their military service.

Since 2018, Andersen has partnered with Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors to help provide accessible, mortgage-free homes designed around the individual needs of severely injured military veterans.

Through the partnership, Andersen has donated windows and doors to 12 veteran families and home projects across the country. The manufacturer also supports the nonprofit through financial contributions and company matches of employee donations.

Most recently, Andersen contributed to a custom home for Marine Lance Corporal Josh Wege in Fond du Lac County, Wisconsin. Josh Wege, who sustained life-changing injuries while serving in Afghanistan, received the keys to the mortgage-free home alongside his family.

The residence was designed around Wege’s accessibility and mobility requirements, with the broader goal of providing greater independence, comfort, and quality of life.

“Building a home that meets the needs of a critically wounded veteran and their family takes a team of people who believe in our mission,” says Jared Allen, founder of Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors since 2009. “Andersen is an important part of that team, and we’re grateful for their support and commitment to the veterans we serve.”

Jared Allen, a Pro Football Hall of Famer and former Minnesota Vikings defensive end, added that the partnership helps create homes “where veterans can live more independently, and families can make memories together for years to come.”

For Andersen, the partnership also provides an opportunity to apply product selection and design considerations to the specific mobility needs of each homeowner. Depending on the project, those considerations can include wider openings, low- or zero-threshold transitions, accessible hardware placement, and patio door configurations intended to make movement easier between indoor and outdoor spaces.

Charlie Jackson, an account sales manager at Andersen, has helped project teams identify window and door solutions based on individual veterans’ accessibility requirements.

“My father was a World War II Marine, so supporting veterans has always been personally meaningful to me,” Jackson shares. “These projects bring Andersen’s work into focus because you can see how thoughtful product choices and accessible design come together to make everyday life easier for a veteran and their family.”

“As a 10-year Andersen employee, I’m proud to contribute my experience to help identify the products and solutions that best support each homeowner’s accessibility, comfort, and long-term needs,” he adds.

The homes are completed through collaboration among Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors, manufacturers such as Andersen, local businesses, tradespeople, and other supporters.

#5612. Invitation Homes Invests in HBI Training for Veterans

The Home Builders Institute (HBI) and Invitation Homes have launched a partnership aimed at helping transitioning military service members, veterans, and their families build careers in construction, property maintenance, and the skilled trades.

The partnership will expand Invitation Homes’ existing Invitation to SkillUp initiative through an investment in HBI’s Military Services program, which provides hands-on, instructor-led skilled trades training, industry-recognized certifications, and job placement assistance.

Through the partnership, HBI and Invitation Homes will connect HBI-trained veterans, military spouses, and family members with career opportunities in the build-to-rent and single-family rental sectors. The organizations also plan to expand recruitment at HBI Military Services locations, including Fort Stewart, Georgia, and Jacksonville, Florida.

Invitation Homes’ Veteran Employee Resource Group will participate in mentorship and career guidance efforts.

“Veterans and their families have dedicated themselves to serving our country, and we are proud to support them as they transition into rewarding civilian careers,” Invitation Homes president and CEO Dallas Tanner says. “Through our Invitation to SkillUp initiative, we are investing in talented individuals whose dedication and service strengthen our communities, while helping create meaningful opportunities in the skilled trades.”

HBI has spent a decade training, certifying, and placing transitioning service members, veterans, and their families in skilled trades careers. According to HBI president and CEO Ed Brady, nearly 90% of graduates from the organization’s military program find jobs, earning an average of more than three times the federal minimum wage.

“We know this model works, and with this important investment from Invitation Homes, we can help more veterans enter the skilled trades every year because the people who served this country deserve a career as strong as their service,” Brady said.

Invitation to SkillUp is Invitation Homes’ national skilled trades development initiative, which works with trade schools and organizations to expand trades education and increase awareness of career opportunities.

Invitation Homes joins other companies supporting HBI’s military programs. The Home Depot Foundation and DEWALT were early supporters, while Google recently provided a $1 million contribution to the effort.

The partnership comes as the housing industry continues to look for ways to strengthen its skilled labor pipeline. For transitioning service members and military families, the effort offers a pathway from military service into construction and housing careers while providing the industry with another source of trained workers.

#5611. Lennar, Operation Finally Home Surprise Two Military Families With New Homes

U.S. Army Specialist Jordan Taylor and U.S. Marine Corps Sergeant Kevin Gallmeier with their families.

Two military veterans and their families received life-changing news ahead of Veterans Day when Lennar and Operation Finally Home surprised them with the gift of new homes.

U.S. Army Specialist Jordan Taylor and U.S. Marine Corps Sergeant Kevin Gallmeier were surprised with the announcement during the inaugural Operation Finally Home Golf Classic reception in Austin, Texas, on Nov. 9.

Neither family knew about the plans beforehand and attended the event as guests of Operation Finally Home.

The announcement followed a live performance by country music artist and Army Reserve soldier Craig Morgan. Operation Finally Home founder Dan Wallrath and Lennar San Antonio division president Brian Barron then revealed that each family would receive a new Lennar home.

The partnership builds on Operation Finally Home’s mission of providing mortgage-free homes and home modifications to wounded, ill, and injured veterans, first responders, and their families.

Gallmeier served in the Marine Corps from 2005 to 2015 after being motivated to enlist by the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. During his service, he deployed twice to Iraq in support of combat operations and later deployed to Okinawa, Japan, as part of the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit.

Gallmeier sustained a traumatic brain injury following a grenade blast during combat operations in Iraq. He also developed post-traumatic stress disorder and continues to manage PTSD, amongst other conditions, according to Operation Finally Home.

Following his military career, Gallmeier earned bachelor’s and master’s degrees in divinity from Biola University and became a pastor. A formal groundbreaking for the family’s new Lennar home is scheduled for Nov. 10 in the Freedom Crossing community in Killeen, Texas.

Taylor enlisted in the U.S. Army in August 2004 shortly after graduating from high school in Washington state. He served as an infantryman and filled roles including Squad Automatic Weapon gunner, driver, and team leader.

From June 2006 to September 2007, Taylor deployed to Baghdad in support of Operation Iraqi Freedom. His unit lost 21 soldiers during the deployment.

After completing his military service in December 2007, Taylor continued serving his community as a firefighter and emergency medical technician.

A serious back injury in January 2024, combined with the lasting physical and emotional effects of his military service, ultimately forced Taylor to medically retire from firefighting in March 2025.

Following the injury, Taylor and his wife, Aylynn, and their four children faced financial uncertainty and eventually sold their home and moved in with relatives. The family’s new Lennar home will provide a fresh start. A groundbreaking for the Taylor residence is slated in December.

#5610. Agile Robots raises $500M funding led by SoftBank at $8.5B valuation

German artificial intelligence robotics startup Agile Robots SE announced today that it has raised $500 million in new late-stage funding at an $8.5 billion valuation.

Japanese multinational investment holding company SoftBank led the Series F funding round. Other participants included AI chip leader Nvidia Corp., Japanese group Hitachi Ltd. and T Capital. The financing brings the total capital invested to $2 billion.

Founded in 2018 as a spinoff from the German Aerospace Center, Agile is one of Europe’s leaders in humanoid and mobile robots, robotic arms and dexterous robotic hands, along with the AI models needed to control them. The company combines robotic hardware with sensing, computer vision and AI software to automate physical work.

At the center of its hardware and software is force-sensitive manipulation. It allows robots to control how much force they use to handle delicate parts, perform precision assembly, and adapt to changing situations.

“Physical AI will fundamentally change how the world builds, moves and makes things,” said founder and Chief Executive Dr. Zhaopeng Chen. “Our vision is intelligent robots working alongside people in factories and warehouses everywhere, and Agile Robots is determined to lead that shift.”

Agile’s established flagship arm Diana 7 allows for precise manipulation and assembly; it includes torque sensors in all seven axes of movement that can detect and respond to the amount of force required to grab, lift and manipulate objects.

Agile One, the company’s humanoid robot, was publicly unveiled in November 2025 as an industrial-first platform. The launch extended the company’s approach into human-shaped platforms intended to carry out tasks across a production floor. It includes dexterous hands, advanced perception and human collaborative capabilities, allowing it to operate readily alongside personnel in manufacturing and logistics settings.

The company now offers an entire family of Agile One human-shaped robots, including the Agile One S, a compact humanoid reference platform built for research labs, universities, and developers. The company also offers Agile One SN, equipped with Dual Wuji five-finger hands and preconfigured for Nvidia Corp.’s Isaac GR00T AI models that act as robot “brains,” designed to let industry developers rapidly train, evaluate, deploy and test new robotic skills.

“We bring Physical AI out of the lab and into industrial production, across logistics, automotive, electronics and manufacturing,” added Chen.

The funding will support expansion into the United States, hiring more engineers and accelerating development of intelligent robotics applications. Additionally, the company said it intends to expand production, including in Germany, where it opened a facility in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich, in early 2026 to meet rising demand. Agile said the site can produce up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots annually.

Agile has deployed around 20,000 industrial robotic solutions for customers across the automotive, consumer electronics, logistics and other industries. It boasts a growing portfolio of subsidiaries, including BÄR Automation, Franka Robotics, Idealworks and Krause Automation. Franka supplies manipulation technology, Idealworks develops mobile robots and coordination software, whereas BÄR and Krause build and integrate interaction capabilities.

In robotics, Agile faces stiff international competition from established automation suppliers such as Universal Robots A/S, ABB Ltd., FANUC Corp. and Yaskawa Electric Corp. Its Agile One humanoid faces rivals that include Figure AI Inc., Apptronik Inc. and Agility Robotics Inc.

#5609. Attached Housing Stands Out in Baltimore’s Housing Market

Annualized new-home sales declined 5.2% in September to 2,613 units. Attached housing accounted for 1,951 sales versus 662 detached sales during the period. However, the Baltimore market is sending mixed signals as 2026 winds down. By comparison, the market’s average new-home sales rate of 2.4 homes per project matched Maryland and remained above the national rate of 2.0.

That aforementioned product split is one of Baltimore’s defining characteristics. Annualized attached sales fell just 0.9% year over year compared with a 16% decline for detached homes as of September data. The strongest sales activity also sits toward the more attainable end of the new home market, with attached homes priced from $350,000 to $450,000 experiencing the most closing activity over the past year.

Related, affordability remains a constraint. As of July, the median new-home closing price stood at $555,337, down 2.9% year over year, compared with $420,000 for existing homes.

The economic backdrop adds another layer. Total nonfarm employment in the Baltimore metro declined 0.6% year over year in August, while the unemployment rate was 4.1%. Households are estimated to decline 0.1% in 2026 and post flat annual growth through 2028.

One potential longer-term catalyst comes from defense manufacturing. Anduril Industries announced a $3.7 billion investment in a high-tech shipyard at Baltimore County’s Tradepoint Atlantic industrial center. The project is expected to create 3,100 direct jobs and support more than 11,000 indirect jobs, while generating more than $2 billion in annual economic output.

Baltimore’s opportunity is therefore less about broad based growth and more about positioning. Ideal locations, attainable price points, and disciplined starts stand out in a market where buyers are still active but increasingly selective.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth market reports published in Zonda Enterprise.

Zonda’s experts provide objective analysis on housing trends, supply and demand dynamics, and economic drivers. The team of economists, researchers, and analysts blends proprietary data with expert interpretation to help you navigate changing markets and make smarter decisions.

#5608. Brooklyn Building Collapse Leaves 8 Dead, Including 2 Children

A three-story building in Brooklyn's Flatbush neighborhood collapsed on Wednesday, killing six adults and two children and injuring 18 others, including four firefighters who joined the rescue effort.

On Thursday afternoon, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the city would be sweeping 100 other sites associated with five "entities" involved in a construction project adjacent to the collapsed building. Mamdani and Department of Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani declined to name the five companies they would be focusing their investigation on.

”If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable," Mamdani said.

“We are launching an extensive, whole-of-government investigation into this,” Tigani said. “As the debris moves, we are continuing to document and look to see what we can find. ... Investigations and interviews are ongoing, so all of that information will have to come together once we are able to get a better and clearer picture of the floor as debris is moved away.”

The FDNY Incident Management Team, created after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, has been activated to manage the response.

More than 250 firefighters along with a canine unit and search drones were on the scene at 1321 Flatbush Ave. combing through debris to search for survivors on Thursday morning. Roads around the collapsed building have been closed to traffic.

So far, only one of those victims has been publicly named. José Luis Caguana, 26, was among the eight victims. He leaves behind a pregnant wife and 4-year-old son.

Ewelina Alvarado-Baczewska, who used to teach the son of Luis Caguana, struggled to contain her emotions as she spoke to Realtor.com® at the scene of the tragedy on Thursday.

"I saw his wife this morning. We embraced each other and cried together. It was an incredibly heartbreaking moment," the teacher said. “We are deeply devastated by the tragic loss of Mr. José Luis."

Alvarado-Baczewska said the family had immigrated from Ecuador.

"They are a truly humble, kind, and warm family. I remember Jose as a father who always greeted us with a smile and showed nothing but kindness and good manners whenever he came to pick up his son. I am struggling to process this tragedy myself, and honestly, I don’t have many more words. My heart is with his wife, their children, and the entire family during this unimaginable time,” she said.

Alvarado-Baczewska and other teachers at the preschool have launched a GoFundMe campaign for the family of Luis Caguana.

At a press conference on Thursday afternoon, FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said that search and rescue efforts would continue until there was no longer hope of finding survivors.

"We always assume that there are more people there until we can access the ground. So until we've removed some of the bigger debris and are able to search beneath them, this will remain a rescue operation," she said.

Incredibly, a woman who is six months pregnant was rescued from the rubble on Wednesday night.

"I have an update. She is alive, she is still alive. I am very happy," her husband told onlookers, according to WABC-TV.

Part of the wall of 1323 Flatbush Ave. also came down in the collapse, leaving apartments in that building exposed to the elements.

Neighbors were evacuated from the property and brought to the nearby Flatbush YMCA as a precaution.

The collapsed building at 1321 Flatbush Ave., in Brooklyn's Little Haiti neighborhood, was built in 1930 and had four apartment units on the second and third floors, while the first floor was a commercial storefront.

At the time of the collapse, workers were excavating a lot adjacent to the property at 2625 Bedford Ave.

Tigani said that the Bedford lot had been approved for a three-story, 64-unit building, but another permit application had been put in for a nine-story building on the site. A stop-work order was issued for that project.

The building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. has 98 recorded violations dating to 1972, according to the city's Department of Housing, Preservation, and Development.

Eleven of those violations are from this year alone and include "unsafe electrical wiring" and a notice to "provide an adequate supply of water for the wet sprinkler and/or standpipe."

Arfan Yasin, owner of Kennedy Chicken & Grill around the corner from the building, has been in the area since 2001 and had customers who lived in the building.“I think they were digging too close to the building," he tells Realtor.com. "The building has been there forever, and nothing like this has ever happened. It’s very sad. Very shocking for this community.

“That building was strong, had a good stable foundation. It didn’t just collapse. And whatever new building that was going up next to it would have been less stable I believe," he continued.

The Brooklyn District Attorney’s Office, alongside the Department of Buildings and local law enforcement, has launched an active joint inquiry to determine whether any criminal negligence or building code violations contributed to the disaster.

Mamdani said in a statement: “There are no words for a loss of this magnitude. My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we have lost, those who are injured and everyone grieving today.“

Andrea Cavallier contributed to this report.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5607. Spec Versus Built-to-Order: Builders Navigate a Changing Market

For builders, the push and pull between speculative homes and built-to-order (BTO) homes is a classic struggle, reflecting the desire to balance operational efficiency against market demand. A favorable mix directly dictates a company’s profit margins, inventory risk, and customer satisfaction.

Spec homes allow builders to more directly compete with resale inventory, offering faster move-ins that can capture demand from buyers looking to move quickly. In strong markets, heavier spec exposure can increase sales velocity. In slower markets, builders with large levels of spec inventory are exposed to carrying costs and pricing risk.

A built-to-order approach reduces that inventory risk and offers buyers greater personalization in their final purchase. Built-to-order homes typically carry higher sales prices and translate into healthier margins while requiring buyers to wait longer to move in.

While several companies are steadfast in their approaches, such as the 100% spec commitments of Meritage Homes and CBH Homes and the 70% BTO target set by KB Home, the spec-BTO balance often shifts over time.

In the immediate post-pandemic period, many builders leaned more heavily into spec production. Unprecedented levels of demand and rapidly rising home prices set a backdrop for many large builders to offer more spec and quick move-in (QMI) homes because homes were absorbed at record levels. Similarly, the standardized production and simplified SKU packages helped builders guard against pandemic-related supply chain disruptions and labor shortages.

When mortgage rates began to spike in late 2023, a go-to-market approach with spec production remained prevalent to help buyers with certainty of price and move-in timing. Public builders at the time noted buyers were less willing to commit many months ahead given rate uncertainty and favored move-in ready homes. Builders favoring a heavier spec production mix were able to lean into financing incentives in the form of price cuts and rate buydowns to capture demand as economic uncertainty began to mount.

At the end of 2025 and beginning of 2026, one of the more notable themes to emerge is a more concentrated shift toward a higher built-to-order mix. KB Home began sharing its goal of a 70% BTO mix in the second quarter of 2025, noting the approach is customer-centric and that a design-forward, personalized approach is a differentiator in a market where incentives were prevalent.

“Our buyers choose their lot, floor plan, and personalized finishes. The result is a home that has a real specific value to the people who will live in it,” president and CEO Rob McGibney said during an earnings call with investors. “Homes built to customer specifications do not require heavy incentives to sell.”

Similarly, in the past couple quarters PulteGroup has highlighted its efforts to skew production more toward BTO homes, targeting a 60-40 mix.

“Our decision to build more spec homes once supply chains collapsed and build cycles effectively doubled was the right one at the time, but we much prefer having a growing backlog of sold homes,” PulteGroup president CEO Ryan Marshall shared during a recent earnings call.

The shift is not just occurring among large public builders, with Texas-based Stylecraft Builders reporting a shift toward the BTO model. After carrying essentially no to-be-built volume as recently as 12 to 18 months ago, the company is targeting a goal of 20% to 25% of sales from BTO orders.

Spec-heavy, BTO-heavy, and hybrid operators are all succeeding in the current challenging market. Rather than converging toward a single model, many builders increasingly view spec and BTO homes as complementary tools that can be adjusted based on market conditions, buyer behavior, and community characteristics.

For many builders, spec homes and BTO homes are not an either-or strategy, and a flexible approach that puts buyers front of mind yields the most successful results.

“They serve different customer needs and we want to execute both approaches well,” David Weekley Homes chief operating officer Ladd Fargo tells BUILDER. “The approximate mix depends on the market, buyer behavior, product type, and price point.”

The by-market approach is one that resonates strongly with Trumark Homes. As a private builder that serves as the western hub for Daiwa House, Trumark Homes leans into the local expertise of its division operators to meet the market with the best approach across its operating platforms in California, Colorado, and Washington.

“We know that we have strong operators in all our markets, and we trust our division teams to understand their buyer profiles, have a pulse on the competition, and utilize the data and tools available to plan accordingly,” Trumark Homes chief operating officer Steve Kalmbach says. “We will continue to be nimble and make the best strategic decisions for each community along the way.”

Fred McConnell, vice president of brand and performance marketing at Risewell Homes, tells BUILDER the company has become more intentional about creating built-to-order opportunities while maintaining a strong offering of quick move-in, spec homes. The mixed approach allows Risewell to be both consumer-led and market-responsive while aligning the company’s core brand platform, Built Well to Live Well.

“Our goal is to maintain the flexibility to respond to both the consumer and the dynamics of each individual market and community,” McConnell says.

Huntsville, Alabama-based Davidson Homes has seen a shift toward more BTO homes, but the company’s core strategy has not changed. CEO Brandon Jones says the company continues to meet buyers where they are, offering a solution for those who need to move in 45 days or those who want to choose every detail from homesite to interior finishes. He says the market has not picked a winner between spec or BTO and has instead rewarded builders who are disciplined about using both approaches.

“We start with the buyer, not the model. A lot of our industry has moved to one way of building,” Jones continues. “We’ve kept real personalization on the menu because buyers still want it, and we keep inventory on the ground because some buyers can’t wait. If we get the buyer right, the mix takes care of itself.”

CBH Homes has been a 100% spec builder since 2019, placing high value on the efficiencies gained in the building process and the simplification it provides to the buyer experience. The efficiencies gained early, from purchasing to scheduling trade partners, provide consistency and synergy that allows real value to be passed on to the buyers.

“Being a spec builder allows us to do what we do best: Build amazing homes quickly, efficiently, and at a price that keeps homeownership attainable,” CBH Homes president and owner Corey Barton explains. “Our buyers can walk through a home, see the finishes, know the price, and know when they can move in. There are fewer unknowns.”

In the current market, where some builders are shifting approaches back toward a heavier BTO mix, Barton says CBH Homes still sees value in its 100% spec approach.

“When rates move or the right opportunity presents itself, our buyers don’t have to wait months for their home to be built,” Barton says. “On top of that, we know if a buyer has the option, they will want to make changes. Not allowing change orders allows us to keep costs down and construction efficiency high. Our goal isn’t to give the buyer a thousand decisions to make. It’s to do the work up front and create a beautiful, professionally designed home they can walk into and say, ‘This is it.’”

“Being a spec builder allows us to do what we do best: Build amazing homes quickly, efficiently, and at a price that keeps homeownership attainable.”

Meritage Homes made a similar transition to an all-spec approach in 2016, focusing on the entry-level segment and leaning into competition with resale inventory. The builder’s shorter cycle times allow it to start homes later while also maintaining its 60-day closing guarantee. CEO Phillippe Lord says that its trade relationships and limited SKU counts set it apart from other builders and provide greater certainty to its vendor partners. While the builder has been market responsive and has increased its portfolio of move-up product given market conditions, Meritage Homes remains committed to its 100% spec approach.

Houston-based David Weekley Homes has leaned more heavily into move-in-ready spec homes to respond to a buyer that is placing more value on speed and certainty. Fargo says the shift has been driven by changes in buyer preferences rather than operational considerations.

“In a more uncertain market, many buyers are less willing to commit far in advance. They want to know what they’re buying, what it will cost, and when they can move in,” Fargo explains. “With quick move-in homes, the goal is not simply to build more inventory. It’s to be thoughtful about which homes we start, where we build them, the price points we target, and when the homes will be available.”

Similarly, Kalmbach notes Trumark Homes is seeing more contingent buyers in the current market. For these buyers, knowing what homes are available within a given time frame can be an important factor when they are looking to move but still must sell their previous home. Spec homes represent a solution for this buyer.

For builders that have leaned more heavily into a BTO approach, most cite personalization, design, and customer centricity as core factors. By allowing buyers to choose lots, floor plans, and personalized finishes, says KB Home’s McGibney, the company is best able to serve its customers.

“Buyers are already invested in and feel a connection to the homes they created,” McGibney said. “This is in contrast to a speculative business model where incentives are used to create value. In that model, the builder increases the incentives to the point at which the buyers believe they have been adequately compensated for features and finishes they did not choose.”

Erlanger, Kentucky-based Fischer Homes has seen an increase in interest in BTO homes in 2026, with the builder noting many buyers are placing an emphasis on personalization. BTO homes utilize Fischer Homes’ Design Studio, giving buyers the opportunity to select finishes and details that bring a unique vision to life and allowing the builder to deliver a home that reflects the specific needs and preferences of a particular buyer.

“The visibility and predictability that BTO provides translates directly into more efficient operations and more dependable margins at delivery.”

Beyond design, KB Home’s McGibney said a BTO-forward approach provides visibility, predictability, and limits risk. When a buyer commits and the company locks in a price, the direct costs can be established before a shovel hits the ground and KB Home knows the margin it will achieve at delivery before a home is started.

“We view this as a fundamentally lower risk profile than a speculative model, where a builder starts a home with an assumption for the future sales price and then finds later, at the time of sale, that market conditions may require price reductions or heavy incentives,” McGibney said. “The visibility and predictability that BTO provides translates directly into more efficient operations and more dependable margins at delivery.”

PulteGroup’s shift toward increasing built-to-order homes reflects the preferences of move-up and active-adult buyers. The builder’s lower cycle time allows it to selectively use rate buydowns to facilitate BTO sales while still achieving higher margins than on spec sales.

“[Move-up and active-adult buyers] are individuals who expect choice, and our operating model allows them to choose their preferred lot and select the options and upgrades they desire,” Marshall said.

For luxury builder Toll Brothers, the company can provide a design-forward experience even to spec buyers given its timing and approach to sales. The builder is focused on selling specs as early as possible in the construction cycle to allow personalization through its design studios, providing an experience that is like the BTO experience in all but name.

Several builders say the spec-versus-BTO decision is often less about philosophy and more about the product being sold and the customer buying it.

Decisions are closely tied to what different buyer segments prioritize in the purchase process. For entry-level buyers, value is often concentrated in price, payment certainty, and speed, characteristics that favor a spec approach. Move-up buyers, by contrast, are often purchasing for the home itself and have greater flexibility to prioritize personalization and design choices over speed.

“A first-time buyer is usually solving for payment and timing. A move-up buyer is solving for the home itself,” Jones of Davidson Homes explains. “Spec answers the first. Built-to-order answers the second.”

Kalmbach of Trumark Homes adds that buyers who are seeking customization in the home buying process are more likely to have the resources and time to engage earlier in the purchasing process, beginning with lot selection and continuing through the full design process. Fargo of David Weekley Homes echoes this distinction: standardized, higher-density, and entry-level products generally lend themselves more naturally to move-in-ready construction while higher-priced, customizable homes are better positioned for BTO.

“In general, building from the ground up allows customers the opportunity to personalize their home and participate more fully in the home building process,” says Fargo. “The longer timeline also gives our team members more time to understand the customer, build a relationship with them, and help create a home that is right for them. That relationship and the experience we provide the home building process are things we value.”

Vincent Salandro is an editor for Builder. He earned a B.A. in journalism and a B.S. in economics from American University.

#5606. Maria Bartiromo Sells Upper East Side Townhouse for $7 Million After Fox News Exit

Former Fox News host Maria Bartiromo has offloaded her Upper East Side townhouse for $7 million, according to property records.

The transaction comes just over two months after the network parted ways with the anchor. On Sept. 3, Fox News Media announced, "We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 ½ years and wish her all the best on her next chapter."

The journalist was the host of three programs on the network, including "Mornings with Maria," "Maria Bartiromo's Wall Street," and "Sunday Morning Futures." In light of the change, Fox replaced Bartiromo with rotating anchors, including Larry Kudlow as a temporary step-in, and renamed the latter two shows to "Mornings with FOX Business" and "FBN's Wall Street."

Prior to the announcement, Baritromo had not appeared on any of Fox News Media's programs since Aug. 9. According to the Los Angeles Times, the move to part with the anchor—who had reportedly been earning about $6 million a year—was "a business decision."

Bartiromo, 59, shared a statement in a Sept. 10 Instagram post, writing, "Before too much time passes, I want to thank all of my friends, followers, and supporters for all of the kind words. I am so grateful for the outpouring of love this week on social media and through texts."

Along with her husband, financier Jonathan Steinberg, Baritromo purchased the five-level townhouse for $6.5 million in 2007.

At the time of the purchase, The Observer described the dwelling as a "five bedroom house" with a "second-floor balcony overlooking the 39-foot-long backyard garden." Nearly 20 years ago, the home had also been equipped with a security system and monitor.

Bartiromo has yet to announce her next permanent gig. Although the sale may indicate a change on the horizon, she is a lifelong New Yorker who has previously spoken about her love for the city.

In a 2019 interview with Resident magazine, she said, "I grew up in Brooklyn and I love New York because of its diversity. You can be in the city and be anonymous yet also visit the greatest landmarks on the planet."

She also opened up about her upbringing, where she worked at the family restaurant her grandfather built after immigrating to the United States from Italy in 1919.

"My first job was in the coat check there, and I watched my entire family work hard to build this business," she said. "This is really who I am. I love working hard, and that's all I know. I am very proud of my upbringing, my Italian heritage, and who my parents are today."

In the interview, Bartiromo also evealed that she and her husband spend their free time in a secondary home, also in New York.

"My husband and I have a home in the Hamptons, and I go there on weekends and bike along the ocean road," she said.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5605. Meritage, PulteGroup Honor Veterans With Mortgage-Free Homes

Two national home builders are honoring military veterans and their families this fall with the gift of mortgage-free homeownership.

Meritage Homes, through its partnership with Operation Homefront, welcomed U.S. Navy veteran Maggie Coleman and her family to a new home in Gulfport, Mississippi, on Veterans Day. Meanwhile, PulteGroup’s Built to Honor program and Building Homes for Heroes will present mortgage-free homes to U.S. Army veterans Carson Shaw and Ryan Heard and their families ahead of Thanksgiving.

The initiatives provide the families with greater housing stability while building on both companies’ long-standing efforts to support military families.

Meritage Homes and Operation Homefront presented Coleman and her two children with the keys to a new, mortgage-free home during a Veterans Day ceremony Nov. 11.

The approximately 2,000-square-foot, four-bedroom, three-bath home is located in Meritage’s Hidden Trails community in Gulfport, Mississippi. The donation marks the 23rd home Meritage has donated to a military family.

Coleman served 13 years in the Navy, including deployments to Italy and Kuwait. The home allows her family to put down permanent roots in her home state of Mississippi.

“I want to give my children everything I didn’t have,” Coleman said. “I want this home to be a place where my kids and I can share stories and make memories.”

“We’re proud to help welcome the Coleman family home to Gulfport,” Meritage Homes CEO Phillippe Lord said. “We recognize the service and sacrifices she and her family have made, and we’re honored to share in this special moment with them.”

The home was provided through Operation Homefront’s Permanent Homes for Veterans program, which works to help military families achieve long-term stability through mortgage-free housing and other support.

PulteGroup will continue the season of giving Nov. 18, when its Built to Honor program and Building Homes for Heroes present the keys to two mortgage-free homes at the builder’s Spencer Glen community in Riverview, Florida.

The homes will go to U.S. Army Sergeant Carson Shaw and his partner, Annalisa, and Purple Heart recipient U.S. Army Specialist Ryan Heard, his partner, Danielle, and their two children.

Shaw joined the Army in 2019 at age 18 and completed deployments to Iraq and Syria and to Africa. A line-of-duty motor vehicle accident in 2024 left him paralyzed from the waist down. He also lives with the effects of a traumatic brain injury and bilateral hearing loss.

Since his injury, Shaw has participated in six adaptive sports at the Warrior Games and plays wheelchair basketball with the Tampa Strong Dogs. His new accessible home will provide a stable foundation as he pursues a bachelor’s degree in finance and economics.

Heard enlisted in the Army in 2007 and completed two deployments to Iraq and one to Afghanistan. During his 2013 deployment to Afghanistan, an improvised explosive device detonated beneath Heard and three fellow soldiers. Despite sustaining a severe traumatic brain injury, Heard helped treat wounded soldiers and coordinate a medical evacuation before losing consciousness, according to the release.

Heard, who received a Purple Heart, also lives with PTSD, chronic migraines, hearing loss, and chronic pain. His new home will provide him and his family with a mortgage-free place to put down roots.

The two homes continue a significant milestone for PulteGroup’s Built to Honor program. Since its launch in 2013, PulteGroup has built and donated more than 100 mortgage-free homes valued at over $40 million to veterans and their families.

Building Homes for Heroes is also celebrating its 20th anniversary and expects to reach its milestone 500th home in December.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5604. Angelina Jolie Snaps Up Connecticut Home—Months After Selling Her $24 Million Los Angeles Estate

Angelina Jolie has picked up a Connecticut mansion—nearly three months after she sold off her Los Angeles home for $24.75 home, according to reports.

In September, Jolie, 51, made headlines when she offloaded her California home, which she purchased in 2017 for $24.5 million.

Now, according to a report from Page Six Hollywood, Jolie has set her sights on a new home across the country in the East Coast.

Insiders told the outlet that Jolie picked up a property in the area, however, it is unclear as to where exactly.

Jolie purchased her Los Angeles home less than a year after she filed for divorce from fellow on-screen star Brad Pitt, and it has served as her primary residence ever since.

However, in August 2025, rumors began to swirl that she was preparing the property for sale, after she admitted to the Hollywood Reporter that she was hoping to leave Los Angeles as soon as the youngest of her six children turned 18.

She then put the property on the market for $29.9 million in May, just two months before her youngest children, twins Knox and Vivienne, celebrated their 18 birthdays.

Then, in September, Jolie officially found a buyer for the six-bedroom, 10-bathroom dwelling, where she has lived with her kids since she and Pitt split.

It came after she told the Hollywood Reporter that, per the terms of her divorce settlement with Pitt, which was finalized in December 2024, she was required to remain in California until all of their children reached the milestone age—but said that she hoped to spend "a lot of time in Cambodia" when she was free to relocate.

"I grew up in this town. I am here because I have to be here from a divorce, but as soon as they’re 18, I’ll be able to leave," she said at the time.

The property—which sits on nearly 2 lush acres—was listed with Jon Grauman of Resident Group and Ernie Carswell of Sotheby's International Realty.

Jolie's name is not mentioned in the listing, which went live on May 4. However, the property's illustrious history is featured prominently in the description, which described the home as an "iconic compound."

"The legendary Cecil B. DeMille estate is now discretely being offered, marking a once-in-a-generation opportunity to own a piece of Hollywood history—an iconic compound from which Hollywood's future was shaped, and where Mr. DeMille helped define the industry as the entertainment capital of the world," the description read.

"Originally conceived in 1913 by architect B. Cooper Corbett, the high-walled estate stands as a cornerstone of Hollywood's architectural and cultural legacy. Acquired by Cecil B. DeMille in 1916, it quickly evolved into a sanctuary of cinematic innovation and social grandeur."

The listing noted that the existing property was expanded by DeMille in 1920, when he acquired a neighboring abode that was once home to Charlie Chaplin. He then set about connecting the two dwellings "by way of a graceful glass corridor."

"This union of artistry and vision transformed the property into a singular masterpiece, embodying the glamour and creative force of Hollywood's Golden Age," the description added.

Among the upscale amenities that were mentioned in the description are a fitness studio, a teahouse, a pool house, as well as a guesthouse studio with its own living room, fireplace, and private gated entry. There is also a "separate garage with security station."

"Perched at the highest point within the prestigious Laughlin Park enclave, the grounds command sweeping views of the Hollywood Hills and Griffith Observatory—adding further romance to this timeless legacy estate," the description added.

DeMille purchased the original property for just $27,893 in 1916—and he lived at the estate until his death in 1959. The extraordinary compound has changed hands on only a few occasions, with records showing that it was sold for just $1.5 million in 1990 and remained with that buyer for nearly 30 years before Jolie purchased it.

When the actress bought the property, it had just undergone an extensive six-year renovation, which included the grounds and the swimming pool.

"A newer classic old Hollywood style pool with arched fountains, surrounded by rolling lawns, specimen trees, rose gardens and dramatic views from the Observatory to Ocean sunsets," the original listing description said.

Last year, Jolie opened the property to loved ones who had been affected by the 2025 California wildfires, with an unnamed source revealing at the time that she had been left "heartbroken for those who lost their homes" and was "doing everything she [could] to help."

The actress later confirmed those reports. In a video obtained by the Daily Mail, she revealed, "Yeah, we're having people at our house. Right now I'm taking care of people close to me and having them at my house."

In a March 2025 interview with the New York Times, the "Salt" star explained that one of her sons had taken up residence at the dwelling, but noted that it was routinely used by all of her children whenever they were in the city.

"The other day I said I was going to pop by, and he was like, 'Can you just give me a day to clean?'" she joked. "I thought, 'I appreciate that, you should clean up for your mother. But also, how bad is it?'"

The actress also owns several properties in Cambodia, purchasing her first dwelling in the country soon after she adopted her son Maddox, who was born in the country. She later noted that she hoped having a home in his home nation would help him to stay connected to his culture.

In 2019, she revealed a very rare glimpse inside the dwelling, when she shot a Guerlain commercial at the home.

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.

#5603. House Plan of the Week: A Starter Home With More to Offer

This isn’t your typical 1950s ranch-style starter home.

To begin with, it’s got two bathrooms, eliminating the need to wait in the hallway.

The guest bedroom rivals the main suite in space, allowing visitors, in-laws, or an older child to live comfortably.

“We designed this country farmhouse for an evolving housing market, where homeowners are looking for smaller, more affordable homes with lasting charm,” says floor plan designer Michael E. Nelson.

Another departure from starter homes of the past: plenty of kitchen space, with seating for six at the island and space for a table to boot.
